stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 20: do you share stories on social media and what kind, what stories do you tell friends and family, and does the telling change between the two. Pairs, three minutes, one answer in open class. The third question is the interesting one and it sets up the text.
stages.aim: To get students talking about the stories they share

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 2A: they read Andy’s story — the two small children, the granddad, the garage, the blue paint on the wall — and choose which of the three final sentences fits best. Alone, then pairs comparing reasons, then open class. Take the reason, not just the letter: the reason is the reading.
stages.avoid: The ending is arguable and they will argue it. That is fine and it is the point, so do not close it down quickly — but do not let it run past five minutes either, because the adjectives are the lesson.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the story

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2B: eight meanings to complete with the adjectives in bold in the story — frightened, amazing, bored, disappointed, annoyed, excited, embarrassing, surprised. Alone with the text open, then pairs. Take the answers and hold the explanation; the teaching is the next stage.
stages.aim: To focus students on the -ed and -ing adjectives in the story

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 2C, the two pictures, is the clarification and it is better than any explanation you can give: which ending describes how a person feels, and which describes what causes the feeling. Let them tell you, then board the pairs — bored and boring, excited and exciting, embarrassed and embarrassing. Concept-check with a question they cannot guess from the grammar: if the film is boring, how do you feel. Then pronunciation, because the -ed ending is not consistent: frightened and bored take a /d/, surprised takes a /d/ after the /z/, disappointed and excited add a syllable. Twelve minutes, not eight, is what lets you drill those four properly and concept-check more than one pair.
stages.avoid: This is the one error that survives to C1 if it is not nailed here. Spend the concept questions on it rather than on the meanings of the individual adjectives, which the story already gave them.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of -ed and -ing adjectives

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3A: eight questions with the adjective ending missing — the most amazing book, a time you were really surprised, the most embarrassing thing, things you find annoying. Pairs, written in, then check in open class. Every item is the -ed or -ing decision you just taught.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the adjectives

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3B: they ask and answer the eight questions from ex 3A in pairs. Insist on a follow-up question after each answer or they will work down the list like a form. Swap partners at four minutes so the better stories get told twice. Monitor and collect.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice using the adjectives

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first and properly, because you have the time here: two or three of the better answers from ex 3B retold to the room. Then four or five things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed, with at least one -ed or -ing pair among them, for the class to sort before you confirm. If you want to give them more feeling adjectives, Vocabulary Bank p. 137 is the book’s own set and it is homework, not lesson time.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using narrative tenses — past simple, past continuous and past perfect — accurately to tell a story.
slots.sub: To develop students’ listening for gist and detail in the context of a travel story.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 21 ex4–7 – audio tracks 2.01, 2.02, 2.03 / Grammar Bank p. 108 ex1

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The six pictures A to F on p.21 on screen, out of order, and in pairs they predict the story — two friends traveling in India, a lake, a train. Ex 4A. Take one version in open class and write its last event on the board so they have something to be wrong about.
stages.aim: To have students predict the story from the pictures

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo:
Play track 2.01, ex 4B: they check their prediction. Then ex 4C with the same track: number the six pictures in the order the events happened. Pairs compare between the plays, then check in open class. Two plays, two tasks, and the second is the one that needs the detail.
Ex 4D: the six detail questions, in pairs, answered with as much detail as they can — how they felt by the lake, what they expected the journey to Varanasi to be like, how they felt on the train, why Beth was worried, what happened to Jane, who helped her. This is still listening work, and it is also where the story becomes vivid enough to be worth analyzing.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist and order

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 6A: two sentences from the story — "They were sleeping on the floor" and "Suddenly, the train stopped in the middle of nowhere" — and the three questions about them: what the tenses are, which sets the scene, which carries the main event. Then ex 6B with "Jane woke up on the railway track. She had fallen off the train.": which happened first, and which tense shows it. Alone, then pairs.
stages.aim: To focus students on the narrative tenses in the story

stages.name: Clarifying TL, with pronunciation
stages.todo:
Three tenses and one timeline. Draw it: the past continuous as the line that was already running, the past simple as the points on it, the past perfect as the point behind the one you are standing on. Build it from their own answers to ex 6A and 6B rather than from the Grammar Bank. Concept-check the pair that matters — she woke up and she had fallen: which do we see first in the story, and which happened first in life. Then the form, briefly: was and were plus -ing, and had plus the participle.
Ex 7A with track 2.02: the three sentences from the story, and what happens to was, were and had when they are not stressed. Let them hear the weak forms before you name them. Then ex 7B with 2.03: they write the three sentences they hear and practice saying them. Drill at speed — the weak form only exists at speed.
stages.avoid: Nine minutes for three tenses means you cannot present each one from scratch. They have met the past simple and the past continuous; the new one is the past perfect, and that is where the time goes.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the narrative tenses

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.108 ex 1. Pairs, and make them read the completed sentence aloud rather than just writing the form, so the weak forms you have just drilled get used. Check in open class, and take only the items where the past perfect was the question.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the narrative tenses

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5 on p.21, which is three questions about a long journey of their own — would you like to make one, when was the last one, was it easy or difficult. Four minutes, in pairs, and ex 7C’s three questions are there too if a pair runs dry. You are listening for narrative tenses in free speech, which is the only place you find out whether the lesson worked.
stages.avoid: Four minutes is short and it is the only free practice in the lesson, so protect it. If the clarification overruns, take the time out of the controlled practice instead — the Grammar Bank can be finished at home.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about a journey

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One or two things on the board from your monitoring, and make one of them a past perfect used correctly in free speech, because that is worth naming. Two minutes.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have improved their fluency telling a personal anecdote, using narrative tenses and time-linking phrases.
slots.sub: To practice using the phrases that order a story — the next thing I knew, and then, in the end, finally — so a listener can follow the sequence of events.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 22 ex8A–8C + the Future Skills box (Communication)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: You tell a short anecdote of your own — ninety seconds, something that went wrong — using two or three of the sequencing phrases deliberately. Then ask them which words told them the order. They will name the phrases, which is a better start than you naming them.
stages.aim: To give students a model anecdote

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 8A on p. 22: they pick one of the five situations — an amazing place, a fun event, meeting someone interesting, something unusual, something that went wrong — or their own, and plan it against the book’s six questions: when, where, who with, what happened, how they felt, how it ended. Notes only, in silence. Go round and feed vocabulary to the ones whose story is hard to tell in English.
stages.avoid: Insist on notes. If they write the anecdote out they will read it aloud in the speaking stage, and a read-aloud has none of the fluency the aim asks for.
stages.aim: To give students time to choose and plan a story

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The Future Skills box on p. 22 gives the phrases that order a story — the next thing I knew, and then, in the end, finally. Board them, add one or two of your own, and drill them as whole units at speed, because that is how they come out in speech. Then a minute on where they sit: at the front of the sentence, with a pause after. Seven minutes buys you the drilling, which five did not.
stages.aim: To give students the phrases that order a story

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 8C in groups of three or four: they tell their anecdotes with as much detail as they can, and the listeners ask questions about each one. Three minutes a speaker for the first round and you keep the clock. Then regroup, so everyone faces an audience that has not heard it, and run it again — the second telling is faster, better, and the one to monitor properly. With the writing lead-in gone there is room for both rounds without hurrying either.
stages.avoid: Eighteen minutes is long enough to sag in the middle. The regroup is what stops that, so call it out loud on the clock rather than waiting for a group to finish.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice telling an anecdote

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first, and properly: two of the best anecdotes retold to the whole room by the person who heard them, not the person who lived them — which is also the only honest check that anybody was listening. Then four or five things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed, with narrative tenses and sequencing phrases among them, for the class to sort before you confirm anything.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

2B.context: Facts and figures – what are you curious about?

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using verbs and nouns related to knowledge — guess, memorize, revise, solution, understanding — to talk about what they know.
slots.sub: To practice reading for detail in the context of two people describing their knowledge and memory.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 32 ex1–2 / Vocabulary Bank p. 138 ex1–2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 32 in groups: do you enjoy quiz shows and are they popular here, what do you know a lot about, and what do you know almost nothing about. The last two are the ones to keep them on — they put the topic in the room and they are honest fun.
stages.aim: To get students talking about quizzes and what they know

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 2A: they read what Marta and Jack say about what they know and decide which of the two they are more like, and why. Alone, then pairs with the reason, then two or three answers in open class. One question across two short texts; keep it to six minutes.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the two texts

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2B: the ten words and phrases in bold matched to their meanings — mind, note down, revise, memory, option, solve, guess, general knowledge, score, data. Pairs, with the texts open, because the context is what decides it. Take the answers and hold the explanation; the teaching is the next stage.
stages.aim: To focus students on the words in the texts

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ten items, and the time goes on the three things the matching cannot give them. Word class, and the words each one lives with: a good memory, note something down, revise for an exam, solve a problem, get a score. Stress: MEMory, GENeral KNOWledge, underSTANDing. And the one that catches everyone — data is normally uncountable in everyday use, so data is rather than data are. Model and drill the three with awkward stress.
stages.avoid: Ten items in ten minutes is the whole stage, so choose four to teach properly and let the other six be recognized. Note down, revise, solve and guess are the four the practice and the next lesson actually use.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the words

stages.name: Controlled, then semi-controlled practice
stages.todo:
Vocabulary Bank p. 138 ex 1, the verb and noun table — the pairs where the two forms differ is the point of the exercise. Pairs, aloud, and check in open class.
Vocabulary Bank p. 138 ex 2, where the words go back into sentences. Pairs, reading the whole sentence out rather than saying the missing word. Check in open class and take only the disputed items.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the words

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2C: each of them picks six of the words from ex 2A and writes a true sentence about themselves with each — the book’s model is "I always note down new English words". Three minutes writing in silence, then they compare with a partner and find two things they have in common. Monitor the writing as well as the talking; the errors are more visible on paper.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice using the words about themselves

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first: two or three sentences read out that surprised a partner. Then three or four things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed, including at least one of the collocations — a good memory, revise for — for the class to sort before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced forming subject and object questions accurately.
slots.sub: To develop students’ listening for detail in the context of a general knowledge quiz.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 32 ex3 – audio track 3.01 / SB p. 33 ex4 / Grammar Bank p. 112 ex1–2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.32: pairs read the seven-question Quick quiz and choose their answers — can fish live out of water, why do we have eyebrows, who wrote the Sherlock Holmes stories, where was paper first invented. Do not confirm a single answer. The recording does that, and their wanting to know is the reason to listen.
stages.aim: To get students doing the quiz

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Track 3.01, ex 3B: two friends discussing the quiz, and they listen for the answers to check their own. Then ex 3C with the same track, six true-or-false statements about what each speaker says and the man’s final score. Pairs compare between the plays, check in open class, and let them keep score.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for specific information

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.33: four questions taken from the quiz and the recording — what do you know a lot about, who wrote the Sherlock Holmes books, why do we have eyebrows, what did Tim Berners-Lee invent — and the three questions about them: which ends in a preposition, which three use an auxiliary and which auxiliary is past, and which uses no auxiliary at all. Alone, then pairs.
stages.aim: To focus students on the questions from the quiz

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 4B is the clarification: the two questions about Tim Berners-Lee, side by side. Who invented the World Wide Web, and what did Tim Berners-Lee invent. Get them to see that the first asks about the subject and needs no auxiliary, and the second asks about the object and does. Board the two word orders in columns — question word, verb, object against question word, auxiliary, subject, verb — and leave them up. Concept-check with a pair they have to build: who ate the sandwich against what did you eat. Then the preposition rule from ex 4A: it stays with its verb and goes to the end. Model and drill the two patterns.
stages.avoid: The error is adding the auxiliary to a subject question — "Who did invent the World Wide Web?" Teach the subject question second, after the object question is secure, and concept-check it rather than explaining it; they can repeat the rule and still not hear the mistake.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of subject and object questions

stages.name: Controlled, then semi-controlled practice
stages.todo:
Grammar Bank p.112 ex 1. Pairs, with the two columns on your board in view, and they say the whole question aloud. Check in open class and take only the subject-question items.
Grammar Bank p.112 ex 2. Pairs, aloud again. If they are quick, go back to the quiz on p.32 and have them say which of the seven questions are subject questions.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of subject and object questions

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: They write their own three-question quiz for another pair, and at least one of the three has to be a subject question — who invented, who wrote, what happened. Three minutes writing, then they swap and answer, then they check. It is the quiz the lesson opened with, now built by them, and it is the only stage where they produce the form without a prompt.
stages.avoid: Ex 6 on p. 33 sends Student A to p. 148 and Student B to p. 146. Those pages are not on your card — the publisher’s own file skips from p. 145 to p. 150 — so plan on them writing their own. Ex 3D on p. 32 is tempting as an extra, but its phrases — by the way, moving on, that reminds me — are conversational signposts, not question forms, and they belong to a different lesson.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice writing their own quiz

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The best question from each pair on the board, and the class answers them. Then one or two corrections, and make one of them a subject question written correctly, because that is the thing they just learned.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have improved their fluency asking and answering questions in the context of a personal quiz.
slots.sub: To develop students’ pronunciation of the stressed words in questions.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 33 ex5–7 – audio tracks 3.03, 3.04

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 3.03: four questions, and the one thing to notice is which words carry the stress — the question word, the main verb, the nouns and the adjectives, and not do, you or a. Play it twice, let them tell you, and mark one question on the board with the stressed words underlined.
stages.aim: To focus students on stress in questions

stages.name: Pronunciation practice
stages.todo: Ex 5B: four more questions — when did people first land on the Moon, who played the Black Panther, where is the Pink Palace, what object related to weather did Benjamin Franklin invent. In pairs they underline the stressed words, then ask and answer them. Then ex 5C with track 3.04 to check both the stress and the answers. Drill the four questions chorally at speed, because stress only shows at speed.
stages.avoid: They will slow down to get the stress right, which removes the stress. Drill fast and accept a rough first attempt rather than a careful slow one.
stages.aim: To give students practice stressing the right words

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 7A on p.33: each of them writes four things on a slip of paper — the name of one person, one object, one date and one place that matter to them — and nothing else. No explanations. The blankness is what makes the questioning necessary in the next stage.
stages.aim: To give students time to prepare their four items

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The Future Skills box on p.33 and its one question: if someone says "I met my partner in 2018", what can you ask next. Collect four or five follow-up questions from the room, board them, and drill two for the stress you taught in the first ten minutes — how old is he, what did you do there. Four minutes.
stages.aim: To give students follow-up questions for the task

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 7C: they swap slips and prepare questions about their partner’s four items, to find out why each one matters. Then ex 7D: two minutes each way, asking, listening and following up, and the book sets a target — find out as much as you can. Run it twice with different partners if the pairs finish early; sixteen minutes is enough for two rounds and the second is better. Monitor with a pen for question forms and for stress.
stages.avoid: Two minutes is the book’s limit and it matters: a time limit is what turns this from an interview into a hunt. Call time out loud and mean it.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice finding out about a partner

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex 7E first: each of them tells the class one interesting thing about their partner, which is the content feedback and takes most of the stage. Then four or five things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed — a subject question from last lesson, a stress pattern, a follow-up question that worked — for the class to sort before you confirm anything.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

s6.from: set six, built 10 Oct 2026 for C/18

1A.context: Communicating – how we keep in touch

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have read a magazine article about digital communication for gist and for detail, and given their own opinions on the questions it raises.
slots.sub: To clarify six adverbs from the article that make another word stronger or less strong – absolutely, really, especially, particularly, pretty and fairly – so that students can use them to give their opinions.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 10 ex 1a–1c, 1f (article: ‘The fast and the furious’) / SB p. 11 ex 2a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Ask how people keep in touch and build a list on the board as they call it out – texts, phone calls, emails, instant messages, Facebook, letters, cards. Then books open at p. 10, ex 1a: in pairs they go through the seven bullet points and say which they do, and what they do instead. Read the two speech bubbles out first, because they show the exchange you want: a fact about me, then my partner’s different answer. Take one or two surprises from the room.
stages.aim: To get students interested in how people keep in touch

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four words block the article and nothing around them explains them: cancel, blog, comment and realise. Give a situation for each and let them supply the word – we planned dinner for tonight, then I sent a message: sorry, I can’t come. What did I do? One concept question each (if you cancel, does the plan happen?) and move on.
stages.avoid: Leave text message and instant message alone. They are two of the four missing words in ex 1b, and teaching them gives away the prediction before anyone has read a line.
stages.aim: To clear the four words that would block the article

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b: they read only the introduction and the four green lines under the photos, and in pairs guess the missing word in each – any sensible guess counts. Board a few. Then the first half of ex 1c: they read the four texts quickly, alone, to check the gaps and nothing else. Give a short time limit and say why. Pairs compare, then confirm in open class: text message, forget, emails, instant message.
stages.aim: To give students a quick first read for the main idea

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: The second half of ex 1c, four questions: why Julie thinks her friend will cancel, what Facebook helps Gin remember, why Marc writes a blog, why Claudio prefers instant messages. They read again, alone, and write short answers, then show a partner the line that gave each one. In open class, ask for the line as well as the answer. For fast finishers, one question of your own that sends them back in: who says Facebook is useful, and who says most of their friends use it but prefers something else?
stages.avoid: Question 4 has a second half the book does not ask about: some of Claudio’s friends do not even send a message, they just stop answering. It is the line the discussion grows from, so make sure someone finds it.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for specific information

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 11: the six highlighted adverbs – really, especially, absolutely, pretty, particularly, fairly. Pairs find each one in its sentence and decide whether it makes the next word stronger or less strong. Check: absolutely, really, especially and particularly are stronger; pretty and fairly are less strong. Then the two things the exercise does not tell them. Pretty here is not beautiful – does pretty sure mean 100% sure? And absolutely goes with strong words: absolutely hate, absolutely love. Drill the long ones inside a short sentence, because the stress is what goes wrong: I absoLUTEly hate it, esPEcially at night, parTICularly in winter.
stages.avoid: This is the sub aim, not a second lesson. Six words in seven minutes; the rest of section 2 on p. 11 is not part of today.
stages.aim: To focus on six adverbs from the text that make a word stronger or weaker

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 1f: four opinions – it’s rude to cancel by text, it’s all right to end a relationship by text, Facebook is the perfect place to say congratulations, I love getting postcards and letters. Check congratulations first: when do you say it? Then groups of three, and each person says how strongly they agree, with a reason. Put two of the adverbs on the board as a nudge – I absolutely hate…, I’m pretty sure… – and say you are listening for them. Walk round with a pen.
stages.avoid: The second statement is the one that wakes a quiet group up. If a group runs dry, send them to it.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to react to the text and give their opinions

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ask each group which statement they argued about most, and take one reason from each side. Then two or three sentences you heard on the board – one adverb used well, one in the wrong place or with the wrong word – and let pairs fix them before you do.
stages.aim: To round off the discussion and correct a few useful errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have revised and practiced the present simple for habits and permanent situations and the present continuous for actions happening now or around now, using the people in the article.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, asking and answering questions about how often they communicate in different ways.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 10 (the article from the previous lesson) / SB p. 11 ex 3a–3c, 4 / Grammar Focus 1B SB p. 142 – audio track 1.14 / SB p. 143 ex a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The article on p. 10 is your way in, and the class read it in the last lesson. Put the four photos up and ask who is who: who is waiting for a text, who is studying in New York, who uses Facebook for birthdays, who ends relationships by instant message. Two minutes – you want them remembering the people, not reading again.
stages.avoid: Do not set the article again. It was the whole of the previous lesson; your minutes belong to the grammar.
stages.aim: To bring back the article as the context for the grammar

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 11: four sentences, and they write present simple or present continuous on each line. Then send them back to the article on p. 10 for two more of each – I’m waiting for her text message, I’m studying in New York, I’m writing a blog, when I check my Facebook page, it tells me, I normally communicate. Board what they find in two columns without naming the columns yet.
stages.aim: To focus students on examples of the two tenses in the text

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first, with ex 3b: pairs match the four sentences to the four uses – habits and routines, feelings and permanent situations, actions right now, temporary actions around now. Then check it with questions, not with the rule. Is Julie waiting now? Yes. Does she always wait for texts from Sara? We don’t know. Is Marc in New York for ever? No – so is his studying permanent or for now? Write questions like these for every sentence on your board before the lesson. Form is a review: be + -ing, and the -s on he, she, it, with Grammar Focus 1B on p. 142 as the reference. Point at the spelling box for writing, studying, putting. Then the tip box – like, prefer, hate, know, need are not normally continuous – which the article shows for you: I prefer writing a blog, never I’m preferring. Pronunciation last, the contractions: play 1.14 for them to repeat the table, then drill two sentences from the article at natural speed – I’m waiting for her text, she’s writing a blog – so the ’m and ’s can be heard.
stages.avoid: They are B1 and have met both tenses. Present the form from scratch and you will spend fourteen minutes on what they know and none on the choice between the two, which is what they get wrong.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning and form of the present simple and continuous

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus 1B on p. 143. Ex a first: four pairs of sentence beginnings, each matched to the ending that fits – I work in a bank… but I don’t enjoy it; I’m working in a café… but it’s only a summer job. It makes them choose by meaning. Then ex b, eight sentences with two choices each. They work alone, compare with a partner, and you go through only the items they disagreed on. Expect 5 and 8 to divide the room: friends who look at their phones every five minutes, and does your brother like.
stages.avoid: Ex c is a fourteen-gap conversation and will not fit. Leave it on the page.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the two tenses

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4 on p. 11: How often do you…? with the nine activities – send a message to say you are sick, share news on Facebook, read English websites, call friends on Skype. Pairs ask and answer, and every answer needs a reason. Put the book’s second speech bubble on the board – Not very often. But I’m planning a holiday in America… – because it shows the move you want: a habit, then something going on in their life now. Change partners halfway so everyone asks the questions twice. Write down sentences as you go round, right ones and wrong ones.
stages.avoid: The questions all start How often, so on their own they produce the present simple and nothing else. Without that second sentence about now, you will hear only half of what you taught.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to use the tenses to talk about their own habits

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A quick survey: hands up for who does each activity most often and least often. Then a state verb you heard in the continuous – I’m knowing, she’s preferring – on the board next to a sentence someone got right. Pairs say which is which and fix the wrong one; you confirm.
stages.aim: To share what students found and correct a few errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have listened for gist and for specific detail to a conversation between two old friends who meet by chance in the street.
slots.sub: To introduce six phrases for greeting someone you know and someone you are meeting for the first time – Long time no see, How are you?, Great to see you, Where are you living these days?, by the way and Nice to meet you – and the usual replies to them.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 12 ex 1a–1d – audio track 1.15 (Part 1) / SB p. 12 ex 2a–2d – audio tracks 1.16, 1.17

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 12: in your country, what do you say and do when you meet someone new, and when you meet someone you know well? Mime hug, kiss and shake hands as you set it, so the words are in the room. Pairs, then two or three answers to the class. In a mixed-nationality class the answers differ and this runs longer – let it, up to five minutes.
stages.aim: To get students talking about greetings and set the context

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the two photos. Do the people in each one know each other well, and how can you tell? Pairs, then board the class’s guesses. Do not say who is right.
stages.aim: To get students predicting what they will hear

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1c: play 1.15, Part 1 of the video or the audio if you have no screen, once. One question: were your guesses right? The two women are old friends; the man is meeting one of them for the first time. Pairs check, then ask what told them – the way they say each other’s names, or nice to meet you.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1d, five true-or-false sentences: when Rachel and Annie last met, where Annie lives, when Rachel and Mark got married, whether Annie has a boyfriend, where the three of them go next. Give them a minute to read first, then play 1.15 again. They answer alone, compare, and correct the false ones – that half of the task is what makes them listen closely. Play it a third time with pauses if pairs still disagree. Answers: 1 true, 2 false (really close to the centre), 3 false, 4 true, 5 false (a café).
stages.avoid: Sentence 3 has a joke in it: Rachel says they married six months ago and Mark says eight. Neither is a year, so it is false either way – but expect the question.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for specific information

stages.name: Language from the recording
stages.todo: Ex 2a: six phrases from the conversation, each with a piece missing. Pairs fill them from the box, then play 1.16 to check. Ex 2b sorts them – the first four for someone you know, by the way and nice to meet you for someone new. Then ex 2c: play 1.17 and they note the reply to each phrase. Collect one or two more replies to How are you? from the class – Fine, thanks, Not bad. Drill the six as phrase and reply, with the voice lifting on the pleased surprise: Long time no SEE! – Great to SEE you!
stages.avoid: Teach these as whole chunks. Long time no see has no grammar worth explaining, and trying to explain it costs you the speaking.
stages.aim: To focus on useful phrases for meeting people from the recording

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Each of them thinks of a friend they have not seen for a long time – who, where they used to meet, what they would ask now. Then groups of three, the same people as in the recording. Two meet in the street as old friends – greeting, how are you, where are you living these days – and the third, standing with one of them, introduces themselves as Mark does: my name’s…, by the way. Nice to meet you, and the conversation carries on with three. About ninety seconds a scene, then rotate so each person is the newcomer once. Books shut for the second round.
stages.avoid: With the page open they read the phrases; shut, they have to remember them, which is the point. Say so before they start.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to use the phrases in a conversation of their own

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One group shows its meeting to the room. Then two things from your notes: a phrase used well, and one used in the wrong place – nice to meet you said to an old friend is the likely one.
stages.aim: To round off the speaking task and correct a few errors

1B.context: Travel and tourism – saying yes to a holiday

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have read the first part of a holiday story for gist and for detail, and predicted what happens next.
slots.sub: To pre-teach the words that would block the story – travel agent, travel agent’s, receptionist and water skiing – so that students can follow Richard’s first two days.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 18 ex 1a–1d (article: ‘Yes Man changed my life’) / SB p. 19 (Day One and Day Two)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Build a list of kinds of holiday on the board as they call them out – beach, city break, camping, cruise, safari, adventure – and take a quick vote on the one the class would choose. Then books open at p. 18, ex 1a, in small groups: where do you like to go, what new things do you try on holiday, what kind of holiday would you hate? Keep the third question until last. The story is about a man who ends up on exactly that holiday.
stages.aim: To get students interested in holidays and the topic of the text

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items: travel agent and travel agent’s, receptionist, water skiing. The pair is the useful part – which is a person and which is a shop? Where do you book a holiday? (In the shop, from the person.) Receptionist from a hotel desk you draw on the board; water skiing from the photo at the foot of p. 18. One concept question each and move on.
stages.avoid: Leave accommodation, check in and unpack for later. They are in the story, but they are also in the vocabulary lesson at the end of this day, and the text makes them clear enough – a hotel? or a…? If anyone asks, a gesture will do.
stages.aim: To clear the four items that would block the text

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b: they read only the introduction, the white text over the photo, and answer the two questions – what is Danny Wallace’s book about, and what did Richard do after he read it? Two minutes, alone, then pairs. Check: a man who said yes to every question for a year; Richard took a week off work and did the same. Then one question to the room before they read on: what could go wrong if you say yes to everything?
stages.aim: To give students a quick first read for the main idea

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c: Day One and Day Two on p. 19, four questions each. Set Day One, check it, then set Day Two – two short reads hold a class better than one long one. Alone, then pairs, with a finger on the line that gives the answer. Day One: he saw a poster in the travel agent’s window, he booked a beach holiday in Greece, no – he prefers cities, the flight was the next day. Day Two: the receptionist asked if he wanted to go, it was about 40°C, he bought two pairs of sunglasses, three hats, a watch and a necklace, and tomorrow is water skiing, which he dreads.
stages.avoid: Day One question 3 hides its answer in a list of things he hates. Weaker readers will say yes because he booked it. Ask them to find what he says about the beach.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for specific information

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 1d: would you like to try water skiing, and will Richard enjoy it? Two minutes in groups. Then take it one step further: each group writes Richard’s Day Three in four or five lines, in his voice – what happened on the water, how he felt by the evening. Groups read theirs out and the class votes on the most likely. End with one question to everybody: would you say yes to everything for a week?
stages.avoid: The Day Threes will be full of past simple slips. That is the next lesson’s target, not yours – note a few for your colleague if you like, but do not teach them here.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to respond to the text in their own words

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first: which Day Three won, and why. Ex 1e on p. 18 has the real Day Three as a recording, but it is not part of this lesson – tell them in one line that he ended up loving it, or leave them guessing. Then a sentence where a pre-taught word was used well, and two that went wrong, for pairs to fix.
stages.aim: To share the groups’ ideas and correct a few errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have clarified and practiced the positive form of the past simple, regular and irregular, including when the -ed ending adds a syllable, to tell the story of a day on holiday.
slots.sub: To give students practice in writing a short story in pairs, about a day on a holiday they invent.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 18 ex 2a–2c (the article from the previous lesson) / SB p. 19 ex 5a–5c – audio tracks 1.27, 1.28 / Grammar Focus 2A SB p. 144 / SB p. 145 ex a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Two sentences on the board with the verb gapped: Richard ___ to change his life. He ___ a Yes Man for a week. They call out what fits, and you board every possible answer. Books open to check against the introduction on p. 18 – wanted, became. Then ask: did this happen now, or before he wrote the article? That one question carries the meaning for the whole lesson.
stages.avoid: The class read this article in the last lesson. One line to remind them who Richard is, then straight on.
stages.aim: To set the context and show the past simple in use

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a: fifteen verbs in a box, and pairs underline the past form of each in the article. They appear in the same order, starting from the introduction, so make it a race. Then ex 2b: which end in -ed, and what happens to the others? Board the answers in two columns, regular and irregular, and leave them up.
stages.aim: To focus students on past forms in the text

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is quick – finished, in the past – and the lead-in has done most of it. Form takes the time. Regular verbs add -ed, and then the three spelling changes from the box on p. 144 that they will need for ever: live, lived; stop, stopped; study, studied. Elicit them from verbs on the board rather than reading the box. Irregular verbs have no rule, so say so: they are learned, not worked out. Then pronunciation, with section 5 on p. 19. Ask where they stayed and what they visited on their last holiday, board stayed and visited, and ask which has an extra syllable. Play 1.27 for ex 5a and they tick the verbs that do – needed, decided, started, wanted. Ex 5b gives the rule: only after t and d. Ex 5c with 1.28: waited, included, shouted, ended. Then drill – as much on the verbs without the extra syllable as on the ones with it.
stages.avoid: The error you will hear all week is ask-ed and play-ed, said as two syllables. That is why asked, changed and played need drilling as much as wanted does.
stages.aim: To clarify the form and spelling of the past simple

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2c on p. 18: six sentences from Richard’s last day with the verb in brackets – worked, spent, stayed, won, took, went. Alone, then read to a partner aloud, so the endings are said and not only written. Then Grammar Focus 2A ex a on p. 145: fifteen verbs to put into the past, spelling included. Check on the board the three where the spelling rules bite: hurried, preferred, danced.
stages.avoid: Ex b and c on p. 145, and section 4 on p. 19, are negatives and questions. Not today – the positive form is the whole lesson.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of past forms, said and written

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Pairs invent a day of their own: a holiday nobody in the class would choose, and someone on it who says yes to everything. Six to eight sentences, every verb in the past. Give them a first line on the board so they start writing rather than discussing: At nine o’clock the hotel manager asked me… Pairs then swap stories and read another pair’s aloud, and the class votes for the worst day.
stages.avoid: Monitor the writing, not only the reading out. A slip in stopped or tried shows on paper and disappears in speech, which is why this stage is written.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to use the past simple in a story of their own

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from the stories on the board, one with a wrong past form or spelling. Pairs correct it.
stages.aim: To correct a few errors from the stories

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learned and practiced the travel phrases in Vocabulary Focus 2A – get a visa, exchange money, book accommodation, check into a hotel, unpack your luggage, do some sightseeing, buy souvenirs, stay in a hostel, stay on a campsite – to talk about their holidays.
slots.sub: To give students practice in speaking for fluency, telling a partner about a holiday they enjoyed and answering questions about it.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 19 ex 6a–6b, 7a–7b / Vocabulary Focus 2A SB p. 133 ex a, c – audio tracks 1.29, 1.30 / Workbook p. 10 ex 2a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 6a on p. 19: which holiday items can they see in the pictures around the article – sunglasses, hats, suntan lotion, the beach chair – and what else do people take? Pairs, two minutes, then board their list. Then Vocabulary Focus 2A ex a on p. 133: eight items matched to the pictures, and play 1.29 for them to check and repeat. Passport, map and suitcase they know, so keep it moving; this is the way into the topic.
stages.avoid: Do not clarify the eight items. The pictures carry the meaning, and the minutes belong to ex c.
stages.aim: To set the context and find out which holiday words students know

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex c on p. 133: ten sentences about one holiday, from the visa to the last week by the beach, each with a noun missing. Pairs fill them from the box; holiday is done for them. Play 1.30 to check. Then send them back into the sentences with one question: which verb goes with each noun? They underline – get a visa, exchanged money, booked accommodation, checked into a hotel, unpacked luggage, did some sightseeing, bought souvenirs, stayed in a hostel, stayed on a campsite, had a great adventure.
stages.aim: To present the holiday phrases in context

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: The phrases are the lesson, not the nouns, so clarify verb and noun together. Meaning, a question for each that needs one: a visa – from the embassy or the airport? A hostel – cheaper than a hotel, and do you share a room? Sightseeing – at home or on holiday? Then form, which is where they go wrong. The verbs: do sightseeing, not make it; stay in a hostel but on a campsite; check into, then check out of. Accommodation, luggage and sightseeing are uncountable – no -s, no a. And campsite, not camping: we stayed at a great camping is the classic mistake. Then stress, drilled inside the phrase: do some SIGHTseeing, book accommoDAtion, buy souveNIRS, have an adVENture. The page prints the phonemes, so point at them as you drill.
stages.avoid: Accommodation, sightseeing and souvenirs are hard to spell because they do not sound the way they look. Write them up slowly and leave them up.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning and form of the verb and noun phrases

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 10 ex 2a: eight sentence halves to match – get a visa from the embassy, do some sightseeing this afternoon, book your accommodation before you go, check out of your hotel by eleven. Alone, then compare. In open class they say the whole sentence, not the letter, so the stress you drilled gets used. Answers: 1d 2e 3a 4f 5h 6b 7c 8g.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the phrases

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 19. First 7a: each of them chooses a holiday they enjoyed and reads the nine questions silently – when, where, how long, who with, what kind of accommodation, any sightseeing, any souvenirs. A minute to think. Then 7b: they tell a partner about it, and the partner asks the questions and some of their own. Swap. Then change partners once, so the phrases come out a second time with more confidence.
stages.avoid: Ex 7 is full of past simple questions. They are printed, so let students read them off the page; correcting did-questions here turns your vocabulary lesson into a grammar lesson.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to use the phrases to talk about a holiday

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One holiday from each pair to the room – whose was the biggest adventure? Then write up two phrases you heard – one right, one with the wrong verb or an extra -s – and let the class decide which needs fixing.
stages.aim: To share a few holidays and correct a few errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learned and practiced nine verbs and phrases for describing a journey – travel around, set off, take off, land, hitchhike, give someone a lift, board a train, change trains, get to – and used them to retell a trip.
slots.sub: To give students practice in speaking for fluency, retelling a journey from a map and talking about how they like to travel.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 20 ex 1a / Vocabulary Focus 2B SB p. 134 ex a, b, f – audio track 1.31 / Workbook p. 11 ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ask how they got here today and list the transport on the board as they answer. Then ex 1a on p. 20 – car, bus, train, plane, coach, on foot: which do they prefer, and why? Three prompts on the board give the pairs more to talk about: every day? on holiday? at the weekend?
stages.aim: To get students talking about transport and set the context

stages.name: Setting the situation
stages.todo: Vocabulary Focus 2B on p. 134 with the nine sentences covered, so they see only the map. Play 1.31 once and they follow the journey with a finger: which cities, and how many kinds of transport? Pairs compare – a plane to Berlin, a car to Frankfurt, then trains to Paris with a change on the way.
stages.aim: To set the situation of a journey before the language

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex a: now uncover the sentences. Pairs match each phrase in bold – travelled around, set off, took off, landed, hitchhiked, gave us a lift, boarded a train, changed, got to – with a definition from a–i, using the map to help. Check in open class: 1h 2i 3d 4g 5e 6c 7a 8b 9f.
stages.aim: To present the travel verbs in context

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning goes fastest in pairs that contrast: set off and get to (start and end a journey), take off and land (only planes), hitchhike and give someone a lift (the same car seen from two sides – who is standing by the road?). Concept-check each pair against the map on the board. Then form. Set off and take off need no object; get to needs a place after it; give takes two – gave us a lift. Write up board a train with no on, because they will add one. The sentences are in the past and three of the verbs are irregular – set off, took off, gave – so point at them. Drill each phrase inside a short sentence: in set off and take off the stress falls on off, in get to it falls on the place – we got to PAris.
stages.avoid: Leave ex c, the travel problems, closed. It is a second set of ten words and will not fit in this lesson.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning and form of the travel verbs

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 11 ex 1a: four short travel stories with ten gaps, and the verbs in the box go into the past – hitchhiked, gave, set off, missed, took off, landed, boarded, changed, got to. Alone, a partner check, then the stories read aloud in open class. Then Vocabulary Focus ex b: sentences covered, and pairs retell the map journey from the pictures alone. Listen for the three irregular past forms.
stages.avoid: Miss is in the Workbook box and not among the nine. It is easy – give it in a line when it comes up.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the travel verbs

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Vocabulary Focus ex f, questions 2 to 5: a country you would like to travel around, the last time someone gave you a lift, how you feel when a plane takes off and lands, and whether hitchhiking is a good idea. New partners. Note what you hear.
stages.avoid: Question 1 is about the pictures in ex c, which you have not taught. Start at question 2.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to use the verbs to talk about themselves

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer to the hitchhiking question that the room should hear, then two slips you caught while monitoring, for pairs to correct – a missing to after got, or boarded on a train.
stages.aim: To share a few answers and correct a few errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have clarified and practiced the past continuous with the past simple, to describe an action that was in progress when something else happened.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, telling a partner about a problem they had while they were travelling.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 20 ex 2a–2b – audio track 1.33 / SB p. 21 ex 3a–3f, 3h–3i – audio tracks 1.34, 1.36 / Grammar Focus 2B SB p. 144 / SB p. 145 ex b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 20: the cartoon and the headline, Woman angry after flight in toilet. Pairs: what happened? Point at the flight attendant and say the word as you do – it is in the story and they need it. Take two guesses.
stages.aim: To set the context of the story and get students guessing

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b: play 1.33 once, and they listen only to check their guess. Pairs, then thirty seconds in open class: why was she in the toilet? A flight attendant’s seat was broken, she was the last passenger to check in, so she lost hers.
stages.avoid: Play it once and stop. Ex 2c is a detail task and the story is not your lesson – the four sentences in ex 3a are. Everything before the grammar should be over inside ten minutes.
stages.aim: To give students a quick listen to check their guesses

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 21: four sentences from the story with the verb missing. Pairs try them from memory, then play 1.34 to check – was raining, were waiting, was reading, was sitting. Ex 3b: they underline the past simple verb in each – left, boarded, spoke, started. Board the four sentences with both verbs marked.
stages.aim: To focus students on the past continuous and past simple in the story

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 3c does the meaning, so put its questions to the room. Which action started first in every sentence? The past continuous one. Then the harder one: did the continuous action stop because of the past simple, or carry on after it? She was reading and the attendant spoke – she stopped. It was raining when she left – the rain went on. Draw the timeline from p. 144 under one sentence, a wavy line for the long action and a cross for the short one, and check two more: was she in the toilet before the turbulence started? Did it stop because of the turbulence? Form next: was or were with -ing, and when joins the two halves either way round. Then ex 3e–3f: play 1.36, and they notice that was and were are weak in the positive sentences and strong in wasn’t and weren’t. Drill the positives at speed: it was RAINing, I was READing my book when…
stages.avoid: Grammar Focus 2B puts positive, negative and question side by side. Teach the positive and let the other two stay on the page – one new structure is enough. Ex 3g is the negatives’ pronunciation and belongs with them.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning and form of the past continuous with the past simple

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3h on p. 21: five sentences, each needing one verb in each tense – the train was leaving when I realised, someone stole my bag when I was standing in the queue. Alone, then a partner. Take the answers aloud so you hear the weak was. Then Grammar Focus 2B ex b on p. 145: seven sentences, choosing the right form for each verb. Check only the ones pairs disagreed on.
stages.avoid: Item 3 of ex 3h has three verbs: I was running for the bus when my bag opened and all my things fell out. Someone will put the third one in the continuous, and it is worth boarding when they do.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the two tenses

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3i: have they had an experience like the ones in ex 3h – a lost passport, the wrong train, a bag that opened? Tell a short one of your own first: I was getting off a bus when my phone fell out of my pocket. Then pairs, and the listener asks one question at the end, as in the book’s speech bubbles: What did you do? Swap, then change partners and tell it again.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to use the tenses to tell a story of their own

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story to the room. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one with the tenses the wrong way round, and pairs put it right.
stages.aim: To share a story and correct a few errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have read a short news story about a difficult journey for gist and for detail, and told it to a partner who read a different one.
slots.sub: To give students practice in using the past simple and the past continuous to retell a news story.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 21 ex 4a–4d / Communication Plus 2B: Student A SB p. 127, Student B SB p. 128

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p. 21: the two headlines and pictures – Did you mean Capri? and Coach passengers asked to get out and push. Ask a student to find Capri and Carpi on the map and spell them both. Then pairs guess what happened in each story. Board one guess for each and leave them there.
stages.aim: To get students interested in the two stories

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items across the two texts, since half the class reads each: GPS, a spelling mistake, break down, push and pull. GPS and a spelling mistake come straight from the map – someone typed CARPI for CAPRI. Break down from a mime of a car that will not start; push and pull with a chair. One concept question each – if your car breaks down, can you drive it? – and move on.
stages.avoid: Five is enough. Coastline, grotto and tonnes can be guessed, and none of the questions turns on them.
stages.aim: To clear the words that would block the two texts

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Split the class into A and B. Students A turn to p. 127, Students B to p. 128. They read once, fast and alone, for one thing: was the guess on the board right? Then A pairs with A and B with B to compare.
stages.aim: To give students a quick first read to check their guess

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: The five questions printed above both texts: where were they going, how were they travelling, what was the problem, who helped and how, what happened in the end. They read again, alone, and make notes – notes, not sentences copied out, because the next stage is telling. Then A with A and B with B check their answers together. Go round the pairs rather than checking in open class; the other half must not hear the answers.
stages.avoid: Question 4 in Text B has two answers – ten passengers pushed, and then a car pulled the coach with a rope. Make sure each B pair has both.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail and taking notes

stages.name: Retelling
stages.todo: Ex 4c: now each A sits with a B. Books shut, notes open. Each tells their story using the five questions, and the listener asks at least two questions of their own. Board the book’s opening – Two Swedish tourists were on holiday in Italy. They… – and one sentence from the coach story: it broke down while it was turning a corner. Those are the shapes from the last lesson, and you want to hear more of them.
stages.avoid: If the notes turn into reading aloud, take the page away. A story told from memory with mistakes is the lesson; a story read out is not.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to retell their story to a partner

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 4d in fours: which journey was worse for the travellers? Each group agrees on one answer and two reasons.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to respond to both stories

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s verdict and one reason. Then two or three sentences from the retelling on the board, one of them a past continuous used well, and pairs correct the others.
stages.aim: To share the groups’ verdicts and correct a few errors

2B.context: Travel and tourism – arriving somewhere new

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced six ways of asking for information in a public place – What time’s the next…?, How often do…?, Could you tell me where…?, How much is…?, Can I…?, Where can I…? – joining the words in them as fluent speakers do.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency in a role play between a tourist and a tourist officer.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 22 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.38 (Part 1) / SB p. 22 ex 2a–2d, 3a – audio tracks 1.39, 1.40, 1.41, 1.42 / SB p. 23 ex 4c–4d / Workbook p. 12 ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 22: train stations, tourist offices, airports – two kinds of information people ask for in each. Pairs, then board a few: train times, platforms, ticket prices, places to visit.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about asking for information

stages.name: Listening for context
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the photo – where is Annie, and what is she asking about? Board their guesses. Then ex 1c: play 1.38, Part 1 of the video or the audio, and they check. She is at a station on her way to Birmingham, asking about the next train, how often they leave, the platform, the ticket office, the price and where to buy a magazine.
stages.avoid: Ex 1d is a second listening for detail. Skip it: this is a functional language lesson, and the recording has done its job once they know who she is and what she wants.
stages.aim: To set the context of the conversation

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the six questions from Annie’s conversation, cut in half. Pairs try to remember the endings before they match, then match, then play 1.39 to check. Then ex 2b: play 1.40 for the assistant’s two questions – How can I help you? Is there anything else I can help you with? Board all eight.
stages.aim: To focus students on polite questions in the conversation

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first, one question for the set: which opening asks about a time, a price, a place, how often, and which asks permission? Then form, where one question needs care. Could you tell me where the ticket office is – not where is the ticket office. After could you tell me the order goes back to a normal sentence; board the two side by side and ask which sounds more polite. Then the pronunciation, ex 3a: play 1.42 – Where can I buy a magazine? How much is a ticket? – and ask what happens between can and I, and between much and is. A consonant at the end of one word runs into the vowel at the start of the next, with no pause: ca-nI, mu-chis. Drill all six questions whole, slowly first, then at speed.
stages.avoid: Ex 3b–3d are different questions – Is anyone sitting here? – from a different situation. Leave them for another day.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the polite questions

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2c: a short dialogue at a tourist office with five gaps from the box. Alone, then play 1.41 to check, which is ex 2d. Pairs read it aloud in both roles; the joining you drilled should be audible. Then Workbook p. 12 ex 1a: eight questions with the words jumbled. Put any slip in item 2 on the board – Could you tell me where the information desk is?
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the polite questions

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4c on p. 23: A is a tourist officer, B a tourist in town. The flowchart gives them the frame, and two lines for coming back with more – Sorry, just one more thing and Actually, there is one more thing. Read those two aloud as you set it up; the task asks for two extra questions of their own. Then ex 4d: swap roles and do it again, books shut the second time.
stages.avoid: The officer has to invent answers. Give the As thirty seconds to decide where they are – which town, which bus station – or they will stall on every reply.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to use the questions in a role play

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One pair performs its conversation for the room. Then one question from your notes that came out wrong – Could you tell me where is… is the likely one – for the class to fix.
stages.aim: To share a role play and correct a few errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have listened for gist and for detail to a phone conversation about arriving in a new country.
slots.sub: To pre-teach rainy season, storm, lightning, delay and turbulence, so that students can follow Karen’s memories of arriving in Jakarta.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 24 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.46

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Say Jakarta and ask which country it is the capital of. Then ex 1a on p. 24, the five photos: what can they see, what do they know about Indonesia, would they like to go? Pairs, then open class – a traffic jam, a beach, a storm over a city, a temple, an orang-utan.
stages.aim: To get students interested in Indonesia and the topic

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items: rainy season, storm, lightning, delay and turbulence. Photo c does the first three – what is happening in the sky? Is a rainy season one wet day or months of them? Delay from a departures board: the train was at ten, it left at eleven. Turbulence from a plane that shakes – mime it. One question each and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach traffic jam. It is in photo a, and ex 1b asks them to find it.
stages.aim: To clear the words that would block the recording

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b, three questions: why is Tim phoning, when did Karen go to Indonesia, and which photos does she describe? Play 1.46 once. Pairs, then check: for advice about arriving, about ten years ago, the traffic jam and the storm. Then ask why each of them went – Tim on holiday, Karen to work.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c, five questions. Let them read them and pencil in anything they remember. Play 1.46 again; they answer alone, then compare. Play a third time with pauses if pairs still disagree. Answers: by taxi; a long delay and turbulence; much noisier and longer than at home; she found them exciting; there was no internet connection in her flat.
stages.avoid: Question 1 is a trap. Karen suggests a bus to save money, but the question asks about Tim’s plan, and Tim says taxi.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for specific information

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: A phone call of their own. Pairs find a town that one of them knows and the other does not. The one who does not know it is going there next week and phones for advice: how to get from the airport or the station, what it is like when you arrive, what to watch out for. A minute to think, then the call – back to back so they cannot see each other, as on a real phone. Swap, with a different town.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to give and ask for advice about a place

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ask a few callers for the best advice they were given. Then three sentences you overheard during the calls, one with a pre-taught word used well; the class corrects the other two.
stages.aim: To share the best advice and correct a few errors

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have written a short travel blog post about a holiday, a new place or a first day doing something new.
slots.sub: To practice using and, but, so, because and when to join short ideas into longer sentences.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 24 ex 1d, 2a (Tim’s blog, which runs on to p. 25) / SB p. 25 ex 3a–3c, 4a–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One line back to the last lesson: Tim has arrived in Jakarta, and Karen never wrote anything down. Then ex 1d on p. 24: do they keep a blog or a diary when they travel, and do they read other people’s? Pairs, two minutes.
stages.aim: To link to the last lesson and get students talking about travel blogs

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 2a: Tim’s two posts, Tuesday on p. 24 and Wednesday on p. 25, and the one topic from the list he does not write about – animals. Three minutes, alone. Then a second pass with a different question: what is each part about? Arriving and the heat; the traffic and the taxi; the meal; the Old Town. Board it as four lines. That is the shape they will use.
stages.avoid: Ex 2b is five detail questions. This is a writing lesson; take two of them orally if you want them, and move on.
stages.aim: To show students a model of the text they will write

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 25: five sentences from the blog, a linking word in bold in each, and five uses – two things at the same time, a similar idea, a different idea, a reason, a result. Pairs, then check and board each word with its use. Then the pair they mix up: so gives the result, because gives the reason – I slept on the plane, so I’m not tired; I’m not tired because I slept. And the comma: a sentence that starts with When needs one after the first half. Ex 3b: they find more examples in the blog. Then ex 3c, eight sentences to complete with but, when, so or because. Alone, then check.
stages.aim: To focus on linking words for the blog

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex 4a and 4b: they choose one of the three topics and make notes under the four headings – where you were, how you felt, what you saw and did, who you talked to. Notes, not sentences. Go round and help with words.
stages.aim: To help students plan their ideas before writing

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4c: they write the post, about 100 words, with a day and a place at the top as Tim has. Ask for at least four linking words, one of them When at the start of a sentence. Silence; answer questions quietly at the desk. Give a two-minute warning.
stages.avoid: Some will write a list of things they did. Point them back at Tim’s four lines: one day, a few parts, and a feeling in each.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to write a travel blog post

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex 4d: pairs swap posts. The reader looks for two things – which linking words did your partner use, and is the post like yours? – and writes a one-line comment at the bottom, as on a real blog. Finish with two sentences from the posts on the board, one that joins two ideas well and one that does not, and fix the second together.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read each other’s posts and correct a few errors

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 28 ex 1a–1e

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a, p. 28: the photo and how the two people feel, to get into the topic of kindness.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Generous, hug and charity, the three words that block the forum.
stages.avoid: Leave the highlighted words in the forum for ex 1d.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b–1c, first question: who helped and who was helped, for gist.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c, second question, plus a few true/false items of your own, for detail.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1d: the nine highlighted items from context, then the verb each one takes.
stages.avoid: The present perfect in the posts is the next lesson’s.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 1e: the most generous writer, and why.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Back to the discussion, and two phrases from ex 1d to judge.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 29 ex 2a–2f – audio track 1.48, ex 5a–5b / SB p. 146 Grammar Focus 3A – audio track 1.47 / SB p. 147 Grammar Focus 3A ex c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Pairs retell one forum post with one fact changed, to bring the context back.
stages.avoid: The forum was read last lesson; do not set it again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a–2b, p. 29: the six forum sentences, and which tense each one is.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 2c: the time expressions and the rule for each tense.
stages.avoid: Been, not gone, and no finished time with the present perfect.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus 3A ex c, p. 147: one wrong tense or form in each sentence.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2e–2f: a present perfect question, then a past simple follow-up.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5a–5b: find someone who…, with a follow-up question each time.
stages.avoid: The follow-up question is where the tense changes.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 30 ex 1a–1c, 2a–2c / SB p. 135 Vocabulary Focus 3B ex a–b – audio track 1.50 / SB p. 130 (3B Results) / Workbook p. 17 ex 1b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: 3 for 2 and BOGOF on the board, then ex 1a, p. 30: is saving money easy?

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 1b, then Vocabulary Focus 3B ex a, p. 135: the two money stories, checked with 1.50.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Seven or eight items from the box: lend and borrow, owe, afford, discount and the rest.
stages.avoid: Fourteen items is two lessons. Choose before class.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 17 ex 1b: saving for a car, eight gaps.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
