s7.name: Pre-intermediate · English File
s7.sources:
Latham-Koenig, C., Oxenden, C. & Seligson, P. (2012) English File Pre-intermediate Student’s Book, 3rd edn. Oxford University Press.
Latham-Koenig, C., Oxenden, C. et al. (2012) English File Pre-intermediate Teacher’s Book, 3rd edn. Oxford University Press.
Latham-Koenig, C., Oxenden, C. et al. (2012) English File Pre-intermediate Workbook, 3rd edn. Oxford University Press.

1A.context: Charlotte’s choice – describing friends and family; who would choose you a better date, your mother or your best friend?

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have clarified and practiced eight adjectives of personality (friendly, talkative, generous, kind, lazy, funny, clever, shy) and their opposites, and revised basic appearance language, to describe a friend or a member of their family.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for specific information in a short conversation about a girlfriend.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 6 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.9 / Vocabulary Bank p. 150 ex 1a–1b – track 1.10, ex 2a–2d – track 1.11 / Workbook p. 6 ex 2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warm-up, books closed: three headings on the board – direct family, other relatives, husband’s or wife’s family – with one example under each (mother, grandmother, mother-in-law). Pairs have one minute to add as many words as they can. Collect them on the board and leave them there; the whole day is about these people.
stages.aim: To get students sorting family words and into the topic

stages.name: Listening – the way in
stages.todo: SB p. 6 ex 1a: before you play anything, pairs describe the three girls in the pictures with whatever words they have. Then track 1.9 once – Luke describing Molly – and they tick her picture (picture 1). Ask what they heard that told them: short dark hair, curly. Second play for ex 1b: the two questions the friend asks – What does she look like? What’s she like? – and how Luke answers the second one (She’s really nice). Board both questions and use the box under 1b to split them: one is about appearance, the other is about the kind of person she is.
stages.avoid: This is a thirty-second clip and it is only the way in. Two plays and out; the lesson is the vocabulary on p. 150, not the listening.
stages.aim: To give students a way into the topic through a short listening

stages.name: Appearance – quick revision
stages.todo: Vocabulary Bank p. 150, section 1 Appearance: ex 1a, pairs match the nine sentences to the pictures, then track 1.10 to check. Most of this they know, so keep it brisk: check beard, moustache, bald and medium height, which are the ones they stumble on, and drill those. Then the two boxes – thin or slim, fat or overweight, and the order of two adjectives before hair (long curly hair, big brown eyes). Do not teach every line; this is revision and the new language is next.
stages.aim: To revise the words for appearance quickly

stages.name: Clarifying personality adjectives
stages.todo: Section 2 Personality on p. 150. Ex 2a in pairs, phones away: the eight adjectives matched to the definitions. Take the answers and check meaning as you go – a generous person gives or keeps? a shy person talks easily to strangers? – and let the definitions do the work. Then ex 2b, the opposites, in the same pairs; track 1.11 to check and repeat. Board the eight pairs. Pronunciation while each is live: stress on TALKative, GENerous, EXtrovert, SErious and hard-WORKing, and the /ʃ/ in shy; drill the pairs that carry stress problems, not all sixteen. Finish with the box on nice, funny and fun – fun is the one they misuse.
stages.avoid: Sixteen words on one board is the top of what fits. Treat the eight in ex 2a as the set and the opposites as extensions of them; if the stage overruns, drop the extra note on silly and leave the box on nice for the next lesson.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of personality adjectives

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 6 ex 2b: six questions matched to six answers – What does your husband look like? / He has short dark hair and a moustache; What’s George like? / He’s very kind and quite hard-working. Pairs. It makes them choose between look like and like with the adjectives attached, which is exactly the confusion from ex 1b. Check in open class and drill the two questions one more time ready for the next stage.
stages.avoid: Questions 1 and 6 are in the past (What did you look like…? What were you like…?). Take the answers and move on; do not open a discussion of the past tense here.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the adjectives

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: P. 150 ex 2d: pairs ask and answer about a member of their family or a good friend, using the two questions and the model exchange printed under 2d. Give them a minute first to pick the person and think of three words. Change partners after three minutes so each of them describes two people. Monitor for the adjectives and for look like against like.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice describing someone they know

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three of them tell the class one thing about their partner’s person. Then three sentences you heard on the board, one of them right, and the pairs decide which is which before you confirm – make one a look like / like mix-up.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist and for detail in a magazine article about a woman whose mother and best friend each choose her a date.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary from the text for talking about people and relationships – get on well with, have a good sense of humour, be into, feel like doing, a date.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 6 ex 2a–2d (article ‘Who knows you better – your mother or your best friend?’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 6 as it stands: who knows you better, your mother (or father) or your best friend, and why? A minute in pairs, then a show of hands for each side and one reason from each. Tell them your own answer – it sets the tone of the article.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about who knows them best

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items, because without them the first task fails: an experiment, single and go on a date. Elicit each from a situation – a scientist tries something to see what happens; she has no boyfriend or husband; two people who like each other meet for dinner. Check meaning with a question and move on. Nothing else: the highlighted words come later and the text explains them.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach the highlighted words and phrases (get on well with, sense of humour, into). Ex 2c is built on guessing them from the context and that stage dies if you have given them away.
stages.aim: To clear the three words the first task needs

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b: they read only the introduction and the first paragraph, alone, two minutes, and answer the four questions – what the experiment is, who Charlotte is, who Alice and Katie are, and what the two women have to do. Compare with a partner before you check. Point at the ’s in Charlotte’s mother when you confirm 3.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for gist

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: The book has no detail task on the second half of the article, so write one: five true-or-false sentences on what Charlotte says – she prefers staying at home to the cinema; she finds it easy to get on with people; she likes men with beards; she wants a man who makes her laugh; she thinks her mother will choose better. Hand it out before they read what Charlotte says, three minutes of reading, compare with a partner, then check and make them point at the line that decides each one.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 2c: pairs guess the highlighted words and phrases from the context. To make the checking work, give them five short definitions of your own to match – have a good relationship with, think something is funny, like very much, want to do something, the ability to find things funny – rather than taking guesses one by one. Check meaning in open class and drill get on well with and sense of humour as whole chunks.
stages.aim: To have students work out words from the context

stages.name: Response – who chooses better?
stages.todo: Ex 2d first, books closed, as a two-minute memory race in pairs: what Charlotte likes doing, what she is like, the kind of men she does and does not like. Then the real response, groups of three or four: would you let your mother or your best friend choose a date for you, which of them would choose better, and what would each of them get wrong? Five minutes of talk; listen in and note what you hear for the new chunks and for the adjectives from the first lesson.
stages.avoid: Do not tell them what happened on the dates. The listening about the two dates is not on your card – it is the next lesson’s and the next day’s business, and the question of who chooses better is what keeps this discussion alive.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to respond to the experiment

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One opinion from each group, then a quick vote: mother or best friend. Two or three sentences from your notes on the board, some right and some not, with at least one use of a chunk from ex 2c, for the class to sort.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have revised and practiced the present simple – third-person forms, and questions and negatives with do and does – to ask about and describe a person they know.
slots.sub: To give students speaking practice asking and answering questions about a person, in an information gap and with question cards.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 7 Grammar ex 3a–3b, 3d–3f (sentences checked in the article on p. 6); Pronunciation ex 5a – audio track 1.16 / Communication 1B Alexander and Oliver: Student A p. 100, Student B p. 106 / Teacher’s Book p. 210 photocopiable ‘Ask me a question’ (instructions p. 198)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3d on p. 7, books closed: in pairs, a minute to remember the kind of men Charlotte likes and does not like. Take three or four sentences and write two of them on the board exactly as they say them – she likes men who…, she doesn’t like… – because they are your first examples of the target language. The article was read last lesson; do not set it again.
stages.aim: To bring back what the article said about Charlotte

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3a: from memory, they complete the five sentences from the article with the present simple – she doesn’t have a partner, she goes on a date, which one does she prefer, what kind of men do I like, I don’t usually like. Alone, then they check against the text on p. 6. Take the answers and put all five on the board; they are the material for the next stage.
stages.aim: To focus students on the present simple in the article

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first, from the sentences on the board: is this every day or always true, or only now? (Always true – she lives in Brighton, she doesn’t like beards.) One concept question is enough; they have met the present simple before and the form is where the errors are. Then ex 3b in pairs as a worksheet: which letter is added for he, she and it; what happens to watch, study, go and have; which auxiliary makes questions and negatives with I/you/we/they and with he/she/it. Board the form in two columns and make the third-person column the loud one – goes, has, does she prefer, doesn’t have. Pronunciation inside this stage: ex 5a, track 1.16, listen and repeat – the final -s as /s/ in likes, /z/ in has, /ɪz/ in relaxes and uses – then drill the five sentences from ex 3a with the -s audible.
stages.avoid: The present simple is not new, so do not present all three forms from scratch. Spend the minutes on the third person and on does, which is what the information gap is about to test.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the present simple

stages.name: Controlled practice – writing the questions
stages.todo: Ex 3e, step one only: A looks at p. 100, B at p. 106, and each writes out the full questions from the prompts in their chart – How old is he? Where does he live? What does he do? What doesn’t he like? Check them in open class and drill four or five, then they keep their questions for the next stage.
stages.avoid: Do not let them start asking until every question is written and checked. The point of the stage is the form of the question, and if they improvise it they produce ‘Where he live?’ and the practice teaches nothing.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice writing questions

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice – information gap
stages.todo: Ex 3e, step two: A asks B about Oliver and completes his column, then B asks A about Alexander. Face to face, books held up. When both charts are full they compare books to check. Then ex 3f in open class: which man is better for Charlotte, and why? One minute of opinions.
stages.aim: To give students practice asking and answering in an information gap

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 210, ‘Ask me a question’, cut up: a set of cards per group of three. Each card is a prompt – What / your mother look like?, How often / you go to the cinema? – and the player makes the full question, with do or does, and asks the others, who answer about themselves. Demonstrate with one card on the board first. Monitor for does and the third-person -s in the answers.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice asking about each other

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One thing each group learned about somebody, then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – a missing does, a missing -s and one that was right – to be corrected in pairs before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

1B.context: Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy – clothes, and describing a painting

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have clarified and practiced the clothes vocabulary they did not already know from the Vocabulary Bank set (eight to ten items such as cardigan, tracksuit, trainers, flip-flops, tights, scarf, gloves, tie, necklace, earrings) to talk about what they wear.
slots.sub: To give students speaking practice talking about the clothes they usually wear in different situations.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 8 Vocabulary ex 1a; Pronunciation ex 2a – audio track 1.20; ex 2e / Vocabulary Bank p. 151 ex a–c – track 1.19 / Workbook p. 8 ex 1a (crossword) / Teacher’s Book p. 249 photocopiable ‘Things to wear’ (instructions p. 245)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warm-up, books closed: CLOTHES on the board. Ask how it is said (/kləʊðz/) and whether it is singular or plural – plural, and there is no singular, so one thing is a sweater or a shirt. Then a line in front of the word: which verbs go there? Wear, buy, try on, put on, take off. Two minutes, and the lesson has its frame.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about the word clothes

stages.name: Test – what do they already know?
stages.todo: This is the diagnostic, so do not teach during it. SB p. 8 ex 1a first, a minute: the six items on the two models. Then Vocabulary Bank p. 151 ex a in pairs, phones away, matching the thirty-two words to the numbered pictures, as far as they get in five minutes. Then track 1.19 to check: they tick what they had right and circle what they had wrong or did not reach. While they match, walk round and note which words the room is missing – that list is the next stage.
stages.avoid: Do not stop to explain a word while they are matching, and do not let a strong pair feed the weak ones – a test they pass together tells you nothing. The teaching happens next, on what you saw.
stages.aim: To find out which clothes words students already know

stages.name: Teach – only what the test exposed
stages.todo: Take the eight to ten words most of the room circled – at this level expect cardigan, tracksuit, flip-flops, leggings, tights, scarf, gloves, tie, bracelet, necklace – and clarify those, not the thirty-two. Meaning with the pictures and the four section headings on p. 151 (clothes, footwear, accessories, jewellery). Form: trousers, jeans, shorts, tights and leggings are plural only – a pair of, some, never a – and that is the error worth boarding. Pronunciation with the book’s own exercise: p. 8 ex 2a, track 1.20, the two sounds /ə/ in trainers, trousers, sandals, sweater, cardigan and /ɜː/ in shirt, skirt, T-shirt; drill the two groups and then the new words individually. Finish with the wear, carry or dress box at the foot of p. 151.
stages.avoid: Anything they matched correctly in the test is not taught again. That is the whole point of the shape, and the temptation is to go through all thirty-two because they are on the page.
stages.aim: To teach only the words the test showed they need

stages.name: Test 2 – controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 8 ex 1a, the crossword, in pairs. Set it as a race with a time limit, then an answer key on the board rather than reading the clues out. It tells you whether the words you taught went in.
stages.aim: To check the words with a quick controlled task

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 249, ‘Things to wear’, one copy per group of three: ten prompts – one thing you wear on your hands in winter, two things you wear on your head, three pieces of jewellery, three things you wear to do sport. Groups write the words, books closed; first group with ten correct wins. Check the answers fast and drill any word that came out wrong.
stages.aim: To give students more practice using the words

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: P. 8 ex 2e: what clothes do you usually wear at work or university, when you go out at night, when you relax at the weekend? Pairs, then swap partners once. Monitor for the new words and for a trousers.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about what they wear

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer from three or four of them about what their partner wears, then three phrases from your monitoring on the board, not all of them wrong, for the class to correct – make one the plural-only trap.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have revised and practiced the present continuous for what is happening now and for describing what people are doing in a picture, in contrast with the present simple for habits.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for specific information in an audio guide to the Hockney painting.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 9 (the painting) / SB p. 8 Grammar ex 3a–3b; Listening ex 4a–4b – audio track 1.24 / Grammar Bank p. 127 1C ex a / Teacher’s Book p. 211 photocopiable ‘At an art gallery’ (instructions p. 198)

stages.name: Lead-in – the painting
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 8 with the painting on p. 9: do they like it? Then in pairs, two minutes on the three questions – what the man and woman look like, what they are wearing, what they are doing. Take answers and write two of them on the board as they say them (the woman is standing by the window, he isn’t wearing shoes). The clothes words come from the last lesson; the sentences are your first examples of the target language.
stages.aim: To get students talking about the painting

stages.name: Listening – the story behind the painting
stages.todo: Ex 4a: who do they think Percy is? Play track 1.24 once; they look at the painting and follow the people and things as they are mentioned, then tell you one thing they remember. Give them a minute to read the twelve statements in ex 4b, play once more, a quick pair check, and check the answers quickly on the board (1 T, 2 T, 3 F, 4 F, 5 T, 6 F, 7 T, 8 F, 9 T, 10 T, 11 F, 12 F). Two plays and out.
stages.avoid: This is the way in, not a listening lesson. If they want a third play to rescue the true-or-false, say no – the clarification and the practice are where the minutes go.
stages.aim: To give students the story behind the painting

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3b: four sentences, present continuous or present simple – the man isn’t wearing shoes, women often wear big hats at weddings, a white cat is sitting on his knee, my son usually sits at the back. Pairs choose and, the part that matters, say why the other one is wrong. Take answers; the reasons are the next stage.
stages.aim: To focus students on the present continuous and present simple

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning from the four sentences: is it happening now, at this moment, in the picture – or is it what usually happens? Concept-check with the cat: is it sitting on him now? does it sit there every day? (We cannot know – the picture shows now.) Then form on the board from their examples: be + verb + -ing, negative isn’t / aren’t, question Is she…? and the spelling of sitting, running, living. Pronunciation is yours to supply – the book has none here: drill the sentences from the board with the contractions, she’s STANDing, he ISn’t WEARing, and the weak are in what are they DOing.
stages.avoid: The present continuous is revision, so do not build all three forms from nothing. The error the Teacher’s Book names is ‘the man in the picture wears a hat’ – present simple for a picture – and that contrast is the one minute of meaning that matters.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the two tenses

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 127, 1C ex a: ten sentences built in the present continuous from prompts – John / wear a shirt today, what book / you read?, she / live with her parents at the moment. Alone, then check with a neighbor, then check only the ones they disagreed on, reading the whole sentence aloud.
stages.avoid: Ex b on the same page mixes in the present simple and is a different lesson. Leave it.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the present continuous

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 211, ‘At an art gallery’: A and B each have a version of the same gallery scene with ten differences. Face to face, pictures hidden, they describe what the people are doing and wearing and circle the differences they find. Demonstrate one exchange first – in my picture a man is reading a newspaper; in mine he’s talking on the phone. Monitor for be and -ing.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice describing a picture

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: How many differences did each pair find? Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – a dropped be, a present simple for a picture, and one that was right – and they find the wrong ones before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced speaking for fluency, describing a painting in enough detail for a partner to draw it.
slots.sub: To revise prepositions of place – in, on, under, behind, in front of, between, next to, on the left, on the right, in the middle – as the useful language for saying where things are in a picture.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 9 Vocabulary ex 5a–5b – audio track 1.25; Speaking box ‘Describing a picture’, ex 6a–6b / Communication 1C Describe and draw: Student A p. 100, Student B p. 106

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put a photo of a room on the screen – your own kitchen or living room is best – for thirty seconds, then take it down and ask where things were: the table, the window, the chairs. They will reach for the prepositions and some will be missing. That gap is the reason for the next stage; say so.
stages.aim: To get students saying where things are

stages.name: Useful language – prepositions of place
stages.todo: Ex 5a on p. 9: eight sentences about the Hockney painting completed from the list – in, on, under, in front of, behind, between, next to, on the right, on the left, in the middle. Pairs, with the painting in front of them. Track 1.25 to check. Then meaning quickly with the classroom (where is the bin? the board?) for any that were wrong, and drill three or four of the sentences whole – in FRONT of the woman, beTWEEN the man and the woman – because the stress and the linking are what they need to say them at speed. Then ex 5b: cover the sentences and say where things are, in pairs.
stages.avoid: This is useful language, not the main aim. Eight minutes is the budget; if they already have the prepositions, take the check and spend the rest on the drilling.
stages.aim: To clarify the prepositions of place

stages.name: Useful language – describing a picture
stages.todo: The Describing a picture box at the top of section 6: there is / there are for what is in the picture, the present continuous for what the people are doing, and the two together – there is a woman standing near the window. Elicit one example of each from the Hockney painting, board the three frames and leave them up for the task.
stages.aim: To give students the language for describing a picture

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: A turns to p. 100, B to p. 106; each has a different painting and the other must not see it. Two minutes looking, then notes only – five things in the picture, where each is, what the people are doing. Monitor and feed in a word where it is missing.
stages.avoid: Keep A and B apart from the moment they open the page. If a partner sees the painting the task has no reason to exist.
stages.aim: To give students time to prepare their description

stages.name: Speaking task – describe and draw
stages.todo: Ex 6a: A describes, B draws without looking and asks questions when the description is not enough; then they swap. Six minutes each way, you keep the clock. The drawing is what makes them be precise – ‘there’s a chair’ is not enough when someone has to put it somewhere. Listen in and note what you hear for the prepositions and the picture language, good and wrong.
stages.avoid: If a pair rushes, do not let them simply show each other the painting. The questions from the drawer are where the speaking is.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice describing a picture for a partner to draw

stages.name: Compare and discuss
stages.todo: They compare the drawings with the originals – similar or not, and what went missing. Then ex 6b in groups of four, two or three of the questions: which of the three paintings in the lesson they prefer, what is on the walls at home, whether they have a favorite painting or painter.
stages.aim: To have students compare and discuss the pictures

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Whose drawing was closest? One minute. Then four things from your notes on the board, at least one of them right and one a preposition that went astray, for the class to sort before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

2A.context: Right place, wrong person – holidays that went wrong, and your own last holiday

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist and for detail in two first-person accounts of holidays that went wrong, and retold one of them to a partner.
slots.sub: To develop students’ holiday vocabulary – the go phrases in the questionnaire, and hostel, atmosphere, flirt, break up, disaster, feel sorry for from the texts.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 12 Vocabulary ex 1a, 1c (questionnaire); Reading & Speaking ex 2a–2d (Joe and Laura)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 12 as the book sets it: one minute to write five things they like doing on holiday, then compare with a partner. Collect six or seven on the board in the -ing form – swimming, going to restaurants, seeing new places – and take a vote on the favorite. The board stays up; it is the vocabulary the day runs on.
stages.aim: To get students talking about holidays

stages.name: Pre-reading
stages.todo: The questionnaire ‘My perfect summer holiday’ in ex 1c: pairs interview each other on the seven choices and ask why each time. Four minutes. Then the title of the lesson and the strapline above the texts – the place is perfect, the weather is wonderful, but… – and one question to the room: what can go wrong on a holiday if you are with the wrong person? Two guesses on the board. Pre-teach nothing; the texts are built for guessing.
stages.avoid: Do not open the Vocabulary Bank (Holidays) here – it is not on your card. The questionnaire already carries the go phrases, and the Bank is the third lesson’s support if it is anyone’s.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about their perfect holiday

stages.name: Reading for gist – jigsaw
stages.todo: Split the room: the As sit together and read about Joe, the Bs sit together and read about Laura. One question for a first fast read, two minutes: did he or she have a good holiday, and who spoiled it? They check inside their own group, and you confirm group by group as you walk round – no open-class answers yet, because the other half has not read it.
stages.avoid: Keep the groups apart and keep the texts covered on the other side of the room. If a B reads Joe now, the retelling in the next stage has nothing to do.
stages.aim: To give students a quick first read of their text

stages.name: Reading for detail and retelling
stages.todo: Ex 2a, still in the two groups: the five questions – where he or she went, who with, where they stayed, what the weather was like, why they did not enjoy it. Four minutes reading and noting answers, then checking inside the group while you monitor each side. Then regroup into A–B pairs, face to face, books closed, and ex 2b: each tells the other the holiday they read, using the five questions as the frame. The listener may ask questions. That retelling is the detail check, so let it run six or seven minutes and listen in.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail and retelling

stages.name: Vocabulary from the texts
stages.todo: Ex 2c: now each reads the other text, and in pairs they guess the seven highlighted items – hostels, atmosphere, flirting, break up, a view of the canals, felt sorry for her, disaster. Give them seven short definitions of your own on a slip to match against, rather than taking guesses one at a time. Check meaning in open class and drill disaster and break up.
stages.aim: To have students work out words from the context

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: The last question of ex 2c first, as a vote: whose holiday was worse, Joe’s or Laura’s, and why? Then ex 2d in groups of three or four: a holiday you did not enjoy – what happened? Tell them one of your own first, in four sentences, so they have the shape. Walk round with your notebook; you want the new words and the past forms, good and bad, for the next stage.
stages.avoid: Do not play or mention the listening in the next section – it is not on your card. Mia and Linda’s side of the story is the next lesson’s way in and the surprise is worth keeping.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to respond to the two holidays

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One bad holiday from each group in a sentence. Then three things you heard on the board, good and bad together, one of them a use of a highlighted word, for the class to sort.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have revised and practiced the past simple, regular and irregular, in positive, negative and question forms, to talk about a trip they went on.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for gist to two people giving the other side of the holiday stories.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 13 Listening ex 3a, 3c–3d – audio tracks 1.34, 1.35; Grammar ex 4a–4c (verbs checked in the texts on p. 12); Pronunciation ex 5a – track 1.37 / Grammar Bank p. 129 2A ex a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: who was Mia, and who was Linda? Two sentences from the room about what Joe and Laura said went wrong. Write one of them on the board as they say it – Mia wanted to go shopping, Linda didn’t pay for anything – because it is the target language and they produced it. The texts were read last lesson; do not set them again.
stages.aim: To bring back the two holidays from the texts

stages.name: Listening – the other side of the story
stages.todo: Ex 3a, track 1.34: Mia. One question only – does she agree with Joe that the holiday was terrible? (Yes.) Then ex 3c, track 1.35: Linda – what is her opinion of the holiday? (She loved it; it wasn’t expensive.) One play each, compare in pairs, quick check. Then ex 3d for a minute in open class: who do they sympathise with? The two gist questions are the whole listening; the detail questions in 3b and 3c are not for today.
stages.avoid: Two short recordings, one play each, nine minutes in all. This is the way in to the grammar, not a listening lesson, and the second play of 3b would cost you the clarification.
stages.aim: To give students the other side of each story

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p. 13: the past simple of twelve verbs, as many as they can from memory in pairs, then checked against Joe’s text on p. 12, and sorted regular or irregular. Then ex 4b: underline the positive past verbs in Laura’s text and give the infinitives. Then ex 4c: find the two negatives – didn’t show, didn’t want – and say how the negative and question are made with ordinary verbs, with was and were, and with could. Take the answers; the teaching is next.
stages.aim: To focus students on the past simple in the text

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is one concept question – last October, last spring: finished, and we know when? Yes – and then form, which is where this class needs the minutes. Board three lines from their examples: regular + -ed (stayed, argued, sunbathed) with the spelling of stopped and studied; irregular (went, spent, took, bought) and the irregular verbs list at the back of the book as their reference; and didn’t + infinitive, Did you + infinitive, with the trap that the irregular form only lives in the positive – went, but didn’t go. Pronunciation with the book’s exercise: ex 5a, track 1.37, listen and repeat the three groups, and the only rule worth boarding – -ed is a syllable, /ɪd/, only after t or d: wanted, decided. Drill the sentences.
stages.avoid: The past simple is revision, so do not re-present it from zero. The two errors to build the stage around are ‘we didn’t went’ and ‘I want-ED’ with a full syllable on every regular verb.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the past simple

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 129, 2A ex a: the Scotland holiday, eighteen verbs into the past simple – drove, broke down, couldn’t find, didn’t know, didn’t have, wasn’t. Alone, then a pair check, then take only the disputed ones in open class and have the whole sentence read aloud so the -ed endings are heard.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the past simple

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: P. 129 ex b: six questions to complete in the past simple – Did you have a good time? Who did you go with? Where did you stay? How much did the ticket cost? Check and drill them. Then pairs use the six to ask each other about the last time they went away for a weekend or a day trip, with one follow-up question each time.
stages.avoid: Keep this to a weekend or a day out, not their last holiday. The full last-holiday interview is the next lesson’s task, and if you use it up here the third teacher has nothing left.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice asking about a holiday

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One thing they found out about their partner, from two or three of them. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – an irregular after didn’t, a question without did, one that was right – which they correct together before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced speaking for fluency, interviewing a partner about their last holiday and showing interest in the answers.
slots.sub: To revise the holiday adjectives (comfortable, basic, crowded, delicious, nothing special…) with What was the … like?, and the phrases for showing interest, as useful language for the interview.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) Teacher’s Book p. 165 photocopiable Grammar 2A, dialogue 3 only (Ruth and Tom) – read as a model / Vocabulary Bank p. 152 ex 3a–3b – audio track 1.33 / SB p. 13 Speaking ex 6a–6c and the ‘Useful language for showing interest’ box

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warm-up: MY LAST HOLIDAY on the board, and they have two minutes to find out as much as they can about it by asking you questions. Answer briefly and keep count of the questions. It models the task they are about to do, and you hear in advance which questions they cannot form.
stages.aim: To get students asking about your last holiday

stages.name: Model – a conversation about a holiday
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 165, dialogue 3 only – Ruth back from a holiday with Tom – cut from the sheet. Pens down, a gist read: did Ruth have a good time, and why not? Then in pairs they fill the eleven gaps with the past simple – did you have, was, stayed, thought, didn’t go, did you do, did you go, spent, argued, bought, didn’t buy. Check fast. Then the question that makes it a model: what does the friend do while Ruth talks? Asks a question after every answer – Why? What happened? What did you do during the day? Board those three.
stages.avoid: Dialogues 1 and 2 on the same sheet are a different lesson. Give them dialogue 3 on its own, or they will fill thirty-three gaps and you will never reach the speaking.
stages.aim: To give students a model conversation

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Two sets. First Vocabulary Bank p. 152, section 3: ex 3a, the five What was the … like? questions matched to the adjectives – comfortable, basic, crowded, delicious, nothing special, foggy – with track 1.33 to check; drill the question frame and three or four of the adjectives. Then the showing-interest box on p. 13: Really? Wow! Oh no! How awful! Was it expensive? – drill these with the intonation exaggerated, because flat they do not work. Board both sets and leave them up.
stages.avoid: Ex 1 and ex 2 on p. 152 are not for today. Section 3 is the one the interview needs.
stages.aim: To give students the language they need for the interview

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 6a: the ten prompts under Your last holiday – pairs write the full questions (did you in most; What was the food like? and What was the weather like? in 5 and 6). Check and drill them round the room. Then ex 6b: two minutes alone, notes against the ten questions about their own last holiday – or another one they remember well, or one in the right place with the wrong person.
stages.aim: To give students time to prepare their questions

stages.name: Speaking task – the interview
stages.todo: Ex 6c: A interviews B with the ten questions and must react to every answer with something from the box and one extra question; then swap. Five minutes each way, you keep the clock. Then change partners for a shorter second round so each of them tells it twice – the second telling is always better. Collect errors and good sentences as you listen for the past forms and for the interest phrases, right and wrong.
stages.avoid: Watch for the interviewer reading the ten questions off the page like a form. The extra question after each answer is the task; without it this is a grammar drill.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice interviewing a partner

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Whose holiday would you most like to have had – and whose would you least? Two or three answers about someone else’s holiday, not their own.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Four things from your monitoring on the board, one of them correct, at least one a question that worked and one an adjective from p. 152 used well. Pairs sort them, you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the language

2B.context: The story behind the photo – two famous photographs, and your own favorite one

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have clarified and practiced the past continuous for an action in progress at a moment in the past, with the past simple for the action that interrupted it, to say what was happening when something happened.
slots.sub: To give students practice in reading for gist in a photographer’s account of election night in Chicago.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 14 Reading ex 1a–1b; Grammar ex 2a, 2c – audio track 1.41 / SB p. 15 Pronunciation ex 4a–4b – track 1.43 / Teacher’s Book p. 166 photocopiable Grammar 2B ex a

stages.name: Lead-in and gist reading
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 14, text covered: the photo Tom Pilston took in 2008 – what is happening? Pairs guess for a minute; two guesses go on the board and you confirm nothing. Then ex 1b: they read the text once, three minutes, to see if they were right, plus one question of yours – why couldn’t he go inside? (He didn’t have his press pass.) Quick pair check, confirm the guesses. That is the whole reading.
stages.avoid: Ex 1c has seven detail questions and ex 1d a discussion. Leave both; eight minutes is the budget for the way in, and the grammar is the lesson.
stages.aim: To get students interested in the photo and the story

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the extract with the highlighted verbs – everybody was looking, people were holding hands and smiling. Pairs decide: did these things happen after he took the photo, or at the same time as he took it? (b.) Then draw the Teacher’s Book timeline on the board – a long line for was looking, a cross on it for took the photo – and let them place the two verbs on it.
stages.aim: To focus students on the past continuous in the text

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning from the timeline: when he took the photo, had the looking started? (Yes.) Had it finished? (No.) So one action is long and in progress, the other short and finished. That pair – was looking / took – is the whole meaning; concept-check it twice with their own examples. Form on the board: was / were + verb + -ing, wasn’t / weren’t, Was she…? and the link they already have – it is the present continuous with was and were instead of am, is and are. Pronunciation with the book’s exercise: ex 4a on p. 15, track 1.43, the short dialogue – Where were you at six o’clock? I was having a meeting – repeated for the rhythm, with was and were weak and the -ing verb carrying the stress. Drill it.
stages.avoid: For some of the class this structure is new, so do not assume it. The error to build the stage around is the past simple for both halves – ‘everybody looked at the screens when I took the photo’ – which loses the meaning; make the timeline do that work.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the past continuous and past simple

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 166, ex a only: six pictures and six sentences to build from the verbs given – she saw the spider when she was buying some fruit; his mobile rang when he was driving. Alone, then compare with a partner, then take the disputed ones and have the whole sentence said aloud with the weak was.
stages.avoid: Ex b on the same sheet is a twenty-four-gap story; cut it off before you copy, or they will be in it for the rest of the lesson.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the two tenses

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice – sound effects
stages.todo: Ex 2c with track 1.41: six sound effects, and after each one pairs write a sentence with the past continuous and the past simple – they were playing tennis when it started to rain. Pause after each sound. Take one sentence per sound on the board and accept any that makes sense; the point is the two tenses in the right places.
stages.aim: To give students more practice of the two tenses with sound effects

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4b on p. 15: seven times from yesterday – 6.30 a.m., 11.00, lunchtime, 4.00 p.m., 6.00, 10.00, midnight. Pairs ask and answer Where were you? What were you doing? for each, taking turns, with a.m. becoming in the morning and so on. Monitor for was and were and for -ing.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about yesterday

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The most surprising thing anyone was doing at midnight, from two or three of them. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – a past simple where the continuous was needed, a missing was, one that was right – and the pairs decide which is which before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for detail to a woman explaining the famous 1968 photo of herself that cost her a fortune.
slots.sub: To focus on the prepositions at, in and on with times, dates and places (in 1968, on May the 15th, at 11 o’clock, in the park).
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 Listening ex 5a–5e – audio track 1.44; Speaking ex 6a (questions 1 and 6) / SB p. 14 Vocabulary ex 3a–3b (answers checked in Tom Pilston’s text)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 5a on p. 15, article covered: the photo of the girl on someone’s shoulders with a flag. Pairs: where are they, and what is happening? Take guesses on the board – Paris, a demonstration, the 1960s – and leave them there unconfirmed.
stages.aim: To get students guessing what is happening in the photo

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items, because the recording turns on them: a demonstration, a flag, a fortune and leave somebody money (when you die). Elicit each from a situation, check with a question – is a fortune a little money or a lot? – and move on. Furious is in the recording too; let it pass, the context carries it.
stages.aim: To clear the four words the recording turns on

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Ex 5b: they read the beginning of the article about Caroline de Bendern – the rich grandfather, the schools in England, New York, back to Paris in 1968 – and in pairs decide why it is called ‘The image that cost a fortune’. Two readings of the title are possible: the photo was expensive, or it cost her money. Collect both; do not say which.
stages.aim: To have students predict how the story ends

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 5c, track 1.44, once through: were they right about the title? (Her grandfather saw the photo on a magazine cover, decided she was a communist, and left her nothing when he died.) A quick pair check, then confirm, and go back to the board to tick or cross the guesses from the lead-in.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 5d: five three-way choices – her politics in 1968, what the students were fighting for, why she was on a friend’s shoulders, why she was carrying the flag, when her grandfather died. A minute to read them, then the second play. Check with a neighbor, a third play only of the parts they disagree on, then check: a, c, a, b, c. Ask for the words that decided 3 and 4 – I was tired; he said could you carry the flag for me.
stages.avoid: Keep to two full plays and a partial third. A full third play is five minutes you need for the language stage and the response.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Language from the texts – at, in, on
stages.todo: Caroline says in 1968, on May the 15th, the next day; Tom Pilston says on 4th November, at about 11 o’clock, in the park. Ex 3a on p. 14 in pairs: which preposition before a date, a time, the morning or afternoon, a room or building. They check their answers in Tom’s text (ex 3b) and then answer the three extra questions – a month, the weekend, home and work. Board the three columns at / in / on with the examples and drill the ones they got wrong, at night and at the weekend above all.
stages.avoid: Stop at 3b. The Vocabulary Bank on p. 153 and the Communication activity are a full vocabulary lesson and they are not on your card; this stage is a follow-up to the listening, not a second lesson.
stages.aim: To focus students on at, in and on in the two texts

stages.name: Response and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 5e first: is she sorry she was in that photo? A minute in pairs, then tell them the Teacher’s Book’s postscript – the press said the inheritance would have been 7.5 million pounds; she says she has no regrets. Then questions 1 and 6 from ex 6a in groups of three: a photo you really like and what was happening when it was taken; other famous historical photos they know. Six minutes of talk, monitored with a pen. Finish with one photo from each group in open class and two sentences you heard on the board, one right and one with a preposition astray, for the class to correct.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to respond to the story

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have written a short blog post describing their favorite photo – what it is, who took it and when, what was happening, why they like it and where they keep it.
slots.sub: To practice the past continuous with the past simple for what was happening when the photo was taken, and the prepositions in, on, of and round from the model text.
slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 Speaking & Writing ex 6a (questions 1, 3 and 4), 6b / Writing p. 112 ‘My favourite photo’ ex a–d and the ‘You can keep a photo…’ box

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Show them a favorite photo of your own on the screen and answer the first question of ex 6a about it in three sentences – who took it, what was happening. Then questions 1, 3 and 4 from ex 6a in pairs: a photo they really like, their screen saver, a childhood photo. Two minutes, then one answer from the room.
stages.aim: To give students a model and get them into the topic

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Writing p. 112, ex 6b’s page: the photo of Anna at Tara and Ellie’s blog post. Pens down, a gist read with one question – why is it Ellie’s favorite? (It is mysterious, like the place, and it reminds her of the holiday.) Then ex a: match the five questions to the five paragraphs, alone, a quick pair check, check. Make the order explicit on the board, because it is the plan they will write to: what the photo is, who took it and when and where, what was happening, why I like it, where I keep it.
stages.avoid: The gaps in the text are ex b. Tell them to ignore the gaps on the first read or they will fill them instead of reading.
stages.aim: To give students a model blog post to read

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex b: the gaps filled with in, of, on or round – in the summer of 2011, on holiday, in Ireland, on top of it, her arms round it, on my phone, on my computer, photos of Ireland. Pairs, then check, then the You can keep a photo box: in an album, on the wall, by your bed, in a frame. Then paragraph 3, the one that matters: Anna was telling us about the stone… when I took the photo we thought she was meditating – the past continuous for what was happening, from this morning’s lesson. Board that frame: when I took the photo, X was …ing.
stages.aim: To give students the language for the post

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Each of them finds a favorite photo on their phone, or chooses one of three or four you bring in for anyone without one. Then notes in pairs against the five questions in order – a partner asking the questions out loud produces better notes than a silent list. Monitor and feed in the words they reach for.
stages.aim: To give students time to plan their post

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Alone, in silence: the blog post, five short paragraphs in the order on the board, about the length of Ellie’s. Give them a handout laid out like the blog page – a box for the photo, a title line – because the audience is what makes them write properly. Walk round and answer questions by pointing, not by speaking to the room.
stages.aim: To give students practice in writing a short blog post

stages.name: Sharing the posts
stages.todo: Posts go on the wall, phones with the photo beside them. Everyone reads at least three and votes for the photo they would most like to have taken themselves. Ex d’s question as they read: is any photo similar to yours?
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read each other's posts

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The winning photo, and why. Then one sentence from the posts on the board with the past continuous or a preposition gone wrong, corrected by the room. Collect the posts and mark them before the next lesson.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language
