1A.context: Lifestyle – meeting people in a new city, daily routines and booking a tour (Unit 2)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced the present simple with I/you/we/they – positive and negative statements and Do you …? questions – to say what they do regularly and to ask about other people’s activities.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, interviewing another pair about what they do and choosing a group for them.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 18 ex 1A–1C (the three Group-meet extracts) / SB p. 19 ex 3A–3B, ex 4, ex 5A–5D – audio track 2.1 / Workbook p. 11 ex 4

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p. 18, which is the book’s own way in: you arrive in a new city and know nobody – how do you meet people? Pairs, two minutes, then take four or five ideas onto the board. If the class is in one city, make it that city. Keep this to four minutes; the lesson is the grammar, not the discussion.
stages.aim: To get students talking about meeting people in a new city

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 1B: the three people and the three Dublin groups. Read the three sentences aloud first so everyone knows who they are looking for, then they read the extracts once and match. Compare in pairs, check: 1 English Italian group, 2 film group, 3 Get fit group. Then thirty seconds on 1C – which group for you – as a quick open-class poll, no more.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach for this. The only word that could block the matching is get fit, and the extract explains it (you don’t do exercise … join our group, get fit). One reading, one task, and move on to the language.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the three extracts

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p. 19: the table of positive, negative and question forms, completed from the extracts – watch, don’t eat, Do. Alone, with the texts open, then compare. Take the answers onto the board in the same table shape and leave it there; it is your board for the next stage.
stages.aim: To focus students on the present simple in the extracts

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 3B gives you the three rules to elicit: regularly (not at this moment), don’t + verb, do you + verb. Spend your time where the errors will be – the positive they have, so one check question on meaning is enough (We watch films: today only, or every week?). Then don’t: show the negative beside the positive on the board and get them to tell you what changed and what did not (no -s, no change to the verb). Then Do you …? and the short answers Yes, I do / No, I don’t – an elementary class says Yes, I like, so drill the short answer as a pair with the question. Pronunciation is ex 5A with track 2.1: they listen and underline the stressed words in the two questions and answers, then 5B, do you as /dəjə/ – say it slowly, then faster, until it links, and drill the two questions that way.
stages.avoid: Three forms in twelve minutes is only possible because two of them are revision. If you present the positive from scratch, you will not reach the question form, and the question form is what the freer stage runs on.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the present simple

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4 on p. 19 first: books closed on p. 18, they complete the text about the three groups with a positive or negative verb – speak, go, don’t eat, don’t like, do, don’t play, go. Four minutes alone, then they open p. 18 and check against the extracts themselves before you say a word. Then Workbook p. 11 ex 4 for the questions: ten prompts to turn into Do you …? questions with a short answer, as far as they get in three minutes. Check only the ones pairs disagreed on.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the present simple

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5C and 5D: each pair writes three Do you …? questions for each of the three groups, using the extracts (Do you like films? Do you go running?). Then pairs join another pair and interview them, and decide which group suits the other two. Monitor with a pen for the question form and the short answers.
stages.avoid: Writing nine questions can eat the whole stage. Two per group is enough; the point is the interview, not the list.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice asking Do you questions

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer from two or three pairs: which group is right for the other pair and why. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort – make one of them a missing don’t or a Yes, I like.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learned and practiced nine daily-routine phrases – get up, have breakfast, leave home, start work/school, have lunch, finish work/school, get home, have dinner, go to bed – to describe a typical day.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, asking and answering questions about their own daily routine.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 1A–1C (Vocabulary: daily routines) / Workbook p. 12 ex 1A

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Write A typical day for your teacher on the board. In pairs they guess what you do and when – get up at six, have lunch at school – and you take six or seven guesses onto the board as a list. Do not confirm any of them: the list is the reading task in the next stage.
stages.aim: To get students guessing about your day

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Hand out a short text you have written about your own day – eight to ten lines, with all nine phrases from the box in ex 1A on p. 20 in it, and clock times only on the hour. They read it once and tick or cross the guesses on the board. That is the whole task; the text is here so the phrases arrive in a day, not in a list.
stages.avoid: Keep the text plain. Every extra word you add is a word someone will ask about, and you have six minutes.
stages.aim: To give students a text with the daily routine phrases in it

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: They go back through your text and underline every phrase that says what you do, then match the nine phrases in the box in ex 1A to photos A–H on p. 20 and find the one that is not pictured (have dinner). Pairs, then the answers on the board under the photos: B leave home, C get home, D go to bed, E finish work, F have breakfast, G start work, H have lunch.
stages.aim: To focus students on the daily routine phrases

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is mostly done by the photos, so put the time into the two things that go wrong. First the verb that goes with each noun: have for the three meals, get for up and home, go to bed, leave home, start and finish work – board them as pairs so get home and leave home sit next to each other. Then the order of a day: get them to put the nine phrases in order on the board, which is also a check. Pronunciation: the stress falls on the noun (have BREAKfast, go to BED, get UP), and get up / get home / go to bed run together as one piece – drill them as whole phrases, not word by word. Quick check that early and late are known; ex 1B needs them.
stages.avoid: This is not a lesson on the present simple. If someone produces he get up, correct it and move on; the he/she form is tomorrow’s grammar lesson.
stages.aim: To clarify the verb for each phrase, and the pronunciation

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Two passes. Workbook p. 12 ex 1A first, the nine phrases with their letters jumbled, done from memory with the book closed on p. 20 – a spelling check, three minutes, then check in pairs and send two or three up to write the hardest ones on the board. Then SB p. 20 ex 1B: cover the box and complete the seven questions with the right verb – have, leave, start, have, get, go. Compare in pairs, then drill the questions: the yes/no ones rising, the wh- ones falling.
stages.avoid: Questions 3, 4 and 6 need clock times to answer. Do not stop to teach the time – lesson 2.3 does that properly; on the hour and half past is all they need today.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the phrases

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 1C: pairs ask and answer the seven questions and find three things they have in common. Model one exchange with a strong student first, using the book’s example (Do you get up early? Yes, I do. I get up at 6. How about you?). Change partners once at the halfway point. Monitor for the phrases and write down what you hear.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice comparing their days

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ask three students for one thing they have in common with their partner. Then two phrases from your monitoring on the board – have a breakfast and go to the bed are the ones you will have heard – and let them fix them.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for specific information to two tourists booking a tour at a tourist information center in San Francisco.
slots.sub: To practice asking for information about a tour with What time does it start?, Where does it leave from?, When does it finish?, How much does it cost? and Do you take credit cards? in a role play.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 22 ex 2A–2B – audio track 2.8; ex 3A (the five questions, written out in order) – audio track 2.10 / SB p. 23 (the three tour leaflets; ex 5B table for the role play)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: where is San Francisco, what is it famous for – the bridge, the cable cars, Alcatraz. Then open at pp. 22–23 and ex 2A: pairs read the three leaflets and answer the three questions – what tours there are, which have eating or drinking, a famous bridge, shopping, and which tour they would choose. Check: all three have food or drink; the bridge is on the bus and boat tours; shopping on the bus and walking tours. Use the photos to check bus route, bay and hop-on-hop-off as you go.
stages.aim: To get students into the topic of San Francisco

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items that the recording needs and the leaflets do not give: book a tour, leave from (the minibus leaves from the front gate), a pier and take credit cards. A situation for each and let them give you the word where they can – if the tour starts at Pier 43, is that a building or a place by the water. One concept question each and move on. The times – ten o’clock, nine forty-five, one p.m. – are in the recording; a thirty-second run over on the hour, half past and quarter to is worth it, because the detail task turns on them.
stages.avoid: Do not teach the language of the questions here. Students will meet it written out in the detail stage; the point of a listening lesson is that they understand it, not that they produce it yet.
stages.aim: To clear the four words the recording needs

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2B with track 2.8: three questions – which tour do they want, do they book it, what is the problem. Say before you play it that the first conversation goes wrong and they only need to know why. One play, compare in pairs, then check: the boat tour; no; he doesn’t understand the woman, she speaks too fast and he feels stupid.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for specific information
stages.todo: The tourists go back, and this time they ask the five questions of ex 3A – but give the questions to the class already in order, on the board or a slip, not as the jumbled words the book prints: What time does it start? Where does it leave from? When does the tour finish? How much does it cost? Do you take credit cards? Read them through together, then play track 2.10 and they write the answers. Check with a neighbour; play it once more for the ones they missed; check: ten o’clock, Pier 43 or the front gate, 1 p.m., 26 dollars each, yes. Leave the five questions on the board.
stages.avoid: Ex 3A as printed is a word-ordering exercise, and 3B–3D and 4A–4B are the pronunciation and functional work of a language lesson. None of that is yours: the questions are a listening task here, not a teaching point.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for specific information

stages.name: Post-listening role play
stages.todo: The role play from ex 5B on p. 23, kept on that page. Student B is the tourist information officer and has the walking tour and rock concert information in the 5B table; Student A is a tourist, draws the empty table, and asks the five questions from the board for each one. Then swap: Student A invents a tour – a name, a start time, a place, a price – and B asks. Sit them facing each other with the book held up so A cannot read B’s table. Monitor and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 5A sends Student A to p. 163 and that page is not on your card. Everyone works from p. 23 and from the questions on the board.
stages.aim: To give students practice booking a tour in a role play

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three tourists say which tour they would book and why. Then read out three things you heard – two with a slip, one asked well – and the class says which is which; the good one gets drilled once more.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

1B.context: Lifestyle – high flyers: unusual jobs and routines; being a good guest (Unit 2)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for detail to a radio program about two people with unusual jobs – a bridge painter and a pilot.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for jobs and working routines – painter, pilot, tour guide, leave home, start work, get home, dangerous – and use it to talk about their own jobs.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 2, ex 3A–3B – audio track 2.2 (Listening: high flyers) / SB p. 21 (the photos of Gonzales, Gagan and Emma for ex 2)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2: the three photos on p. 21. Elicit where each person is and what the job is – Gonzales paints bridges, Gagan is a mountain guide, Emma is a pilot – and write the three jobs under the photos. Then the book’s question in pairs: one good thing and one bad thing about each job. Take one of each in open class. High flyer, the title, is worth thirty seconds: people who work high up, and people who are very successful.
stages.aim: To get students talking about the three jobs

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Only what blocks the two tasks: dangerous (the wife thinks the job is dangerous), fresh air, fly between small towns, and a sandwich on the bridge is clear from the photo. Elicit each from a picture or a situation – the Gonzales photo gives you dangerous in one question – one concept question each and move on. Days of the week come up in 3B (Monday, Thursday): a ten-second check is enough.
stages.avoid: The routine phrases – leave home, start work, get home – were taught yesterday. Point at the board where they were, do not teach them again.
stages.aim: To clear the words that would block the tasks

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3A with track 2.2: two questions only – do the people like their jobs, and do their families think the jobs are good. Tell them the program is about two of the three people, not all three, so they listen for which two as well. One play, check with a neighbour, check: Gonzales and Emma; yes, both like their jobs; Gonzales’s wife thinks it is dangerous but loves the money, Emma’s daughter does not like her being away.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3B: the true/false table, four statements for Gonzales and four for Emma. Give them a minute to read it first and to guess, then play the recording a second time and they mark T or F. A quick pair check and – the instruction that matters – tell each other why: he leaves home at four, not five. Check on the board: 1 Emma T; 2 Gonzales F, Emma F; 3 Gonzales T, Emma T; 4 Gonzales T, Emma F. If a line splits the room, play only that part again.
stages.avoid: Two full plays plus one short replay is the budget. A third play from the top takes the time from the speaking, which is where the lesson ends.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Post-listening speaking
stages.todo: Their own jobs. Two minutes alone to note one good thing and one bad thing about their job, then groups of three tell each other and decide who has the best job in the group. For a student without a job: the job they want, or a job someone in their family does. Model it with your own job first – the good and the bad in two sentences – so they see the shape. Monitor with a pen; you want the job words and the routine phrases coming back.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to talk about their own jobs

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One student from each group: who has the best job and why. Then a quick vocabulary check from your notes – say the wrong version you heard (he is pilot, a danger job) and let the student who said it put it right.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced present simple positive and negative statements with he/she/it – he works, she doesn’t like – including the third-person -s ending, to describe another person’s job and day.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken accuracy, telling a partner about a family member’s job and daily life.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 4A–4C (Grammar: present simple he/she/it) – audio tracks 2.3, 2.4 / SB p. 169 (audio script 2.2 for ex 4A) / SB p. 21 ex 5 (Gagan text) / Workbook p. 12 ex 3A

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The three photos on p. 21 are back on the board. Ask what they remember about Gonzales and Emma from the last lesson and write three or four of their sentences up as they say them – He works on bridges. She flies. His wife doesn’t like it. Do not correct the -s yet; the sentences on the board are your evidence for the next stage.
stages.avoid: The recording was played twice in the previous lesson. Do not play it again – send them to the script.
stages.aim: To bring back the jobs from the last lesson

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p. 20: audio script 2.2 is on p. 169. They find the lines and complete the table – works, has, loves, watches, doesn’t like – and then the three rules under it. Alone, then compare in pairs. Take the answers and put the five verbs on the board beside the sentences from the lead-in.
stages.aim: To focus students on the third person in the script

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is the same as yesterday’s I/you/we/they – a routine, a fact – so one check question and move to form, which is the whole difficulty. Board the positive beside the I/you form and let them find the -s: works, loves; -es after -ch, -sh, -s: watches, finishes; has for have. Then the negative: doesn’t + the bare verb – She doesn’t like flying, and NOT doesn’t likes – which is the error that will follow this class for a year, so make the comparison with don’t explicit. Pronunciation: ex 4B, track 2.3 – the four verbs into /s/, /z/ and /ɪz/ – then ex 4C, track 2.4, eleven more verbs sorted into the three columns, and they repeat after the recording. Put a hand on the throat for /s/ against /z/ if they cannot hear it.
stages.avoid: Questions with does and the short answers are ex 7 on p. 21, and they are not in this lesson. If someone asks, say so and keep to statements; the freer stage needs none.
stages.aim: To clarify the form and pronunciation of the third person -s

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: SB p. 21 ex 5, the text about Gagan: twelve verbs in brackets, positive or negative, in the third person – doesn’t have, leaves, goes, meets, puts, walk, stop, makes, doesn’t eat, walk, doesn’t go. Look at the photo first and guess his day, then write. Alone, then pairs, then an answer answers on the board. Watch out for items 7, 8 and 11, where the subject is they and the -s must NOT appear. If that goes well, Workbook p. 12 ex 3A, Al the hot dog seller, is the same thing with fresh verbs; prepare it and use it only if there is time.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the third person

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Each student picks a family member with an interesting job or an unusual day and writes four or five notes – not sentences: nurse, nights, home at 8. Then they tell a partner about the person, change partners and tell someone new. Model with one of your own relatives first. You are listening for the -s and for doesn’t, so stand where you can hear.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice describing a family member's day

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four sentences from your monitoring on the board, two with the -s missing or doubled (she don’t work, he doesn’t works) and two correct. Pairs decide which are wrong and fix them; then you confirm and drill the corrected ones once.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have developed their spoken fluency, discussing what a good guest does and agreeing five top tips for guests in their country.
slots.sub: To practice the key phrases for giving and reacting to an opinion – What do you think?, I agree, I don’t agree, It depends, For example …, I think it’s important to … – in a group discussion.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 25 ex 4A–4B, ex 5A–5D (speakout: a good guest) – audio track 2.13

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Check guest first – draw a house, someone arriving with a bag, a week. Then ex 4A: the four questions in pairs – do you like having guests, what is good, what do you not like, three problems with bad guests. Take the problems in open class and board the new words as they come (noisy, late, dirty).
stages.aim: To get students talking about having guests

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 4B: pairs finish the sentence A good guest … three different ways, choosing from the topics in the box – bring a small gift, arrive early or late, help with cooking, speak in your language. Check the box together first; most of it is transparent, give money and stay a short time are the two to check. Collect one ending from each pair and leave them on the board; they will compare them with the recording.
stages.aim: To give students time to prepare their ideas

stages.name: Listening for a model
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 2.13: two people doing exactly what the class has just done. Which topics from the box do they talk about – arrive early or late, give money, stay a short or long time, speak in your or their language. One play, pairs compare, check. Then 5B on a second play: tick the key phrases they hear – all of them except What do you mean?
stages.avoid: This recording is a model for speaking, not a listening lesson. Two plays, two quick tasks, and no detail questions of your own.
stages.aim: To give students a model of the discussion

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The key phrases box, cut to the six that run a discussion: What do you think?, I agree / I don’t agree, It depends, For example …, I think it’s important to … Meaning they have from the recording; the work is saying them – mark the stress (I AGREE, it dePENDS) and drill them as you would want to hear them in the groups, fast and natural. Point out that For example and It depends buy thinking time. Board them and leave them up.
stages.avoid: Useful language is not target language. If a group does the task well without It depends, that is fine; the aim is the discussion.
stages.aim: To give students the phrases they need to discuss

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 5C in groups of three or four: five top tips for being a good guest in their country – or, in a mixed class, in a country they know. The book’s model (A good guest in Poland … brings flowers for the hostess) goes on the board. Eight minutes to argue and agree, one person writing. Then ex 5D, shortened: each group reads out its five tips, the others listen and ask one question. Keep the clock and monitor with a pen; you want the discussion phrases and the present simple with a good guest.
stages.avoid: Five tips in eight minutes means the group must disagree and decide, not list. If a group finishes in three minutes, they have listed – send them back to find the one tip they do not all agree on.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice agreeing on tips for guests

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A class vote on the best tip, which is the content feedback. Then four things from your notes on the board – one good use of a key phrase, one he bring, one a good guest don’t – for pairs to sort and correct before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

2A.context: People – big families and real friends (Unit 3)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist and for specific information in two short articles about very big families, the Bonells and the Radfords.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for family life – parents, children, bedrooms, housework, neighbour, bakery – and use it to talk about their own family.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 28 ex 2A–2D (Reading: the Bonell family) / SB p. 167 (Student A text: the Radford family, for ex 2B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2A: big family or small family – what is good and what is bad about each. Write the two headings on the board, pairs talk for two minutes, then one good and one bad thing for each from the room. Have the photo on p. 28 visible: it is the Bonells, and someone will count the children.
stages.aim: To get students talking about big and small families

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items, two from each text and one shared: bakery and minibus from the Radford text, neighbour and housework from the Bonell text, and noisy. Elicit from a picture or a situation – the shop where you buy bread; the person who lives in the next house – with one concept question each, and move on. Check the list with your tutor at planning; the texts have more unknown words than this, and the task does not need them.
stages.avoid: Have got is all over both texts (they’ve got sixteen children, the house has got seven bedrooms). Leave it alone; it is the grammar of this lesson in the book and it is not on your card. If someone asks, give the meaning in one word – have – and move on.
stages.aim: To clear the words that would block the texts

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Split the class: Student A reads the Radford text on p. 167, Student B the Bonell text on p. 28. One question on the board for both: How many children, and are the parents happy with a big family? Three minutes, alone, no dictionaries. Then A tells B and B tells A, in a sentence each. Check: sixteen children in both families, and yes, both sets of parents say they love it.
stages.aim: To give students a quick first read of their text

stages.name: Reading for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 2B: each student circles the numbers from their box that are in their text and notes what each number refers to – a two-column grid, number and meaning, that you give them on paper. Model one for each text first (A: 17 – a seventeen-seat minibus; B: 600 – food shopping costs $600 a week). Four minutes reading, then regroup A with A and B with B to compare. Then back into A/B pairs for ex 2C: tell your partner about your family using the numbers. Not every number in the box is in the text – say so.
stages.avoid: Keep the A/A and B/B check short, or the A/B exchange that follows it – the point of a jigsaw – gets squeezed out.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for specific information

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2D: the six phrases joined to the right family. Now the pair has both texts between them, so they can check each other’s claims against the page. Answers: the Bonells don’t all live together, all do housework together, like their big family; the Radfords have got a bakery, sometimes make pizza, like their big family. Check in open class, and ask them to point at the line that proves each one.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Their own families. Ex 5A on p. 29 is not on your card, so build the prompts yourself from the texts – how many people, who lives in your house, who does the cooking and the housework, is it noisy. Two minutes alone to think, then groups of three with new partners talk and decide whose family is most like the Bonells. Model with your own family first. Monitor and write down what you hear.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to talk about their own families

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One finding from each group – the biggest family, the noisiest house. Then a word check: say five of the pre-taught words in a sentence with a gap (the … lives in the next house) and the class fills them – that is the sub aim coming home.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for detail to three people – Hakim, Bridget and Jane – talking about their friends.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about friends – close friend, best friend, online friends, visit / phone / text each other – and use it to say which speaker they are most like.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 30 ex 1A–1B, ex 2A–2C (Listening: real friends?) – audio track 3.2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A: the three photos on p. 30 – Hakim, Bridget, Jane – with the three labels online friends, have-fun friends and real friends. In pairs: what is each type of friend, and one example of each. Then 1B, the three questions, quickly – have you got a lot of online friends, friends you see every week, one real best friend. Take a show of hands on each; it tells you what the room will say later.
stages.aim: To get students talking about types of friends

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: From the script: close friends (Hakim hasn’t got many), personal things (he never talks about them), add someone as a friend (Mark adds people he meets at parties) and each other (we visit / email / text each other). Each one from a situation, with one concept question, and move on. Four items; you have five minutes.
stages.avoid: Usually, sometimes, often, hardly ever and never are in every speaker’s lines and they are the next lesson’s grammar. Do not board them, and do not explain them if asked – they are not needed for either task.
stages.aim: To clear the words the script needs

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2A with track 3.2: draw a line from each name to the topic – who talks about online friends, who about a friend they do things with, who about a best friend. One play, a quick pair check, check: Hakim b, Bridget a, Jane c.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2B: six lines, each with three alternatives to tick. A minute to read them first; let them guess from the first play. Then play it again and they tick. Pairs compare, and play the part they disagree on once more. Check: 1 go running, 2 doesn’t want, 3 thirty-five, 4 doesn’t know, 5 talks to, 6 doesn’t see.
stages.avoid: Two plays and one short replay. If the whole room wants a third full play, the task was not read before the recording started – that is the thing to fix next time, not the number of plays.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Post-listening speaking 1
stages.todo: Ex 2C: which of the four people – Hakim, Bridget, Mark or Jane – is most like you, and why. Pairs, then three or four answers in open class. It is a short stage; its job is to move the words from the recording into their own mouths.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to compare themselves with the speakers

stages.name: Post-listening speaking 2
stages.todo: New groups of three or four. Online friends: how many have you got, do you know them all, are they real friends, what is a real friend. Give them a minute to think before anyone speaks. Monitor and listen for the four pre-taught items coming back; note what you hear.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice talking about friends

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The class answer to one question – what is a real friend – from two groups. Then two things you heard said well, repeated to the room as praise, and one error written up with a gap where the mistake was, for someone to fill.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced adverbs of frequency – always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never – and their position before a main verb and after be, to say how often they do things with their friends.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, telling a partner what they do with a close friend and how often.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 30 ex 3A–3C (Grammar: adverbs of frequency) / SB p. 170 (audio script 3.2, to check the gapped sentences) / Workbook p. 17 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The three photos again. Pairs: one thing you remember about Hakim, one about Bridget, one about Jane. Take a sentence for each on the board exactly as it comes – if someone says Hakim plays football with Tomi at the weekend, you have your first example waiting.
stages.avoid: Do not play the recording again. It has been heard twice this afternoon; the language is on p. 170 in print.
stages.aim: To bring back the three speakers from the last lesson

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The four sentences of ex 3A, on a handout with the adverbs taken out and the four adverbs in a box: At the weekends we ___ play football … Mark is ___ on his computer … We ___ visit each other … We ___ see each other … They fill the gaps from memory of the listening, then check against audio script 3.2 on p. 170. Then the line in ex 3A: they put usually, sometimes, often and hardly ever where they belong between never and always.
stages.aim: To focus students on the frequency adverbs in the sentences

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Draw the 0–100% line on the board and let them place the six adverbs – hardly ever at 10%, sometimes around 40%, often 60%, usually 80% – with a check question on the two they confuse: hardly ever, is that a lot or almost nothing. Then form, which is ex 3B: Mark IS sometimes on his computer, but we SOMETIMES play – the adverb goes after be and before every other verb. Board the two patterns one above the other with the adverb in a different color, and get a second example of each from the class. Pronunciation: word stress on USually, HARDly ever, SOMEtimes, and the whole sentence drilled once so the adverb does not get its own stress.
stages.avoid: An elementary class puts the adverb at the end – I play football sometimes – and hears nothing wrong, because it is not wrong, only informal. Say that it is possible but that the middle position is what the book and the test want, and drill the middle.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of frequency adverbs

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3C: six jumbled sentences about real friends to put in order, each with an adverb in it. Do the example together – A real friend often helps you with problems – then four minutes alone, compare in pairs, answer read the answers out. Items 3 and 6 have be in them; those are the two to watch.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of word order with adverbs

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 17 ex 2: ten facts about colors where they choose the adverb that is true – apples are sometimes / hardly ever / never purple. It tests meaning, not position, which is why it comes second. Pairs, aloud, and let them argue about the eggs and the taxis.
stages.aim: To give students practice choosing the right adverb

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: A grid you have made: six activities down the side (watch films, play sport, go to a café, text each other, talk about problems, visit each other) and the six adverbs along the top. Each student thinks of one close friend and ticks a box per line, then tells a new partner about that friend in full sentences – We often go to a café. We never talk about problems. Model it about a friend of yours first. Monitor for the position of the adverb and write down what you hear.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about a friend

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two students say one surprising thing about their partner’s friend. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one correct, for the class to sort – make sure one has be in it.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

2B.context: Places – unusual places around town, what you can do there, and shopping (Unit 4)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist, for specific information and for reference (what they, it and one refer to) in a short article about three unusual places – an underwater post office, a tiny free library and a solar-powered cinema.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for places in a town – post office, library, cinema, supermarket, bank, school – found in the text.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 40 ex 1A–1E (Reading: around town); ex 2A (places in the text)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Do you live in a village, a town or a city – has it got a cinema, a post office, a library? Then open at p. 40, ex 1A: the three photos only. In pairs: what are these places, and why are they unusual? Collect the guesses on the board and leave them there; the first reading checks them.
stages.aim: To get students talking about places in their town

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book names the four that block: plastic, maximum, for free and solar powered. Add underwater and borrow, which the tasks turn on. Six items, from a picture or a situation each – the sun gives the energy; you take the book and bring it back – with one concept question each, and move on. Check the list with your tutor at planning.
stages.avoid: Can is in every paragraph (you can send a postcard, you can borrow a book). It is the next lesson’s grammar: give the meaning in a word if someone asks and do not board it.
stages.aim: To clear the words that would block the text

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1B: read once and check the guesses on the board. Two minutes, no dictionaries. Swap and compare, then tick or cross the board: an underwater post office in Vanuatu; a free library in Pakistan, one of 12,000; the smallest cinema in the world, in Wales.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for gist

stages.name: Reading for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 1C: six things someone might say, each matched to the post office, the library or the cinema. Do the example together (They’re plastic, not paper – PO). Four minutes alone with the text, check with a neighbour and point at the line that proves it, then check: 2 L, 3 C, 4 PO, 5 C, 6 L.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for specific information

stages.name: Reading for reference
stages.todo: Ex 1D: what do they, one, it stand for in the six sentences. Explain in one line what you are doing – a word like it points back at something – and do number 1 with them (They = postcards). Pairs do the rest with the text open; then put the sentences on the board and send students up to draw the arrow to the word. Answers: 2 a book, 3 a film, 4 a postcard, 5 a library, 6 a book.
stages.aim: To focus students on what the reference words stand for

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: First ex 2A in pairs, two minutes: how many words for places in a town can you find in the text – post office, supermarket, school, bank, cinema, library – which is the vocabulary the text has given them. Then ex 1E in groups of three: which of the three places would you like to visit or use, and why. Then one more question of your own: is there an unusual place in your town? Monitor and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 2B–2D are the vocabulary section proper, ten place words with can in every sentence. They are not on your card.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to respond to the three places

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A show of hands for each of the three places, then one reason from each camp. Then the vocabulary: cover the board, give the meaning of each of the six place words, and let them call the words back.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the vocabulary

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced can and can’t for possibility – You can send a postcard, you can’t borrow DVDs – to say what is and is not possible in the places in a town.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, describing a place they often go to and what you can and can’t do there.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 41 ex 3A–3E (Grammar: can for possibility) – audio tracks 4.5, 4.6; ex 4A–4C / SB p. 40 (the article as the source of the examples; the list of places in ex 2B for ex 4A) / Workbook p. 26 ex 4A, 4B, 4D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A thirty-second quiz on the article they read last lesson, books closed: where is the underwater post office, how long is a film at the Sol Cinema, how much does a Little Free Library book cost. Three questions, hands up. The text is done; this only puts it back in the room.
stages.avoid: The text was read three times in the last lesson. Do not set it again – go straight from the quiz to the sentences.
stages.aim: To bring back the article from the last lesson

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3B gives you two sentences about the library and the post office with can/can’t gapped; add four of your own from the article on p. 40 so that both forms appear – You ___ send a postcard from the beach. You ___ buy a paper postcard. You ___ take a book for free. You ___ watch a long film at the Sol Cinema. They complete them from the text, alone, then compare. Then ex 3A, the one-line meaning check: it’s possible or not possible.
stages.aim: To focus students on can and can't in the article

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first, from their own sentences: can = it is possible, can’t = it is not possible – one check question on each (You can send a postcard from the beach: is it possible? Can you buy a paper one? No). Then form, which is where the errors live: can + verb without to, and the same word for every person – he can, they can, no -s, and the negative is can’t, not don’t can. Board a positive, a negative and a question (Can you …?) one under the other. Pronunciation is ex 3C with track 4.5 – can is weak /kən/, can’t is strong /kɑːnt/ – then ex 3D with track 4.6, six sentences to mark positive, negative or question by ear, and ex 3E, repeat after the recording. Drill the pairs: you can / you can’t.
stages.avoid: Do you can and You can to buy are the two errors the Teacher’s Book warns about. Put both on the board crossed out before the practice, not after.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of can and can't

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 26: ex 4A, the five quiz questions completed with where, can and a verb from the box; then ex 4B, they answer the quiz in pairs; then ex 4D, can put into the five answer sentences (You can eat it in China …). Answer key on the board; take only the disputed ones.
stages.avoid: Ex 4C on the same page is the quiz’s answer key. Hold it back until 4B is done.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of can and can't

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p. 41: each student picks a place from the list in ex 2B on p. 40 and writes two sentences, one can and one can’t, without naming the place (You can buy stamps there. You can’t play tennis there). Then ex 4B: partners read their sentences and guess the place. Monitor the writing for to after can.
stages.aim: To give students practice describing a place with can and can't

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4C with a new partner, turned into their own lives: think of a place you often go to in this town – a café, a gym, a library – and tell your partner what you can and can’t do there; the partner asks Can you …? questions to find out more. Model with a place of your own on the board first. Monitor and collect what you hear.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about a place they go to

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort – make the wrong one a can to or a don’t can if you heard it. Confirm and stop.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced the language of buying something in a shop – Have you got it in large / in black?, It’s too small, How much is it / are they?, I’ll take it, and the polite refusals No, thanks, I’m just looking and I’m not sure, I need to think about it.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for specific information – the item, the price and whether the customer buys – in four short shop conversations.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 42 ex 1A (questions 1–2 only), ex 3A–3D (Function: shopping) – audio track 4.9 / SB p. 171 (audio script 4.9 for ex 3C) / SB p. 43 ex 4A–4B, ex 5A–5B – audio track 4.10, ex 6A–6B / Workbook p. 27 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p. 42, questions 1 and 2 only: do you enjoy shopping, and is there a big shopping center in your town. Pairs, two minutes, hands up for the shoppers. Then the three photos: where are these people – a clothes shop, an electronics shop, a sports shop – which are the three shops in the recording.
stages.avoid: Ex 1B and ex 2A–2D are a twelve-item vocabulary section and not this lesson. The recording needs sweater, SIM card and trainers; check those three from the photos and leave the rest.
stages.aim: To get students talking about shopping

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3A with track 4.9: four customers; for each, the item and whether they buy it. One play, pairs compare, check: 1 a sweater, no; 2 a SIM card, yes; 3 trainers, no; 4 nothing, no. Then ex 3B on a second play: the prices – 19.99, 8.99, 120 euros, and nothing for the fourth. That is the listening done.
stages.avoid: This is the way in, not a listening lesson. Two plays, two quick tasks, no gist question of your own, and no third play – the clarification is where the minutes belong.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3C: the four customer lines with a word gapped – It’s too small. Have you got it in large? How much is it? That’s fine, I’ll take it. They try from memory first, then open audio script 4.9 on p. 171 and check. Then ex 3D, the same four with different words in the gaps (too long, I’ll have, in medium, How much are they), which shows them the slots that change.
stages.aim: To focus students on the customers' phrases

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Six phrases on the board, customer’s side only: Have you got it in … ? / It’s too … / How much is it? – How much are they? / I’ll take it / No, thanks, I’m just looking / I’m not sure, I need to think about it. Meaning from the conversations they have just heard, with a role play for too – try to lift the table and say it’s too heavy, as the Teacher’s Book suggests. Form, briefly: too + adjective; it or them after take and in How much; a size or a color after in. Then the pronunciation, which is ex 5A and 5B on p. 43 with track 4.10 – the three polite refusals, intonation high and friendly, because a flat No, it isn’t right is rude in English. Drill all six as whole lines, fast.
stages.avoid: Do not teach the shop assistant’s side as well. Can I help you? and Here you are are for the role play card; the aim is the customer.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the shopping phrases

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p. 43: the flowchart, where they write the customer’s four lines from the prompts (Have you got this sweater in size forty-two? … That’s too small. I’ll have the gray one.). Then 4B, read it aloud in pairs, once each way. If a pair finishes early, Workbook p. 27 ex 2: two shop conversations with the missing words in a box.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the phrases

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 6A and 6B, kept on p. 43: Student A is the assistant in a sports shop and writes a price on a slip for each of the four things in 6A; Student B is the customer and tries to buy them, writing the price when they do. Then swap for 6B, the electronics shop. Tell the assistants to make one thing very expensive, so the customer has to say no politely. Model the first exchange with a strong student. Listen in and note what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 6A sends Student A to p. 164 and that page is not on your card. The assistant invents the prices; it works just as well.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice buying in a shop role play

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who bought the most, who said no best. Then two lines from your monitoring on the board, one a refusal that worked and one with a mistake, for the class to fix.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the task and the language

Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 78 ex 3A–3D (Grammar: present continuous) – audio track 8.1 / SB p. 79 ex 4A–4D / Workbook p. 46 ex 1, 2A / Teacher’s Book p. 176 photocopiable ‘I’m on the phone!’ (present continuous) for the freer stage
Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 80 ex 1A–1E (Listening: what a difference!) – audio track 8.3

Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 88 ex 1 (lead-in); ex 3A–3D (Reading: Mexico’s bike revolution) / SB p. 89 (the last paragraph of the article – the taxi driver)
Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 89 ex 4A–4E (Grammar: can/can’t, have to/don’t have to) – audio track 9.2; ex 5A–5B; ex 6C / SB p. 88 (the article as the source of the examples)

slots.watch:
