s9.name: Upper-intermediate · Language Hub
s9.sources:
Brinks Lockwood, R. et al. (2019) Language Hub Upper Intermediate Student’s Book. Macmillan Education.
Language Hub Upper Intermediate Teacher’s Book (2019). Macmillan Education.
Language Hub Upper Intermediate Workbook (2019). Macmillan Education.

1A.context: Connections – meet-up groups, and two people who took the long road to success

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for the main ideas and for detail in three conversations at Get Together meet-up groups.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for everyday conversation taken from the recording: sign in, how come, fair enough, get on with, give it a go and no rush.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 4 Listening ex A–D – audio track 1.1 (three conversations: ukulele group, running group, book club)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ask the room how they meet new people in a new city, then put up the logos of two or three meet-up sites they will know (meetup.com and a local one). In pairs: have you used one, and what happens on it? Two answers in open class, then Listening ex A on p. 4: they read the Get Together box in two minutes and answer the three questions with a partner. Take the answers quickly – the box exists to set up the recording, not to be read for its own sake.
stages.aim: To get students talking about meeting new people

stages.name: Listening for the main ideas
stages.todo: Ex B with track 1.1: three conversations matched to the three pictures a–c. Tell them before you press play that they only need to decide which group each conversation is at, nothing more. One play, a thirty-second pair check, then confirm in open class (1b, 2c, 3a).
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for the main ideas

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: six true-or-false statements, two per conversation. Give them a minute to read the statements first, then play the track again. Pair check with the instruction that they must also correct the false ones – it is the woman’s first meet-up, the flat is a long way from the station, and there is no rush to return the form. In feedback nominate someone for each statement and ask what the speaker actually said. If the room splits on one item, replay that conversation only.
stages.avoid: Do not play the whole track a third time. The recording is nearly six minutes and a third play costs you the vocabulary and the speaking.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: Prepare a handout with six lines from the audioscript (it is in the Teacher’s Book, TB4) that carry the phrases: could you tell me where I sign in, how come, fair enough, I don’t really get on with my flatmates, I thought I’d give it a go, no rush to return it. Pairs match the phrases to six short definitions, working from the lines, not from memory. Check, then say each phrase at natural speed and have them repeat it – fair enough and how come only exist as whole chunks.
stages.aim: To focus students on useful phrases from the recording

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in groups of three: the benefits of joining a group like this, whether it is the best way to meet people here, and which Get Together group they would join and why. Add one question of your own about a group they have actually been part of. Listen with a pen for the phrases from the previous stage and for anything worth the whole room hearing.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to discuss joining a group

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One group’s choice of meet-up and why, then three sentences from your notes on the board, one of them correct, for the class to sort in pairs. Make one of the three a use of fair enough or how come so the vocabulary gets a second outing.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have reviewed and practiced question forms – indirect questions, questions ending in a preposition, subject questions and negative questions – using the Get Together conversations as the model.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice asking and answering questions while planning a new meet-up group.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 4 Grammar ex A – audio track 1.2 (four extracts from the conversations) / SB p. 5 Grammar ex B, ex D; Pronunciation ex A–B – audio tracks 1.3, 1.4; Speaking Hub ex A–C / Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A–B (1.1 Question forms, controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The three pictures from p. 4 on the screen. What do they remember about each conversation – who was new, who was moving flat, which book they talked about? Three minutes; the recording was taught in the previous lesson, so this is a reminder, not a listening stage.
stages.avoid: Do not set the gist or detail tasks again. Your lesson starts at the grammar.
stages.aim: To bring back the three conversations

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 4 with track 1.2: four short extracts with the question gapped. A minute to read them first, one play, and they complete the questions – who’s leading the group tonight, why don’t you like them, who do you live with, could you tell me where I sign in. Pair check, then put the four questions on the board exactly as said; they are your examples for the whole lesson.
stages.aim: To focus students on the indirect and subject questions

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B on p. 5: alone, then in pairs, they choose the options that complete the four rules – indirect questions keep statement order and drop do; the preposition goes at the end; a subject question keeps statement order with the question word as subject; negative wh-questions keep the auxiliary. Confirm each rule against the example on the board. Meaning is mostly known at this level, so the time goes on form and on the one meaning that is new: a negative question like who doesn’t want pizza expects the answer to be almost nobody – check it with a question, not an explanation. Then Pronunciation ex A and B (tracks 1.3, 1.4): they mark whether each question rises or falls, listen, and say how they decided. Drill the eight questions with the intonation; make the contraction in who’s and don’t audible.
stages.avoid: Four question types is a review, not four presentations. If the ex B answers show they already have one of them, say so and move on.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the question forms

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 5: five jumbled questions to reorder, one of each type. Alone, pair check, then confirm with an answer key on screen rather than reading them out. If they finish early, Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A – eight questions with a mistake in each – is the second pass and catches the preposition and the subject-question errors.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the question forms

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking Hub ex A–C on p. 5 as the base: groups brainstorm a meet-up group, choose one and plan what they would do, where, how often and what it costs. Then each group presents in two minutes and the listening groups must ask three questions – that is the stage’s purpose, so tell them before the presentations and keep a tally on the board of questions asked. Listen for the question forms, right and wrong.
stages.avoid: Without the three-questions rule this is a presentation lesson and the questions never happen. Set the rule when you set the task.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice planning a meet-up group

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which group would the class actually join? Then four questions from your notes on the board, two right and two wrong, for pairs to sort and correct before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist, scanning and reading for detail in an article about two people who overcame challenges to succeed.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about success and setbacks from the article: overcome, adversity, eccentric, gifted, groundbreaking, self-made.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 6 Reading ex A–C and the article The long road to success / SB p. 7 Reading ex D–E (top of the page only)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Photos of Stephen Hawking and Vera Wang on the screen, names covered. Ex A on p. 6 in groups: who are they and what do they know about them. Collect one fact for each on the board and leave the board up – the text will confirm or correct it.
stages.aim: To get students talking about the two people

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items that the text does not explain: overcome, eccentric, groundbreaking. A situation for each and let them give you the word – a family that keeps bees in the basement and drives an old London taxi, is that normal or unusual; if you overcome a problem, does it still stop you. One concept question each and move on. Gifted, adversity and self-made come out of the text later; leave them.
stages.aim: To clear the three words the text does not explain

stages.name: Reading for gist, then scanning
stages.todo: Ex B first: read the article once and choose the sentence that connects the two people – famous people who overcame challenges to succeed. Three minutes, no dictionaries, a quick pair check, confirm. Then ex C: six statements ticked against Hawking or Wang. Say what scanning is and give them four minutes, because the task is to find, not to read everything again. Pair check with the rule that they point at the line that proves each tick, then check in open class. A variation if the room is strong: give the text with its five question-headings removed and have them put the headings back before ex B.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for gist and scanning

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 7: eight sentences completed with no more than two words from the article – lazy, an hour, two, awards, figure skater, sales assistant, 17 years, $600 million. Do the first one together so they see the two-word limit means the words as printed, not a paraphrase. Alone, then pairs, then take only the ones that split the room.
stages.avoid: The Grammar section at the bottom of p. 7 belongs to tomorrow’s first lesson. Do not touch the highlighted sentences or the tense review.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail

stages.name: Post-reading task
stages.todo: Ex E widened into a task: groups of three choose a well-known person, from here or anywhere, who overcame a serious setback and succeeded, make notes for three minutes and present the person to the class in one minute each. Every other group asks one follow-up question. Put overcome, gifted, self-made and groundbreaking on the board as words they could use.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to tell a story of their own

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which story did the room find most surprising? Then two or three sentences from the presentations on the board, one of them correct, for pairs to sort before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

1B.context: Connections – who we are: tenses from the success article, the six friends everyone needs, and what runs in the family

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have reviewed six tenses – present simple and continuous, past simple and continuous, present perfect and past perfect – and practiced choosing between them to tell a short biography.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice summarizing a biography to a partner and comparing the two people.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 6 the six highlighted sentences in The long road to success / SB p. 7 Grammar ex A, B, D; Speaking ex A–C (bottom of the page) / Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A–C (1.2 Tense review, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 149 (Student A – Emily Blunt) and p. 152 (Student B – Jean-Dominique Bauby)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Hawking and Wang on the board, a column each. Groups of three have two minutes to write down everything they remember from yesterday’s article – include anyone who was absent in a group that was there. Collect four or five facts under each name. The text has been read; your lesson starts with the sentences in it.
stages.avoid: Do not set a reading task. The article was taught yesterday and the time is needed for the clarification.
stages.aim: To bring back the article from the last lesson

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 7 with the article open at p. 6: the six highlighted sentences matched to the six tense names. Name the first one together – while each of them read a book, past continuous – then they do the rest alone and compare. Put the six sentences on the board under their tense names; they are the examples for the next stage.
stages.aim: To focus students on the narrative tenses in the article

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B: they complete the six rules with the tense names, alone and then in pairs, and you confirm each rule against its sentence on the board. It is a review, so teach where the matching showed gaps and pass quickly over what they had – at this level the pairs that still go wrong are present perfect against past simple with a finished time, and past perfect for the earlier of two past events; build a concept question for each of those. Form on the board for the two perfect tenses only. Pronunciation is yours to supply: the weak and contracted auxiliaries – she’d completed, he’s admitted, she’s built – said at speed and drilled, because the contraction is what hides the tense when they listen.
stages.avoid: Six tenses is the book’s review, not six presentations. If you present each from scratch you will not reach the practice.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the narrative tenses

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 7, the Saroo Brierley text: ten verbs in the right tense across one continuous story. Alone, pair check, answer key on screen; take only the ones they disagreed on and make them say which rule decides it. Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A (1.2 Tense review) is a second pass for anyone who finishes early.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the tenses

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking ex A–C on p. 7. A/B pairs: Student A reads about Emily Blunt on p. 149, Student B about Jean-Dominique Bauby on p. 152, and each makes notes under the three bullet points – notes, not sentences, four minutes. Books closed, they tell their partner the story from the notes; the partner notes the tenses they hear. Then ex C: what the two people have in common and who faced the bigger challenge. Monitor for the tenses, especially the past perfect where one event came before another.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice telling a true story

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two pairs say who faced the bigger challenge and why. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, for pairs to sort before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for the main ideas and for detail in a radio interview about the six types of friend successful people have.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary of personality adjectives from the interview: loyal, open-minded, easy-going, arrogant, self-centred, stubborn, down-to-earth, witty.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 8 Listening ex A–D – audio track 1.5 (interview with the psychologist Richard Bonnel); Vocabulary ex A – audio track 1.6 (listen and check) / SB p. 9 Vocabulary ex B (top of the page only)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Describe one close friend of yours in three sentences – how you met, how you are alike, how you are different. Then Listening ex A on p. 8 in pairs: their closest friends, and whether it matters to have different types of friend. Ask two people what their partner said, not what they said themselves.
stages.aim: To get students talking about close friends

stages.name: Listening for the main ideas
stages.todo: Read the skills box on listening for the main ideas with them first – the next is, another one is, the last is are the signposts – then ex B with track 1.5: six friend types numbered in the order the psychologist mentions them. Say it is a number, not a tick, and that there are six to find. One play, pair check, confirm.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for the main ideas

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: five three-option questions. A minute to read them and underline the key words, then play the track again. Pair check; in feedback ask what else the speaker said that supports each answer – 50 people, new situations do not stress them, brutally honest, neighbors, feeling part of a group. Replay a short section if an answer splits the room, not the whole interview.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A on p. 8: eight extracts from the interview gapped with the eight personality adjectives in the box. Pairs complete them from what they remember and from the sense of the sentence, then track 1.6 to check. Meaning they can mostly work out from the extracts, so the time goes on the three that look alike and are not: self-centred against arrogant, stubborn against determined, and easy-going against open-minded. Drill the stress – ARRogant, self-CENtred, down-to-EARTH, open-MINDed – then ex B at the top of p. 9, eight sentences choosing between two adjectives, alone and compared.
stages.avoid: Stop at ex B. Ex C sends them to the Vocabulary Hub and ex D is the personality quiz; neither is on your card and the lesson is the listening.
stages.aim: To focus students on the personality adjectives in the recording

stages.name: Post-listening task
stages.todo: The six friend types on the board: loyal best friend, open-minded adventurer, honest friend, complete opposite, dependable neighbor, witty colleague. Two minutes alone to think of a real person for as many of the six as they can and a word on why. Groups of three tell each other, using the adjectives from the previous stage. Then ex D question 2 if a group finishes early.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to describe their own friends

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two people describe one of their partner’s friends to the room. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, with an adjective in each, for the class to sort.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced developing a topic and changing the subject in conversation using speaking of which, talking of …, actually, that reminds me of …, strange you should mention that and anyway.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice in a role play about the things that run in their families.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 11 Family matters ex A; Speaking Skill ex A (the printed extract, completed and used as the text), ex B and the box Developing and introducing new topics, ex C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tell them one thing that runs in your family – a talent, a habit, a flaw – in two sentences. Then ex A on p. 11 in pairs: the job they have or want and what makes them suited to it. One or two answers, then ask whether that suitability came from their parents; the extract they are about to read is two friends having exactly that conversation.
stages.aim: To get students talking about what runs in their family

stages.name: Text
stages.todo: The Café Hub video is not in our files, so the Speaking Skill ex A extract is your text. Prepare it with the three gaps filled – speaking of which, strange you should mention that, talking of – and give it out as a handout. Two questions on the board before they read: what is Sam busy with (opening a new café) and what runs in Harry’s family (untidiness). Two minutes, pair check, confirm. That is all the reading the lesson needs.
stages.avoid: This is a language lesson. Keep the text stage to its two questions and do not turn the extract into a reading lesson.
stages.aim: To give students the extract as the context

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex B in pairs: what the three phrases are doing, and what is different about anyway. Elicit the answers and board the exponents under two headings – developing the topic: speaking of which, talking of which, talking of [topic], actually, that reminds me of …, strange you should mention that (because) …; changing the topic completely: anyway. Then the box to confirm.
stages.aim: To focus students on the phrases for developing and changing the topic

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Check meaning with the extract: when Sam says speaking of which, is the hand soap connected to the paper towels (yes); when he says anyway, is Harry’s progress connected to the café delivery (no). Form: talking of takes a noun or -ing, that reminds me of takes a noun. Pronunciation is yours: the phrases are said fast and low before the new topic, with the stress on the topic that follows – drill all five as chunks.
stages.avoid: One function, five exponents. Do not add the idioms from the Café Hub page opposite; they are a different lesson.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning and pronunciation of the phrases

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex C: Student A talks about one of the six topics – a film, a news item, a restaurant – and Student B has to either develop it with one of the developing phrases or change it with anyway. Swap after each topic. Keep the board up and listen for the phrases; stop the room once to correct a phrase that is not landing before you continue.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the phrases

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: A role play in pairs about things that run in their families: one partner keeps developing the subject, the other keeps trying to move off it. Three minutes to plan, four to run it twice with roles swapped, and a sentence of brief each time on who they are – two colleagues at work, two cousins at a wedding. If the group is small, two pairs perform for the room; otherwise monitor and collect what you hear.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice in a role play

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which pair managed the most topic changes? Then three lines from your monitoring on the board, one of them right, for pairs to sort before you confirm – the one worth time is a developing phrase used where anyway was needed, or the reverse.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the task and the language

2A.context: Lifestyles – a full life: health and fitness, six ways to live longer, and what people give up for the new year

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learned and practiced six health and fitness nouns – calorie, cholesterol, obesity, depression, stress, anxiety – and used them to argue about health.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice agreeing and disagreeing with statements about health.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 14 Vocabulary ex A–C, ex E (the Vocabulary section only) / Workbook p. 11 Vocabulary ex A (controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tell the room two things you do to stay healthy and one you know you should. Then Vocabulary ex A on p. 14: pairs brainstorm things with a positive or a negative effect on our health. Two columns on the board, healthy and unhealthy, and collect their ideas; if any of the six target nouns come up, leave them on the board and say nothing yet.
stages.aim: To get students talking about health

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: The six sentences in ex B carry the words in context, so present from them rather than from a list. Read sentence 1 together and let the clue – a lack of healthy lunch options, worrying levels – give them definition c, obesity. Then they match the other five alone and compare. Meaning is settled by the definitions, so your time goes on what the definitions cannot give them: the two that overlap, stress against anxiety (pressure from outside against worry from inside – ask which one a deadline causes and which one keeps you awake with no reason); the collocations the words live in – suffer from depression, under stress, high cholesterol, levels of obesity; and the sounds – cholesterol has four syllables with the stress on the second, anxiety is /æŋˈzaɪəti/, obesity /əʊˈbiːsəti/. Drill the six, board them with the stress marked and the collocation beside each.
stages.avoid: Six items and their collocations is the lesson. The Vocabulary Hub (ex D) adds seven more phrases – that is a second lesson, not an extension of this one.
stages.aim: To present the health words in context

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex C: six gapped sentences, one word each. Alone, pair check, then answers on screen. Then Workbook p. 11 Vocabulary ex A, the Staying healthy as a student article with the same six nouns to place across one continuous text – harder than ex C because the clues are spread out. Pair check and take only the disputed ones.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the words

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Four or five provocative statements about health on the board, each built around one of the words – eating meat causes obesity; meditation should be taught in schools to cut students’ stress; most anxiety is caused by phones; a diet is more important than exercise. Groups of three agree or disagree with each and must give a reason. Then ex E as the last round: the effects of junk food, smoking, lack of exercise and a poor work-life balance. Listen for the nouns and their collocations.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice discussing statements about health

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which statement did the room disagree about most? Hear both sides for a minute. Then four sentences from your monitoring on the board, two right and two wrong – make one of them a collocation error, such as suffer depression or in stress – for pairs to sort, then confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced predicting, scanning and reading for detail in an article about six ways to live longer.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about health from the article – life expectancy, processed foods, mental health, physical activity, reduce the risk, slow the ageing process.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 14 Reading ex A–D (the Reading section only) / SB p. 15 the article Six ways to live longer / Vocabulary Hub p. 143 (2.1 Health and fitness – vocabulary from the text)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One question on the board: how can we live longer? Collect six or seven ideas from the room fast and leave them up – the article will agree with some and surprise them with others. The health words from the previous lesson are fresh; use them yourself as you write.
stages.avoid: The source document opened with a six-minute taboo game. Leave it out: it spends the pre-reading time on the last lesson’s aim, not yours.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about how to live longer

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items only, because they block the gist and the text does not explain them: life expectancy, sedentary and immune system. A context for each and let them give you the word – the average age people live to in a country; a job where you sit all day; the part of your body that fights illness. One concept question each and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach processed foods, optimist or pessimist – the text makes them clear and they come back in the vocabulary stage.
stages.aim: To clear the three words that block the gist

stages.name: Prediction and scanning
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 14 with the six pictures and sub-headings on p. 15: pairs say how a pet, moving to Japan, thinking of the details, helping others, singing and not moaning could each lengthen a life. Board one guess per heading. Then ex B: scan the article in three minutes to check the guesses – a scan, so they are looking for their guess, not reading every line. Pairs compare what they found before you give the answers.
stages.aim: To have students predict, then scan the text

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: six questions, one per section, with the instruction to underline the part of the text that answers each. Alone, then compared in pairs pointing at the lines. Check in open class and ask for the evidence – less risk of heart disease from walking the dog, less fat and smaller plates, better sleep and less comfort eating, volunteering, stress, their own physical health.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Vocabulary Hub p. 143, the 2.1 exercise: seven gapped sentences with the box – level of fitness, life expectancy, mental health, physical activity, processed foods, reduce the risk, slow the ageing process. All of them are in the article they have just read, so pairs do it with the text open and find each phrase in it. Check, then drill the stress on the longer chunks – slow the AGEing process, reDUCE the risk.
stages.aim: To focus students on the collocations in the text

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex D questions 3 and 4 in groups: which of the six changes they would actually make and what else they could change. Then the source’s find-someone-who, if there is time: six lines on a handout – find someone who exercises every day, who never eats processed food, who sings – and they mingle to fill it. Close with the question who is the healthiest person in the room.
stages.avoid: Do not open the Speaking section at the foot of p. 15. The discussion in ex D is the response this lesson needs.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to discuss the changes

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist, for the main ideas and for reasons in a radio program about people who gave something up for the new year.
slots.sub: To develop students’ language for giving and recognizing reasons – because of, as, since, that’s why, due to the fact that, in order to, and the infinitive of purpose – from the skills box and the interviews.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 16 Listening ex A–E and the box Listening for reasons – audio tracks 2.1 (first part of the programme) and 2.2 (the five interviews)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Write New Year’s resolutions on the board and elicit what one is. Tell them something you once gave up and whether it lasted. Then Listening ex A on p. 16 with the six pictures a–f: pairs pick the one they would find hardest to give up and say why. Two answers in open class.
stages.aim: To get students talking about resolutions

stages.name: Prediction and listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex B: pairs guess what percentage of people break their resolution within a month and within a year. Put three or four pairs’ figures on the board. Then ex C with track 2.1, under a minute long: they listen for the two numbers and check – 43% and 86%. Whose guess was closest?
stages.aim: To have students predict, then listen for gist

stages.name: Listening for the main ideas
stages.todo: Ex D with track 2.2: five speakers matched to the things they gave up, with one picture left over. Tell them there is one extra before you play. One play, pair check, confirm – smartphones, coffee, sugar, shampoo, meat.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for the main ideas

stages.name: Listening for reasons
stages.todo: Before the second play, the box Listening for reasons: ask how a speaker signals a reason and collect the signals on the board – because (of), as, since, that’s why, due to the fact that, in order to, and the infinitive of purpose (I stopped … to help …) – then the box’s point that a reason is often implied and has to be inferred. Then ex E: track 2.2 again, notes on each speaker’s reason. Pair check, then open class – more family time, better sleep, sugar’s health effects, a friend’s advice about hair, carbon footprint and health. Replay one speaker if the room missed the reason, not all five.
stages.avoid: Two plays of the interviews is the budget. The recording is long; a third full play eats the discussion.
stages.aim: To focus students on the ways speakers give reasons

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: The five things given up back on the board. Groups of three or four decide which of the five they could give up and which they could not, and must give a reason for each using the language from the box. Each group agrees on one thing they could all give up and tells the room why.
stages.avoid: Stop before the Grammar section on the right of p. 16. The present perfect extracts are tomorrow’s first lesson.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to discuss what they could give up

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s choice in one sentence. Then three reasons from your monitoring on the board, one of them correct – look for in order to with -ing, or because of followed by a clause – for pairs to sort before you settle it.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

2B.context: Lifestyles – change: advice for a new year, a family that moved from London to a remote island, and what they used to do

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have written a short article giving advice on a lifestyle change – reducing stress, improving their diet or getting fit – organized under headings with bullet points.
slots.sub: To practice the structures for giving advice from the model article: why not …?, don’t forget to, make sure you, remember to, try to, avoid + -ing, and if + present simple + imperative.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 155 Unit 2 Writing ex A–D (the model article Clear the mess and clear your mind and the box Using different structures to give advice); Writing ex A–D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The five things given up in yesterday’s radio program on the board – smartphones, coffee, sugar, shampoo, meat. Which worked, and what advice would they give someone trying one of them? A minute in pairs, two answers, and the word advice stays on the board; the day is still about changing how you live.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about advice

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 155 in pairs: the title Clear the mess and clear your mind – what advice will the article give? Then ex B, read it quickly to see which of their ideas it has. Now the shape of the thing, because that is what they will copy: an introduction that says why, three headings, and bullet points under each. Ask them to count the headings and the bullets and to say what the introduction does. Keep it to ten minutes – the model is there to be copied, not studied.
stages.avoid: Do not turn the article into a reading lesson. Two quick tasks and the structure, then the language.
stages.aim: To give students a model article

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex C: the table completed with examples from the text – if + present simple + imperative (if you don’t watch it, sell it), negative imperatives (don’t keep broken things), positive imperatives (make sure you …, remember to …) – plus why not …?, try to and avoid + -ing from the bullets. Board the seven structures in two columns, soft and strong, and the form that trips them: avoid takes -ing, try to and remember to take the infinitive, why not takes the bare verb. Then ex D, six sentences rewritten with the word in bold, in pairs, as the controlled check. Drill the three that run together in speech: don’t forget to, make sure you, why not.
stages.avoid: This is the sub aim, not a grammar lesson. Ten minutes and the structures are on the board for the writing; the writing is the lesson.
stages.aim: To give students the language of advice from the model

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Writing ex A: pairs choose one of the three topics – reducing stress, improving your diet, getting fit – and brainstorm six to eight pieces of advice as notes. Then ex B: they sort the notes under three headings of their own. Notes and headings only; the sentences get written in the next stage.
stages.avoid: If they start writing full sentences here, the writing stage becomes a copying stage. Notes only, and say so.
stages.aim: To give students time to plan their article

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex C: each student writes the article alone – an introduction of two or three lines, three headings, two or three bullet points under each, and at least five of the seven structures from the board. Around 150 words. Silence, the model and the board in front of them, and answer questions by walking over, not by speaking to the room.
stages.aim: To give students practice in writing an advice article

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex D: articles swap with someone who chose a different topic, and the reader checks three things from the book’s list – spelling and punctuation, the advice structures, and whether the advice is clear and good. One line on the board from what you saw while they wrote – it will be -ing after try to or avoid – and let them correct it. Collect the drafts and write on them before the next lesson.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the writing

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for detail in an interview with a family that moved from London to a remote island.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about a change of life from the interview: the rat race, take the plunge, a midlife crisis, out of the question, better off, homeschooled.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 18 Listening ex A–D – audio track 2.5 (interview with Frank and Katie Gerrard)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Where do they live now, and would they move to a small island or somewhere remote near here? Then Listening ex A on p. 18 in groups of three: the advantages and disadvantages of a family moving from a city to a remote island. Two columns on the board and collect four ideas in each. Keep it to six minutes – the source gave this ten and paid for it later.
stages.aim: To get students talking about moving somewhere remote

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex B with track 2.5: which members of the family are happy with the move and which are not. One play, notes only, check together, confirm – Frank and the young son are happy, Katie is not, and the mother is not clear. Make them say what they heard that told them.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: six three-option questions. A minute to read them and underline the key words, then play the interview again. Pair check, then open class with the reason for each answer – the demanding job, growing and catching food, the money, the internet, UK exams, playing outside all day. If one question splits the room, replay just that part.
stages.avoid: Two plays. A third full play of a long interview costs the vocabulary and the response.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: A handout with six lines from the audioscript (it is in the Teacher’s Book notes for the lesson) that carry the phrases – escaping the rat race, taken the plunge, a midlife crisis, out of the question, better off, homeschooled – and six definitions to match. Pairs, from the lines. Check, then drill the ones that are chunks: the RAT race, take the PLUNGE, out of the QUEStion.
stages.aim: To focus students on the phrases from the recording

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in pairs: imagine moving to a small island far from here – what would you miss, and what would you be glad to leave behind? Push for the vocabulary from the previous stage; put it on the board again if it has gone.
stages.avoid: Stop before the Grammar section at the foot of p. 18. The used to extracts are the next lesson’s.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to discuss a move of their own

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three people say what their partner would miss most. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced used to and would for finished habits, and be used to and get used to for familiarity, to talk about how their own lives have changed.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice explaining the biggest changes in their lives over the last ten years.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 18 Grammar ex A–B (extracts from the interview) / SB p. 19 Grammar ex D; Pronunciation ex A–B – audio tracks 2.6, 2.7; Speaking ex A–C / Workbook p. 13 Grammar ex A (controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Frank and Katie on the board. What was Frank’s life like before the move, and what is it like now? Collect two sentences for each and write them as they come – if anyone produces used to or is used to, leave it on the board untouched. The interview was taught last lesson; this is a reminder of the context only.
stages.avoid: Do not replay the interview. The listening tasks were done in the previous lesson.
stages.aim: To bring back Frank's life before and after

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 18: four extracts from the interview matched to four meanings. Pairs, then confirm – used to work: true in the past, not now; I’m used to getting up at six: strange at first, normal now; we’re getting used to it: still strange, becoming familiar; he’d complain: a past habit. Board the four extracts under their meanings.
stages.aim: To focus students on used to, would, be used to and get used to

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B: they complete the four rules with the box, alone, then pairs; confirm against the extracts. The meaning split that matters is past habit against familiarity, and it is the form that carries it: used to + infinitive against be/get used to + -ing or a noun. Concept-check the dangerous pair on the board – I used to get up early (do I now? no) against I’m used to getting up early (do I now? yes, and it is easy). Would takes habits but not states – they would complain, not they would live in London – say it once with an example. Then Pronunciation ex A with track 2.6: is the /d/ in used to heard, strong or weak to – no, and weak, /ˈjuːstə/ – board it in phonemics, then ex B with track 2.7 and drill the five sentences.
stages.avoid: Four forms with two meanings is what 45 minutes holds. Do not add didn’t use to and the question forms as separate teaching points; mention the form once and let the practice carry it.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the four forms

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 19: eight sentences with used to, would, be used to or get used to and the verb in brackets. Alone, a quick comparison in pairs, answer key on screen; take only the ones they disagreed on and make them say whether it is a past habit or a familiarity. Workbook p. 13 Grammar ex A – ten sentences, some wrong, to correct – is the second pass for the fast finishers and catches didn’t used to and get use to.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the forms

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking ex A–C on p. 19: a minute to list changes in their lives in the six areas, then notes on the three biggest using the book’s questions – what prompted it, how it affected them, whether they are used to it yet. Groups of three take turns explaining their changes and ask each other follow-up questions. Monitor for the target forms and write down what you hear.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about changes in their lives

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One change from each group that surprised the others. Then three sentences from your notes on the board, right and wrong mixed – the one to expect is I’m used to get up – for the class to correct, then confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

5A.context: Community – how we live: a moneyless community, the phrasal verbs its founder uses, and a phone call about shared housing

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 80 Listening ex A–D and the article How We Live returns – audio track 7.5 (interview with Callum Castling)

Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 86 the highlighted sentences in the article / SB p. 87 Grammar ex A–B, D; Speaking ex A–B / Grammar Hub p. 137 ex A–B (8.1 Past modals of deduction, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 151 (8.1 – the answer to the Hopkinsville goblin case)
Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 88 Listening ex A–D – audio track 8.1 (interview with Phillip Norris on myths and legends); Vocabulary ex A (Word families – the table)

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.)
