s11.name: Upper-intermediate · Empower B2
s11.book: Cambridge English Empower B2 Upper Intermediate, 1st edition (Cambridge, 2015)
s11.sources:
Doff, A., Thaine, C., Puchta, H., Stranks, J. & Lewis-Jones, P. (2015) Cambridge English Empower B2 Upper Intermediate Student’s Book. Cambridge University Press.
Cambridge English Empower B2 Upper Intermediate Teacher’s Book (2015). Cambridge University Press.
McLarty, R. (2015) Cambridge English Empower B2 Upper Intermediate Workbook. Cambridge University Press.

1A.context: Outstanding people – taking on a challenge, and Becky’s first day at the café

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using eight verbs and phrases for trying and succeeding – give up, manage to, keep to, keep it up, work out, have a go at, try out, make an effort – to talk about challenges they have taken on themselves.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for the main point and for specific information in a podcast about the 30-day challenge.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 11 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.10 (podcast: Alison and the 30-day challenge) / SB p. 12 Vocabulary ex 2a–2d – audio track 1.11 / Workbook p. 5 Vocabulary ex 2a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Write A CHALLENGE on the board and give pairs one minute to agree a definition and one example; take two or three. Then books open at p.11: photos a–c, and the short box The 30-day challenge. Pairs read it and answer question 2 only – why might thirty days give you a better chance of succeeding? – and you take one answer. That is enough context; the podcast is the next stage.
stages.avoid: Question 1 under the photos asks about activities they have taken up and how successful they were. It is the freer practice in different clothes, so leave it for the end of the lesson rather than spending the vocabulary on it now.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about challenges

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 1b with track 1.10: three possible main points, and they tick the one Alison makes. Read the three aloud before you press play, one play, pair check, confirm (it is 3). Then ex 1c: Alison’s seminar notes with six gaps, one or two words each. Give them a silent minute to read the notes first, play the track once more, pair check, then answers on the board. Keep it brisk: the lesson is the vocabulary and you want ten minutes of this, not twenty.
stages.avoid: Do not explain give up, keep to or make an effort if they come up while checking the notes. Those are the target language and the next two stages exist to teach them. A nod and move on.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for the main point

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ask what Alison said about starting something new and sticking with it or not; prompt with give, keep and make if nothing comes. Then p.12 ex 2a: eight sentences from the podcast, gapped, and the nine words and phrases in the box. Alone, then pairs, then track 1.11 to check – the recording reads the completed sentences, so they hear each phrase in its sentence. Confirm the answers on the board and leave the sentences up: the clarification works from them.
stages.aim: To focus students on the phrases about trying and succeeding

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 2b first, in pairs: five meanings – succeed, stop trying, not stop trying, try hard, try to see if it works – matched to the phrases. That settles most of the meaning, so spend the time on what the matching cannot give them. Form: manage to takes a verb, keep to takes a noun (keep to a diet, keep to a plan), keep it up carries the pronoun inside it, have a go at takes -ing, try out splits round its object (try it out), make an effort is a fixed noun phrase, work out here has no object – it worked out, it didn’t work out. Concept-check the two pairs they confuse: keep it up versus keep to, and manage to versus work out (who is doing the trying?). Pronunciation: the stress on the particle – keep it UP, work OUT, give UP – and the weak have a GO at. Drill the sentences from ex 2a, not single words.
stages.avoid: Nine phrases are in the box and eight sentences, which is the top of what a slot holds. If you are running late, treat successfully as a passive item: it is the adverb they already know, and the practice does not need it.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the phrases

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2c on p.12: three half-sentences about 30-day challenges to finish with a phrase from 2a and their own idea – there is more than one right answer, so take two or three endings for each. Then Workbook p.5 Vocabulary ex 2a: six picture sentences, one phrase each from a box of seven, one extra – Sandra at the gym, Simon’s lemon cake, fast food, the Smiths’ kitchen table, the diet. Alone, pair check, and only the disputed ones in open class.
stages.avoid: Workbook p.5 ex 2b on the same page is nine more gaps with a different box. It is not on your card and it is where the time goes if you let it: 2a and stop.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the phrases

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 2d: groups of three or four tell each other about a time when they found something difficult but didn’t give up, made a real effort, had a go at something unusual, did something that worked out, or tried something that didn’t. Model one yourself first – the Teacher’s Book has a driving-test story and your own is better – so they hear two or three of the phrases inside one story. Six minutes talking while you listen with a pen. Then three minutes: one story the room should hear, and three sentences from your notes on the board, right and wrong mixed, for pairs to sort before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about a challenge of their own

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have revised the form of direct questions – auxiliary before the subject, subject questions with no auxiliary, the preposition at the end – and used them to interview a partner about a challenge.
slots.sub: To give students practice in reading for gist and for detail in three interviews about 30-day challenges.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 12 Reading ex 3a–3b / SB p. 13 ex 3c–3d – audio track 1.12 (the three interviews), Grammar ex 4a–4c, 4d (role-play) / Grammar Focus SB p. 134 (1B, the rules) and p. 135 ex a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p.12: the three challenges in the margin – Farah has stopped eating meat, Mona draws something every day, Steve is learning Italian. Pairs decide who will find it easy and who will find it hard, and whether they would try any of the three. One minute of answers in open class, no confirming: the reading does that.
stages.avoid: The class did the 30-day challenge podcast last lesson, so do not rebuild the idea from scratch. One sentence – you remember the thirty days – and straight to the three people.
stages.aim: To get students guessing who will find their challenge hard

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 3b: they read the three interviews once to check their guesses (Farah easy, Steve difficult, Mona mixed). Then ex 3c on p.13: the five missing questions a–e put back into the interviews – which question does each answer fit? Alone, then pairs, then track 1.12 to check. This is reading for detail, but it is also where they meet the target language, so do not take answers before the track: let the recording confirm it.
stages.avoid: Seven minutes for both tasks. If the gist read drifts into a line-by-line discussion of vegetarianism, you have started a reading lesson; the grammar has not begun yet.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the interviews

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Use the Teacher’s Book’s own device. Three or four true statements about yourself on the board – I haven’t had a coffee today, I ate a chocolate bar for breakfast, my friend in New York emailed me this morning – and the first word of the question for each (Have…, What…, Who…). Students come up and complete the questions. Then ex 4a: the four rules about questions, read together, and in pairs they find an example of each in the interviews and in 3c. Check: rule 2 is What made you decide…, rule 3 is Who do you practise with?, rule 4 is Do you think you’ll carry on…?
stages.aim: To focus students on the question forms

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 4b and 4c, in pairs then confirmed: a neutral question against a negative one that expects yes (Didn’t you see her?), and which versus what for a limited choice against an open one. Then the clarification proper on the board, from their examples: auxiliary before subject, and do/did when there is none; the subject question keeps statement order and takes no auxiliary – Who spoke to you?, never Who did speak; the preposition sits at the end – Who do you practise with? Concept-check the subject question with one pair: Who did you phone? (you phoned) against Who phoned you? (they phoned). Pronunciation: drill four of the questions from 3c at speed, the auxiliary weak – did you /dɪdʒə/, do you think – and the fall at the end of a wh- question. Grammar Focus p.134 (1B) is the reference they can read after.
stages.avoid: Keep to direct questions. Indirect questions (Can you tell me…) are on p.134 too and in Grammar Focus ex c, but they are not in the interviews and they are a second structure; forty-five minutes holds one.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the question forms

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus p.135 (1B) ex a: seven questions, two options each – are we / we are, didn’t you, Who from?, What happened – alone, then compared, then the disputed ones only. Then ex b: six statements with an underlined part, and they write the question that asks about it – Who discovered pulsars? is done for them. Make them read their questions aloud to a partner, because word order has to pass through the mouth, not only the pen.
stages.avoid: Ex c on the same page is the indirect questions. Stop at b.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the question forms

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4d on p.13: pairs choose one of the three interviews and role-play it – A interviews, B answers with their own ideas – and A must add three questions of their own beyond the ones in the text. Then they swap: a second interview, B asking. Give them two minutes first to write their extra questions down, because that is where the grammar is used. Six minutes of interviewing while you note questions, good and wrong. Close with three questions you heard, written up exactly as they were said; pairs decide which one is right and fix the other two.
stages.avoid: Part 5 Speaking at the bottom of p.13 is three challenges of their own. It is not on your card: 4d gives the practice and the day already has a speaking lesson.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice in an interview role play

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have improved their spoken fluency explaining a process they know well to a partner, emphasizing what matters and checking the partner has followed.
slots.sub: To introduce three expressions for emphasizing the important points of an explanation (the most important thing is…, remember to always…, another thing to remember is…) and four questions for checking understanding.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 15 Listening ex 4a–4c – audio track 1.19 (Part 3: Sam shows Becky the café) / Useful language ex 5a–5f – audio tracks 1.21, 1.22 / ex 5g–5h (role-play) / Speaking ex 6a–6c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The photos on p.15: a café, a young woman, a man at the counter. Who are they, and where is she? Tell them it is Becky’s first day at her cousin Sam’s café, then ask what might be hard about a first day in a café and what someone would have to explain to you. Two or three ideas on the board – you will come back to them.
stages.avoid: Pages 14 and the first two parts of the story are not on your card. One sentence of back-story – her cousin’s café, her first day – is all they need.
stages.aim: To set the scene of Becky's first day

stages.name: Listening as a model
stages.todo: Ex 4a with track 1.19 (Part 3 of the video, as audio): one of two summaries – she learns how to handle food and meets a customer. Play once, confirm, and ask whether any of their board ideas came up. Then ex 4b, the four questions – what does Sam explain, what does Phil do, why JK, who is Emma – on a second play, pair check, quick answers. Finish with ex 4c in pairs for one minute: will Becky be good at the job? This is the model: they have now heard a process being explained before they do it.
stages.avoid: Part 4 (ex 4d–4e, track 1.20) is Tom and Becky at the counter talking about the wedding. It is not about explaining anything, so it is not on your card. Two plays of Part 3 and move on.
stages.aim: To give students a model of explaining how to do something

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 5a: Sam’s three expressions, words jumbled – the most important thing is, remember to always, another thing to remember is. Alone, then track 1.21 to check. Ex 5c asks why he uses them: to emphasize important points, and that is the meaning done. Form: all three sit at the front of the sentence and take a clause or an imperative after them. Then ex 5d: the four checking questions completed from the box – Is that clear? Do you understand what I mean? Have you got that? Do you get the idea? Then ex 5e, track 1.22: each question said two ways, which is friendly, and does the voice go up or down – up is friendly. Ex 5f: drill all four, rising, until the room sounds polite rather than threatening. Board the seven and leave them up.
stages.avoid: This is the sub aim, so it gets eleven minutes and a drill. But it is the sub aim: if the clarification runs to twenty minutes the speaking has lost its time, and the speaking is what you are assessed on today.
stages.aim: To give students the phrases for explaining a process

stages.name: Speaking task 1 – role-play
stages.todo: Ex 5g: three more things Sam could explain to Becky – clearing a table when a customer leaves, the coffee machine at closing time, things customers leave behind. Pairs prepare what Sam says, with the three expressions, and what Becky says to show she has followed. Then ex 5h: they act it, swap roles, act it again. Three minutes’ preparation, four of talking. Keep it short; it is the warm-up for the real task.
stages.aim: To give students practice explaining in a role play

stages.name: Speaking task 2 – explain a process
stages.todo: Ex 6a: each student picks a process they really know – a sport or hobby, a machine or device, how to make or cook something. Ex 6b: three minutes alone to plan it, deciding which two points matter most (that is where the emphasizing phrases go) and where they will check. Then ex 6c in new pairs: take turns explaining, and the listener must ask at least two questions. Eight minutes of talk. Walk round with a pen: fluency first, the seven phrases second, and anything else wrong third.
stages.avoid: If they choose something nobody could explain in four minutes – how to play chess – the task collapses. Set a size when you set the task: a process with four or five steps.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice explaining a process they know

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first: two listeners tell the room one process they could now do, in two sentences. Then language: four lines from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, at least one a checking question with the wrong intonation to say aloud. Pairs sort, you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

1B.context: Modern life and survival – a day without technology, then getting into trouble and getting out of it

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have written a short article about a week without a device they depend on, organized the way the model is – dependency, the experience, an evaluation – and sequenced with the model’s linking phrases.
slots.sub: To introduce six comment adverbs – inevitably, not surprisingly, naturally, strangely, predictably, undoubtedly – and where they sit in a sentence.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 16 ex 1a–1b (the survey results only; the listening is not played) / SB p. 16–17 Reading ex 2a–2b (Tech free!), Writing Skills ex 3a–3f, Writing ex 4a–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: everyone writes down the one gadget they could least do without and two reasons. Compare in pairs, take the most popular in open class. Then p.16 ex 1a, the two questions – how much do you depend on technology, which parts of it make life easier – for a minute in the same pairs.
stages.avoid: Ex 1c–1g on p.16 is a listening about Gitta and Derek and it is not on your card. The only thing you want from the top of p.16 is the survey box.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about the gadgets they depend on

stages.name: Preparing to write – the model
stages.todo: Ex 1b: pairs list the five things they hate most about modern life, you collect the class’s top three on the board, then they read the survey box – self-service check-outs, sales calls, selfies, slow internet, battery life – and say whether they agree. Then the model: p.17, Tech free!. Ex 2a, one question, two minutes: is anything from the survey mentioned? (the self-service check-out). Then ex 2b, seven true-or-false sentences, read in detail, alone, then pairs. Confirm quickly: 2, 4 and 6 are false.
stages.avoid: Ten minutes covers the survey and both reads. This is the model for the writing, not a reading lesson: if the true-or-false check becomes a discussion of each line, the writing stage shrinks.
stages.aim: To give students a model article to read

stages.name: Noticing the organisation
stages.todo: Ex 3a: three summaries of how Sam organizes his article; pairs choose – it is 2: his level of dependency, his day, then an evaluation. Ex 3b: how does he get attention at the start? A direct question to the reader. Put the three-part shape on the board, because it is the plan they will write to.
stages.aim: To focus students on how the article is organized

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3c, alone: underline the phrase that sequences each of paragraphs 2–5 (The first thing…, After breakfast, Then, Afterwards) and the phrase that signals the summary (All in all). Point out that after needs a noun and afterwards does not. Then ex 3d: Inevitably is the example – the writer saying this was always going to happen – and they find five more: Not surprisingly, Naturally, Strangely, Predictably, Undoubtedly. Elicit the position: the front of the clause, with a comma. Ex 3e in pairs: add amazingly, naturally, inevitably, (not) surprisingly to the four sentence pairs; more than one works. Drill the six adverbs once for the stress – inEVitably, preDICTably, unDOUBTedly.
stages.aim: To give students the sequencing language from the model

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4a: a week without one device, from the survey, the article or their own life; two minutes of notes. Ex 4b: one minute telling a partner the idea, so the content exists before they write. Then ex 4c: write the article, in silence, to the three-part plan on the board, with at least two of the sequencing phrases and two comment adverbs. Eleven minutes of writing; you walk round and answer questions at the desk.
stages.avoid: Set a length – ten to twelve sentences – or the strong writers will still be on paragraph one when the time ends. And no dictionaries: the language they need is on the board.
stages.aim: To give students practice in writing an article

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: First ex 3f, thirty seconds in pairs: which of the seven pieces of advice is wrong? (5 – be as objective as possible; an article wants opinions). Then ex 4d: swap with a new partner, read, and answer the book’s questions – does it follow the advice, is it interesting, what would make it more so. One comment each. Collect the articles and write on them before the next lesson.
stages.avoid: Four minutes is one reader’s comment, not a correction session. Save the language errors for the written feedback.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the writing

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using ten expressions with get – get away, get to do, couldn’t get over, get into trouble, get hold of, get swept away, not get anywhere, get the feeling, get someone’s attention, get over it – to talk about getting into difficulty and out of it.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for gist and for the order of events in a story about a surfing accident.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 20 Listening ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.25 (Abby’s surfing story) / SB p. 20 Vocabulary ex 2a–2b (not 2c)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s own lead-in, books closed: elicit two or three places it might be dangerous to visit – the jungle, the desert, the open sea – pick one, and pairs choose the five things they would take to survive there. Thirty seconds of reasons in open class. Then p.20 ex 1a: pictures a–d, and what they would be most afraid of in each one.
stages.aim: To get students talking about dangerous places

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 1b with track 1.25: which picture is being described, and where was the holiday – d, South Africa. One play, pair check, confirm. Then ex 1c: events a–h numbered in the order they happened, from buying a surfboard to being rescued. Read the eight aloud first, play once more, pause after three or four if they are struggling, pair check, answers on the board. Two plays and that is the budget.
stages.avoid: If get into trouble or get hold of come up while checking the order, leave them. The next two stages teach them; the listening is the way in.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist and order

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Write get on the board and two sentences with uses they already have – I got to know Sandra well, I got the time wrong. Ask what Abby and Rob said with get; take whatever they remember and board it. Then ex 2a: the ten sentences from the conversation, expressions in bold, matched to meanings a–j. Pairs, with the sentences, because the context decides it. Check quickly and leave the ten up.
stages.aim: To focus students on the expressions with get

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 2a has done the meaning; spend the eleven minutes on what it leaves. The pair that trips them: couldn’t get over (surprise – I still can’t believe it) and got over it (recovered). Concept-check both with Abby: did she recover from the bad experience? did she believe how strong the waves were? Then form, which is where the errors live: get to + verb (I’ll get to do it), get hold of + noun, get into trouble with no article, get someone’s attention with the possessive inside, get swept away with no object (the wave did it), not get anywhere mostly in the negative. Pronunciation: get links to a vowel after it – get_over, get_into, get_anywhere, get_away – and the stress falls on the content word, not on get. Drill the ten sentences from 2a.
stages.avoid: Ten expressions is the cap, and ex 2c sends them to Vocabulary Focus on p.155 for eight more. That page is not on your card. Stop at ten.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the get expressions

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2b: ten sentences, one word in each gap, all ten expressions in the right form – ran out to get the policeman’s attention, soon got over the experience, got into trouble skiing off the trail. Alone, then pairs, then hand out a paper key rather than reading ten answers aloud, and take only the ones they disagreed on. Ask two of them for the base form of what they wrote, so the past forms do not hide the expression.
stages.avoid: The Workbook page for 2A mixes in the Vocabulary Focus expressions (get rid of, get on my nerves, get through), so it does not fit this lesson. The ten gaps in 2b are the controlled practice.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the expressions

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Six personal questions on a slip, one expression in each: Have you ever got into trouble for breaking a rule? How would you get someone’s attention if you were stuck in a lift? What is something you couldn’t get over when you first saw it? When did you last feel you weren’t getting anywhere with something? Where would you most like to get away to? What have you always wanted to get to do? New pairs, five minutes, ask and answer and ask one more. Walk round with a pen. Then four minutes: one answer the room should hear, and two errors with get read aloud as you heard them – the class gives you the correction before anything goes on the board.
stages.avoid: Write the slip before the lesson, not on the board during it. Six questions on the board is three minutes of silence while they copy.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice answering personal questions

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have revised the four narrative tenses – past simple, past continuous, past perfect simple and past perfect continuous – and used them to tell a survival story, with the weight on when the past perfect continuous is the one to choose.
slots.sub: To give students practice in reading an article about a diver lost at sea for gist and for specific numbers.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 21 Reading ex 3a–3b (Lost at sea) / SB p. 22 Grammar ex 4a–4b – audio track 1.29, ex 4d–4g (Eric and Ricky), Speaking ex 5a–5b / Grammar Focus SB p. 136 (2A, the rules – reference only)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Has anyone been scuba diving, and how deep? Would the rest like to? Then one question for the room: what can go wrong for a diver? Three or four dangers on the board – you will check them against the text. Keep the surfing story from the last lesson in view in one line: Abby got into trouble in the water; this man had it worse.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about what can go wrong for a diver

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Pre-teach three words only, with a sentence each: tide, vision (what he thought he saw), nap. Then p.21 ex 3a: they read the first paragraph to see if his problem is one on the board, then the whole article for the two questions – how long was he in the water (four days and three nights) and what he had to overcome (currents, no food or water, sunburn). Then ex 3b in pairs, from memory: what do 200 metres, seven kilometres, the fourth day, three hours, half a kilometre, the third day refer to – a sentence each, checked against the text. Confirm in open class.
stages.avoid: Ex 3c, the four discussion questions, is where the time goes. It is not on your card: the text is the way in to the grammar, and you have eight minutes for it, not twenty.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the story

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 4a: the verbs in bold in Lost at sea – came to the surface, had been diving, had decided, was wearing – matched to uses a–d. Pairs, with the text. Then students come up and write the four verbs on the board with the tense name next to each; you confirm the matching (1 d, 2 c, 3 a, 4 b).
stages.aim: To focus students on the narrative tenses in the story

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: A timeline from the four board sentences: the main events in the past simple, the background in progress in the past continuous, and the two past perfects before the main events. Give the weight to the pair that is new at this level: past perfect simple for an earlier completed action and its result (he had decided to swim alone), past perfect continuous for an earlier activity and its duration or effect (he had been diving for sea urchins). Concept-check with one pair: he had read the book / he had been reading the book – did he finish? Watch for the two errors you will get: the past simple where the continuous belongs (I arrived, Jacky played) and the present of be in a past story (I am walking home when…). Then ex 4b with track 1.29: which verb is stressed (the main verb) and how had been sounds – /hədbɪn/. Play again and drill the three sentences, then two more of your own with the same rhythm. Grammar Focus p.136 is the reference they read after the lesson.
stages.avoid: Four tenses is a revision lesson, not four presentations. Past simple and past continuous need a sentence each on the board and no more; the ten minutes belong to the two past perfects.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the narrative tenses

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: The pictures on p.22: where are the two men and what is their problem? Then ex 4d: A reads about Eric Le Marque, B about Ricky Megee, each answering the two questions – where, and does he survive. Ex 4e, alone: underline the correct verb in the five choices in their text; pair A with another A to check before you confirm (Eric: was going, came, remembered, ’d seen, had been searching; Ricky: had been living, was driving, stopped, had eaten, ’d lost). Then ex 4f–4g: two minutes of notes, and they tell their original partner the story they read, in their own words, with the tenses. The retelling is where you hear whether the past perfect has arrived.
stages.avoid: The underlining alone is recognition, not practice. The retelling in 4g is the practice, so do not let the underlining swallow the twelve minutes.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the tenses

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 5a: a dangerous situation they or someone they know was in, or one from a book or film; two minutes of notes against the book’s prompts – where and when, who, the background, the events, the outcome. Ex 5b in new pairs: tell it, with at least one past perfect, and the listener asks two questions. Four minutes. Then two minutes of feedback: one story for the room, and a slip for each pair with one sentence from the stories and a tense wrong in it, to fix and read back.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice telling a story of danger

2A.context: Survival – surviving an animal attack, a tiger’s revenge, and agreeing with a friend

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for detail in a radio interview about The Tiger, the true story of a hunter and a Siberian tiger.
slots.sub: To clarify the words for animals and the environment the interview carries – at risk, creature, endangered, environment, extinct, habitat, hunt, natural, protected, rare, species.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 25 Listening and Vocabulary ex 3a–3e – audio tracks 1.34 (part one), 1.35 (part two) / ex 3f–3g – audio track 1.36

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A story or film with an animal as the main character – what was it, and did they like it? Pairs for one minute, two answers in open class. Then the book cover on p.25: what is the animal, and what does the title Vengeance and Survival suggest?
stages.aim: To get students talking about stories with animals

stages.name: Prediction and pre-teaching
stages.todo: Ex 3a: the nine words in the box – tiger, mattress, attacked, hut, forest, wounded, shot, killed, boots – and pairs build the story of the hunter and the tiger from them. Mattress and wounded will stop them, so give those two before they start: a sentence each. Three minutes of inventing, then each pair tells its story in two sentences and the class votes on the likeliest. Then one more word for the listening: drag – pull something heavy along the ground.
stages.avoid: The source document sent you to the Workbook for vocabulary support; the support is in the Teacher’s Book notes, not the Workbook, and three words is the budget. The vocabulary set comes later, after the listening.
stages.aim: To have students predict the story and clear the words

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3b with track 1.34, the first part of the interview: was the story like yours? One play, pairs compare their version with Miles’s, and the room decides whose guess came closest. Keep the feedback to the story itself – the tiger waited two days, dragged the mattress out, left only the boots.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3c: four questions, and which one Miles does not answer. They guess first from the first play, then track 1.34 again to check (it is 3 – how many people have been killed). Then ex 3d with track 1.35, the second part: five topics, tick the ones he talks about. Read the five aloud first, one play, pair check, confirm (3 and 4). Three plays in all across the two stages, and that is the whole budget.
stages.avoid: Do not play part two twice. Ex 3e asks what Miles would think, and they answer that from what they remember, not from a fourth hearing.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Vocabulary from the listening
stages.todo: Ex 3f: the eleven words in the box sorted into animals and places – the box is on paper, cut up, and pairs stick each word under ANIMALS or PLACES on the board; some go under both (at risk, protected). Then meaning where it is needed: endangered against extinct (still alive, or gone?), species against creature (a kind, or one animal?), habitat against environment. Stress on enDANgered, exTINCT, HABitat, SPEcies – drill them. Then ex 3g, alone: six sentences from the interview completed with the words, and track 1.36 to check.
stages.avoid: The box is the book’s set and it is eleven. Treat natural and protected as words they have, and spend the time on the other nine.
stages.aim: To focus students on the words from the listening

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 3e: five statements – it was right to kill the tiger, the tiger was only behaving naturally, humans are more dangerous – and alone they write Yes or No for whether Miles would agree. Then groups of three or four: do they agree with Miles, and why? Six minutes of talking, with the eleven words in sight on the board. Then three minutes: one position from each group, and the three strongest sentences you heard, boarded as they were said, for the class to say what makes each one good.
stages.avoid: Section 4 Speaking on p.25, advice to a visitor, uses the if/unless box from the grammar lesson that follows and is forty minutes on its own. It is not on your card.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to respond to the story

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have revised future time clauses and conditionals with if, unless, as long as, provided, as soon as and in case – a present tense in the clause, will or an imperative in the main clause – and used them to give advice on surviving a wild animal.
slots.sub: To give students practice in reading a survival guide for gist and for detail.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 23 Reading ex 1a–1d (How to survive an animal attack) / SB p. 24 Grammar ex 2a–2b, 2d / Grammar Focus SB p. 136 (2B, the rules) and p. 137 ex a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Which animal are you most afraid of, and why? Pairs, one minute, then three answers in open class and let the room react. Then p.23 ex 1b: pictures a–e – a bear, a wolf, a shark, a tarantula, a crocodile – and in the same pairs, which is the most dangerous and which the least. Take a vote, board it, and do not confirm.
stages.avoid: Ex 1a, the three wild places, is a second lead-in. One is enough; the text is waiting.
stages.aim: To get students talking about dangerous animals

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Pre-teach two words with a sentence each, no more: harmless and weapon. Ex 1c: read once to check the vote – tigers and crocodiles the most dangerous, tarantulas the least. Two minutes, no dictionaries. Then ex 1d: six sentences, tick the true ones, read in detail. Alone, pairs, confirm (1, 2, 4, 5). Ex 1e, thirty seconds in open class: what kind of text is it? Written for amusement, which is why the examples are so quotable.
stages.avoid: Nine minutes for the text and no more. Ex 1f and the answers on p.127 are a separate activity and not on your card. The grammar has not started yet.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the text

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s device: five sentence beginnings on the board – Bears will only fight if…, They won’t attack people unless…, Bears will usually move away as soon as…, Provided you stay absolutely still, the bear…, As long as you don’t panic, a shark… – and pairs finish them from memory. Exact words do not matter; the verb forms do, and you are listening for them. Then p.24 ex 2a: the five sentences in print, and questions a–e in pairs. Then ex 2b: one more example of as long as, unless and provided from the text, alone.
stages.aim: To focus students on the conjunctions in the text

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Work from their answers to 2a. Meaning on the board as a set: unless = if not; provided and as long as = only if; as soon as = immediately after; in case = because something might happen (take a stick in case you meet one – the text has it). Concept-check the two that go wrong: unless (Sharks won’t attack unless they think you’re food – do they attack if they don’t? no) and in case against if (take tablets in case you get bitten – do you take them before or after?). Form, which is the whole point of the lesson: a present tense after the conjunction, will or an imperative in the other half, and never will in the if-clause. Watch for when in place of if: When the bear comes toward you… means it will. Pronunciation: the conjunctions are unstressed and run together – as soon as /əzˈsuːnəz/, as long as, provided – and ’ll is swallowed before the verb. Drill three of the sentences from 2a. Grammar Focus p.136 (2B) is the reference they read after.
stages.avoid: The first conditional is not new at this level; the conjunctions are. If you present if from scratch you will have taught them what they know and skipped what they do not.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the conjunctions

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus p.137 (2B) ex a first: seven sentences, tick the correct ones and correct the rest – when we’ll be on holiday, unless you don’t study, in case it’ll get damaged. Alone, pair check, and ask for the reason with each correction. Then ex b: eight pairs of sentences joined with the word in brackets, which is the harder half because they have to choose the clause the present tense goes in. Take the disputed ones only.
stages.avoid: Ex c on p.137 is 2A, narrative tenses, done yesterday. Stop at b.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the conjunctions

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 2d on p.24: four sentence beginnings – Sharks won’t attack you unless…, Wolves will only attack if…, Tarantulas won’t bite you provided…, If you hit a crocodile on the nose… – finished with their own ideas, then compared in groups of three, who choose the best ending for each. Then one more of their own for an animal from their country, with as soon as or in case. Six minutes while you listen with a pen. Then three minutes: the best endings read out, and two of the wrong ones you heard said back with a questioning intonation – the room corrects them aloud.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice finishing sentences about animals

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced agreeing with what someone says by repeating it with a question tag and a fresh adjective – Yes, it’s lovely, isn’t it? / No, they weren’t helpful, were they? – said with a falling tone.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency talking about people, places and films they know.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 26 Listening ex 1a–1d – audio track 1.37 (Part 1: Becky and Tessa take photos) / Conversation Skills ex 2a–2e / Pronunciation ex 3a – audio track 1.38, ex 3b–3c / Workbook p. 12 Conversation Skills ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.26: do you like taking photos, what makes a good one, are you good at it? Pairs, two minutes, then two answers for the room. Then ex 1b, the photo: what is Becky doing, and why does she need Tessa? Take guesses and do not confirm.
stages.aim: To get students talking about photos

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 1c with track 1.37 (Part 1 of the video, as audio): check the guesses – she is measuring the tripod, and it is difficult. Then ex 1d: four true-or-false sentences, read first, second play, pair check, confirm (2 is false). That is the way in; the language is next.
stages.avoid: This is a function lesson and the recording is two minutes long. Two plays, no third.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist and detail

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 2a: Becky says It’s quite difficult – how does Tessa answer? Play the line again if they did not catch it: Yeah, it’s hard, isn’t it? Board it. Then ex 2b, the two choices – the tag agrees, and a different adjective is more interesting – and ex 2c, alone: the two tags completed (isn’t she, were they). Pairs compare.
stages.aim: To focus students on question tags for agreeing

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 2d, the rule: a positive statement takes a negative tag and a negative one a positive tag. Form on the board from their three examples: the auxiliary comes back in the tag – is / isn’t, were / weren’t, do / don’t – and the subject becomes a pronoun. Meaning: this is agreeing, not asking; the speaker already knows. Ex 3a with track 1.38 makes that audible – does the tone go up or down on the tag? Down, because it is not a question. Contrast it yourself once: the same tag said rising is a real question. Then drill with the Teacher’s Book’s prompts – It’s a great camera… / She wants to be a photographer… / He hasn’t published a book… – the class supplying the tag, falling, and then a few individually. Finish with the adjective swap: lovely becomes charming, difficult becomes hard, and that is what makes the reply sound like a friend rather than an echo.
stages.avoid: Tags are the trainee’s trap because every auxiliary in English is in play. Keep the clarification to the four auxiliaries in the material – be, do, have, modal – and resist the full table. The controlled practice has eight tags, which is plenty.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and intonation of question tags

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.12 Conversation Skills ex 1a: Mike and Lucy at the beach, eight tags from a box of nine – isn’t, shall, aren’t, didn’t, did, haven’t, could, wasn’t, don’t. Alone, pair check, paper key; ask which ones they still want explained. Then SB p.26 ex 2e, in pairs: four exchanges completed with an adjective from the box (soaking, breathtaking, welcoming, worried) and the tag. Ex 3b: they read the four exchanges aloud to each other, tag falling.
stages.avoid: Ex 1b in the Workbook plays the Workbook’s own recording to check. Use a paper key instead; the only recordings on your card are the Student’s Book’s.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of question tags

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 3c: in new pairs they talk about people and things they both know – a person, a café, a film, a car – and the listener agrees each time with a tag and a stronger adjective from the five pairs: amusing / funny, frightening / terrifying, cheerful / happy, exhausting / tiring, interesting / fascinating. Six minutes, swapping roles halfway, while you listen for the tag, the tone and the adjective. Then four minutes: one exchange the room should hear, and three tags from your notes said by you with the wrong tone, for the class to say back with the right one.
stages.avoid: Section 2 Useful language on p.27, giving compliments, is the second function in this lesson. It is not on your card: one function, four to six exponents, forty-five minutes.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice agreeing with question tags

2B.context: Survival and talent – lost in a Canadian forest, a safety leaflet, and what it takes to learn something well

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for detail in Luiza’s story of getting lost in a Canadian forest, and predicted how it ends before they hear it.
slots.sub: To recycle four of the expressions with get from 2A as Luiza uses them – got in trouble, wasn’t getting anywhere, get its attention, couldn’t get over.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 28 Speaking and Listening ex 1a–1g – audio tracks 1.41 (part one), 1.42 (part two)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed, LOST on the board, and thirty seconds on a time you got lost yourself. Then pairs: a time they were lost – as a child, as a tourist, on a walk – where, why, and what happened. Two stories for the room. Then p.28 ex 1a, the three questions about the last natural place they went to, one minute.
stages.aim: To get students talking about getting lost

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three words the story needs and does not explain: short cut, clearing, forest ranger. A sentence or a quick board sketch for each – the clearing is a drawing, not a definition – and let them give you the word. One concept question each and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach the get expressions. They are the sub aim and they come out of the text at the end; the class met them in 2A.
stages.aim: To clear the three words the story needs

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b with track 1.41: which natural environment, and what was the trouble she got in – a national park in Canada, and she got lost. Read the two questions first, one play, pair check, confirm. Keep it to the two answers.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c: three questions – why she got lost (a short cut), how she chose a direction (the sun sets in the west), what led her to the clearing (a stream). They try from memory first, then track 1.41 again to check. Pairs compare, confirm.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for detail

stages.name: Prediction and part two
stages.todo: Ex 1d: read them her last line – I suddenly had this strange feeling I was not alone – and groups of three decide what happened next, in two sentences. Regroup so each new group has one member from each old one, and they compare endings; the room votes on the likeliest. Then ex 1e with track 1.42: who was closest? Then ex 1f, four true-or-false sentences, read first, second play of part two, pair check, confirm (2 and 3 are false).
stages.avoid: Two plays of part two and no more. The prediction is the stage that makes them want to listen; if you cut it to save time you have cut the wrong thing.
stages.aim: To have students predict how the story ends

stages.name: Response and language from the story
stages.todo: First the language, three minutes: four phrases from the story on the board with get gapped – I … in trouble in the forest, I wasn’t … anywhere, it flew away before I could … its attention, what I couldn’t … over – and pairs complete them from memory. They met all four in 2A; this is a second outing, not a lesson. Then ex 1g: what would you have done in Luiza’s situation, and then their own – a time they were lost or in real difficulty, told to a group of three with at least two of the four phrases. Six minutes while you listen. Then three minutes: one story the room should hear, and one get expression that went wrong, reformulated by the class before you give the line.
stages.avoid: They will stumble on would have done. It is not today’s language – note it, do not teach it.
stages.aim: To focus students on the language and respond to the story

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have written a short safety leaflet with headings, modeled on Be wise and survive, for a situation of their choice.
slots.sub: To revise the four imperative forms a leaflet uses – positive, negative, with always or never, and if + present tense + imperative.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 28 Reading ex 2a–2c / SB p. 29 (Be wise and survive), Writing Skills ex 3a–3c, Writing ex 4a–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One line back to Luiza from the last lesson – she took a short cut and lost four hours – then p.28 ex 2a: you are going hiking in a forest; what do you need to remember to stay safe? Pairs list five things, you collect them on the board. Leave the list up: the leaflet will confirm or add to it.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about safety in a forest

stages.name: Preparing to write – the model
stages.todo: Ex 2b: read Be wise and survive on p.29 once, quickly – are your ideas in it? – then the three headings into gaps a–c, one heading spare (Preparation, In the forest, If you get lost). Ask why headings matter in a leaflet. Then ex 2c, the four questions – what to take, what not to do, food and drink, move or stay – read in detail, alone, then pairs, then confirm. Ten minutes for both reads.
stages.avoid: This is the model, not a reading lesson. If the detail questions turn into a discussion of each tip, the writing time is gone.
stages.aim: To give students a model leaflet to read

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3a: the four verb forms the leaflet runs on – positive imperative, negative imperative, always or never plus imperative, if plus present tense plus imperative – and pairs find one more example of each in the text. Ex 3b: what are they for? Advice, made clear and direct. Then ex 3c, alone: six sentences, three of them wrong – Not eat any plants, If you will hear a rescue team, Always carries – corrected. Pairs compare, confirm. The three errors are the three you will see in their leaflets, so name them on the board.
stages.aim: To give students the verb forms the leaflet uses

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4a: one of the four situations – camping in a forest, backpacking abroad, swimming in the sea, hiking in the mountains – and three minutes in pairs noting six to eight pieces of advice. Then ex 4b, alone and in silence: the leaflet, with two or three headings, the four imperative forms from 3a at least once each, and the information clear and direct. Twelve minutes of writing; you walk round and answer at the desk.
stages.avoid: Set the size – eight to ten guidelines under two or three headings – or they will write an essay. A leaflet is short, and that is the point of it.
stages.aim: To give students practice in writing a safety leaflet

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4c: swap with a partner who chose a different situation, with a three-line checklist on the board – headings? all four forms? clear and direct? – and one suggested improvement each. Then ex 4d: leaflets passed round the room for two minutes, and the class names the clearest and the most useful. Collect them and write on them before the next lesson.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the writing

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using seven adjectives for ability and achievement – talented, skilled, brilliant, exceptional, outstanding, successful, potential – and the nouns skill, talent, brilliance and ability, with their prepositions, to talk about people they admire.
slots.sub: To give students practice in reading three short texts about learning for gist and for specific answers.
slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 32 Reading ex 2a–2c (Learning to learn) / SB p. 33 Vocabulary ex 3a–3e / Workbook p. 16 Vocabulary ex 2a, 2c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p.32: how long does it take to learn something well, when in the day is best, how much does memory matter? Pairs, two minutes, then one answer to each question in open class. Do not settle anything – the texts answer the three questions, which is the gist task.
stages.avoid: Section 1 Listening at the top of p.32 is a different lesson and not on your card. Start at section 2.
stages.aim: To get students talking about learning well

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 2b: three texts across pp.32–33 – It’s all about rhythm, Give me strength, A question of talent? – matched to the three questions in 2a. Three minutes, headings and first lines only, pair check, confirm. Then ex 2c, two questions only – 3 (natural talent for tennis, do I need to practise?) and 6 (how do I become brilliant, not just good?) – because both send them into A question of talent?, which is where the vocabulary lives. Pre-teach stick with for the others if anyone asks; answers in pairs, confirm.
stages.avoid: All six questions in 2c is a reading lesson and fifteen minutes. Two questions, and the discussion in 2d is not yours. The language has not started yet.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the three texts

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p.33: seven lines from the talent text with an adjective in bold in each, and four questions – which two mean a good level of ability (skilled, talented), which one a good level of achievement (successful), which three a very high level (outstanding, exceptional, brilliant), and is potential now or later (the future). Pairs, then confirm, and board the seven in three groups.
stages.aim: To focus students on the adjectives for ability

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 3b: the noun for each – skill, talent, brilliance, ability – elicited and boarded next to the adjective, and a sentence each. Then ex 3c, the prepositions, in pairs: talented AT, potential TO, talent FOR, ability TO. That is the form, and it is where the errors are: at and for are followed by -ing (talented at playing), to by the verb (the ability to become). Add that potential is a noun here but an adjective elsewhere (a potential problem). Pronunciation: the stress shifts – TALent / TALented, SKILL / SKILLED, BRILLiant / BRILLiance, but aBILity, exCEPtional, outSTANDing, sucCESSful, poTENtial. Drill the adjective with its preposition as one chunk, because that is how it has to come out.
stages.avoid: Outstanding and exceptional are near-synonyms and the practice does not separate them. Teach them as a pair and spend the minutes on the prepositions, which is what the Workbook tests.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the adjectives and nouns

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.16 Vocabulary ex 2a: Mariana and Louis on the writer Daniel Kalder, eight choices between two words – talented or brilliant, ability or potential, successful or exceptional. Alone, pair check, take the disputed ones. Then ex 2c: eight sentences with one mistake each, mostly the preposition – a talent to it, exceptional for their field, skilled for the game, brilliant on ball sports. Alone, then compared, then confirm, with the reason each time.
stages.avoid: Ex 2b in the Workbook plays the Workbook’s recording to check 2a. Use a paper key; there is no track on your card.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the words

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 3d: five people – someone skilled at a sport or an art, someone with a talent for an instrument, someone famous they think is brilliant, someone exceptional in their field, the most successful person they know – two minutes of notes. Then ex 3e in pairs: tell each other, with a reason for each, and the listener asks one question back. Five minutes while you listen with a pen. Then two minutes: one person the room should hear about, and a preposition error from your notes written up with the preposition missing – pairs fill the gap, and you say whether the speaker had it right.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice describing talented people
