1A.context: Questions and answers – extreme job interviews, then making conversation with someone you have just met (File 1A)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist and for detail in the context of ‘extreme’ job interview questions.
slots.sub: To develop students’ ability to work out the meaning of unknown words from context, using the ten highlighted items in the article (demanding, flustered, bizarre, think on your feet, approach …).
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 6 ex 4a–4b (photo and article ‘Extreme interviews’) / SB p. 7 ex 4c–4d, ex 4e – audio track 1.8, ex 4f–4g

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Project the photo on p. 6 with the article covered: an interviewer asking ‘So, what sort of dinosaur would you be?’ Ex 4a in pairs — what is happening here, and would anyone really ask this in a job interview? Take two or three guesses, write the vote on the board (real or not) and leave it there; the gist reading settles it.
stages.aim: To get students interested in the interview question

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the text does not explain: merely (line 11), pioneer (line 19) and stranded (line 16). Elicit each from a short situation — if you are stranded on an island, can you leave? — one concept question each and move on. Headhunter and Silicon Valley are in the glossary, so point at it rather than teaching them.
stages.avoid: Leave the ten highlighted words alone. Guessing them from context is ex 4c–4d and the sub aim of the lesson; if you pre-teach them there is nothing left to guess.
stages.aim: To clear the three words the text does not explain

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 4b: read the article once to answer the question from the lead-in — is the dinosaur question real — and decide how you would answer it. Three minutes, alone, no dictionaries. Quick pair check, then settle the board vote (yes, it is a real interview question) and hear two or three of their dinosaurs.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for gist

stages.name: Reading for detail: words from context
stages.todo: Go through the Guessing the meaning box on p. 6 with them: the words around it, the part of speech, a similar word they know. Demonstrate with flustered (line 26): what has just happened to the candidate, is it an adjective, a good feeling or a bad one. Then pairs read again and guess the other nine highlighted items, and do ex 4d, matching them to definitions 1–10. Play track 1.8 (ex 4e) to check, and they underline the stressed syllable. Drill demanding, bizarre, flustered and recruitment agency.
stages.aim: To give students practice working out words from context

stages.name: Reading for detail: the questions
stages.todo: Ex 4f: the three questions — what extreme interviews are, which companies started them, why some people think they are better — answered in their own words, not read out from the text. Pairs, then check in open class. Push them to use the words from ex 4d in their answers (candidates have to think on their feet, the approach comes from Silicon Valley).
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail

stages.name: Discussion and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4g in groups of three or four: are extreme interviews a good way to choose people, and which of the real questions in the circles would work — room, desk or car, which TV character, does life fascinate you. Give them a job to decide for: each group picks the most and the least useful question and says why. Eight minutes talking while you listen and note what to correct. Then three minutes of content feedback — one group’s choice and the room’s reaction — and two or three sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, corrected in pairs before you confirm.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to discuss extreme interviews

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have developed their spoken fluency, interviewing a partner with ‘extreme’ questions and answering under pressure with reasons.
slots.sub: To practice listening for detail: five people describing the strangest question they were asked at an interview, as the model for the interviews.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 7 ex 5a–5d – audio track 1.9 (played twice), ex 6a–6d / Communication Extreme interviews: p. 104 (Student A) and p. 108 (Student B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Point back at the dinosaur question from the last lesson, then ex 5a in pairs: have you ever been for a job interview, what did they ask, did you get the job. Two minutes, then two answers in open class. If the class is young and has not been interviewed, ask about any interview — university, a visa, a flat.
stages.aim: To get students talking about job interviews

stages.name: Listening as a model
stages.todo: The chart on p. 7 is too small to write in, so give them an enlarged copy or project it. Pre-teach reincarnated (the Teacher’s Book flags it; nothing else in the recordings blocks the task). Ex 5b, track 1.9: five speakers, and they complete the five gapped questions in the first column — Do you still practice philosophy? What would make you kick a dog? How tall are you, how much do you weigh? Pause after each speaker. Pairs compare, then show the five questions. Ex 5c, the same track again: notes on how each person answered and what happened in the end. Pairs compare, check. Ex 5d as one open-class question: which were good or bad questions to ask.
stages.avoid: Two plays is the whole budget. The listening is the model for the interviews, not the lesson; a third play comes straight out of the speaking task.
stages.aim: To give students a model of the interview

stages.name: Preparation and useful language
stages.todo: Pairs A and B. A reads the eight questions on p. 104, B the eight on p. 108, silently, and marks anything unclear — the Teacher’s Book expects aspect and deserted on A’s list, lead role and financial limitations on B’s. Clear those in open class. Then board the interviewer’s follow-ups they heard in the recordings and will need: Why? Can you give me an example? Tell me more about that. The task is answers with reasons, so the interviewer has to push.
stages.aim: To give students time to prepare their questions

stages.name: Speaking task: the interviews
stages.todo: Seat the pairs face to face like an interview. Demonstrate with one student: ask question 1 from p. 104, push for a reason, react. Then A interviews B with the p. 104 questions, B answers quickly and gives reasons, and A ends by saying whether B gets the job and why. Swap: B interviews A from p. 108. Five minutes each way; you keep the clock. Monitor with a pen for question forms — the Teacher’s Book says to correct those — and for good answers to use in feedback.
stages.avoid: Do not let the As read all eight questions in a row and the Bs answer in one word each. Say before they start that every answer needs a reason, and that the interviewer asks a follow-up before moving on.
stages.aim: To give students fluency practice in an interview

stages.name: Second task: their own questions
stages.todo: Ex 6b: each student writes three extreme questions of their own that would tell them something about a person — elicit one or two first so they have the idea. Then ex 6c: stand up, mingle, ask as many people as possible and answer theirs. Four minutes of mingling is enough.
stages.aim: To give students practice asking questions of their own

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Ex 6d: which questions were the most interesting and how did people answer them — two or three answers worth the whole room hearing, and a quick vote for who got the job. Then three questions from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, and the class decides which is which.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced forming questions accurately — auxiliary word order, negative questions, questions ending in a preposition and subject questions — to keep a conversation going with someone they have just met.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, keeping a conversation on one topic going with follow-up questions.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) Teacher’s Book p. 188, photocopiable Communicative 1A ‘Ask me a question’ (one copy per student) / Grammar Bank 1A, SB p. 132, rules 1–4 and ex a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The photocopiable has no context of its own, so give it one: a dinner party. Show a picture of two guests at a table, one of them plainly bored. Elicit what is wrong and how you keep a stranger talking — you ask them things. Then in pairs: which topics are safe with someone you have just met and which you would avoid. Board the safe ones; the sheet’s eight topics (home, getting around, free time, lifestyle, travel, family, childhood, a relative) will mostly come up.
stages.aim: To set the context of a dinner party

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Give out p. 188: eight topics, five gapped questions each, with the question words and auxiliaries missing. In pairs they work out the missing words — saying them, not writing them in, as the Teacher’s Book insists, so the sheet stays usable for the speaking. Five minutes. Walk round and note which questions go wrong; the sheet is built to catch the preposition at the end (Who do you live with? What did you want to be?), the negative question (Is there anything you don’t like …?), the indirect form (Do you think it’s better to travel alone?) and the subject-free How long does it take? Confirm nothing yet.
stages.avoid: Do not correct while they work and do not let them check with another pair. The test only tells you something if it is theirs.
stages.aim: To find out what students know about question forms

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Teach only what the test exposed, against the four rules of Grammar Bank 1A on p. 132: inversion with an auxiliary or modal and do/does/did for the simple tenses; negative questions for surprise or when you expect agreement; the preposition at the end, never at the front; who/what as the subject with no auxiliary (Who lives there?). Board three or four of the sheet’s questions as the models, elicit the pattern under each, then drill the ones with a preposition at the end and the negative question, because the rhythm is what goes wrong in speech — what do you, who do you, isn’t there. Then confirm the full questions on screen.
stages.avoid: At B2 they can form most questions, so do not present question formation from scratch. If the test showed only the preposition and the negative question, those two are the lesson.
stages.aim: To clarify the form and pronunciation of what the test exposed

stages.name: Second test: controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 132 ex a: ten jumbled questions to put in order. On their own first, then compare; open class only for what split them. Items 3, 8 and 10 are indirect questions (Could you tell me when …?), which the sheet only touches; take them if the test showed a need, otherwise skip them and say so.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of question forms

stages.name: Freer practice: dinner-party conversation
stages.todo: Groups of three; each group takes one or two topics from the sheet. Model with the Family questions: ask one student, then a follow-up, then another, and show that the aim is to stay on the topic as long as possible, not to get through the five questions. Then each student finds someone from another group and interviews them on their topic; on your signal they swap roles, on the next they change partner. Three or four rounds. Monitor for question forms.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice keeping a conversation going

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which topic was easiest to keep going and which died — one answer each. Then three or four questions you heard, on the board, right and wrong mixed; pairs sort them, you confirm.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

1B.context: Do you believe in it? – what your signature says about you, true stories of the paranormal, and reacting to strange news (File 1B)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced listening for gist and for detail, taking notes from a graphologist explaining what a signature reveals about personality.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, interpreting a partner’s signature from the notes they have taken.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 10 ex 6a–6c, ex 6d – audio tracks 1.17, 1.18, 1.19, 1.20 (the notes on the right of the page), ex 6e–6g

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 6a is the book’s own way in and it does the work: everyone writes I look forward to hearing from you on a slip of paper, signs underneath as they would a formal letter, and swaps slips with a partner, who keeps it safe for later. Then ex 6b: the ten famous signatures — pairs identify any (Tolstoy, Obama, Paris Hilton, Usain Bolt, Dickens, McCartney, Connery among them) and say what they know of the person. Ex 6c, the short extract: read it and answer one question in open class — can a signature say something about personality?
stages.aim: To get students writing and looking at their signatures

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Graphology itself and three words the notes need: initials, legible/illegible and self-esteem. Elicit each from an example — write your name on the board as initials, write something unreadable — one concept question each and move on. Everything else in the four recordings is either on the page already or can be guessed.
stages.aim: To clear the words the notes need

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: The book has no gist task, so make one from the page: notes covered, one question — which four features of a signature does the expert talk about? Play tracks 1.17 to 1.20 straight through (about four minutes). Pairs compare their four, then uncover the notes and check against the four headings on the right of p. 10: what is in it, its size, its legibility, its angle.
stages.aim: To give students practice in listening for gist

stages.name: Listening for detail: taking notes
stages.todo: Go through the Taking notes box first: key words, not sentences. Then ex 6d one part at a time, the way the Teacher’s Book does it — read the notes for that section, play the track, pause for them to write, play again if they ask. Track 1.17 (what is in your signature), 1.18 (size), 1.19 (legibility), 1.20 (angle). Pairs compare after 1.18 and again after 1.20. Check on screen; the answers are short — your surname = your public self, capital letters = big-headed, illegible = you may be disorganized or secretive, rising = determined and optimistic.
stages.avoid: Two plays of each part is the budget and the notes are key words. If a pair wants a third play of 1.19 to get the full sentence, they have missed the box — point at it rather than pressing play.
stages.aim: To give students practice in taking notes for detail

stages.name: Response: interpreting signatures
stages.todo: Ex 6e: pairs go back to the famous signatures and interpret two or three from their notes — do the readings match what they thought of the person? Then ex 6f, the real task: take out the partner’s slip from the lead-in and read their signature to them, feature by feature; the partner says whether they agree. Sign your own name on the board first and let the class read you — it shows the language they need (your surname is bigger, so …). Monitor and collect.
stages.aim: To have students interpret signatures from their notes

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two people say one thing their partner’s signature revealed and whether it was true. Then two or three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one of them right, and the class decides which is which.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist and for detail, in the context of three true stories about the paranormal, and retelling one of them.
slots.sub: To give students practice in writing a short narrative collaboratively, continuing a spooky story one sentence at a time.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 8 ex 1a–1c (the quote, the story beginnings, The Coffee Cup Reading) / Communication Hard to believe?: p. 104 Noises in the Night (Student A) and p. 109 The Strange Object on the Hill (Student B) / SB p. 9 ex 1d (the rest of The Coffee Cup Reading, read aloud by you from the script on p. 120 — recording 1.10 is not in our audio set), ex 1e – audio track 1.11

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s own lead-in: the Stuart Chase quote on p. 8 on the board, books closed — for those who believe, no proof is necessary; for those who don’t, no proof is possible. What does it mean, and do they agree? Then the lesson title, Do you believe in it? — elicit paranormal, and hands up: believers and sceptics. Ex 1a: the two story beginnings — what might they have in common.
stages.avoid: Keep religion out of it. If it comes up, steer back to ghosts and UFOs — the stories are about unexplained happenings, nothing more.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about believing without proof

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items only: fortune-teller, clairvoyant and spooky. Elicit from a situation — who reads your palm at a fair — one concept question each and move on.
stages.avoid: The highlighted words in the two Communication stories — curtains, estate agent, dragging, dome, gliding, hallucinating — are not for pre-teaching. Guessing them and filling the glossary is the reading task on those pages.
stages.aim: To clear the three words the stories need

stages.name: Reading for detail: the jigsaw
stages.todo: Ex 1b: pairs A and B, face to face. A reads Noises in the Night on p. 104, B reads The Strange Object on the Hill on p. 109 — ex a on each page: read, guess the highlighted words, complete the glossary. Five minutes, time limit on the board. Then the stories get covered and A retells from the bullet questions on the page (when, what happened, how they feel now) while B listens and asks; then B retells. Finish with one open-class question: what do they think the noises and the object really were.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail in a jigsaw

stages.name: The third story: reading, then listening
stages.todo: Ex 1c on p. 8: everyone reads the beginning of The Coffee Cup Reading and answers the question — would you have let Fatos read your cup, and why. Then ex 1d on p. 9: they read the nine questions, and you read the rest of the story aloud from the script on p. 120, at a storyteller’s pace, pausing twice to let them write. The recording for this part (1.10) is not in our audio set, so this is a live listening — rehearse it. Pairs compare, then check the nine answers.
stages.aim: To give students the third story through reading and listening

stages.name: Vocabulary from the story
stages.todo: Ex 1e with track 1.11: five short extracts from what they have just heard, one word missing in each — spot on, laid-back, weird, spooky (coincidence), sceptical. They fill the gaps on the first play, and in pairs work out the meaning from the extract. Check, then drill sceptical and laid-back.
stages.aim: To focus students on the words from the story

stages.name: Response: a story in a chain
stages.todo: Groups of four, and one sheet per group with the first line of a strange story already on it — write your own, something like It was nearly midnight when I heard the knock. Each student adds one sentence and passes the sheet on; four rounds, a minute each, then the sheets go back to the group that started them, who read theirs out. Two minutes for the reading. Do not open the discussion of the three stories — the next teacher starts with it.
stages.avoid: Ex 2 on p. 9 (which story is spookiest, any explanation) is the next lesson’s lead-in. Leave it.
stages.aim: To give students practice telling a strange story together

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using auxiliary verbs to react to what someone says — reply questions (Did you?), So / Neither do I, and a stressed auxiliary for emphasis (I did see one) — in conversations about strange experiences.
slots.sub: To practice the sentence stress and intonation of reply questions and emphatic auxiliaries, copying the recordings.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 9 ex 2 (the Reacting box and the first two questions, as the lead-in), ex 3a, ex 3b – audio track 1.12 / Grammar Bank 1B, SB p. 133, rules 2–6 and ex a / SB p. 9 ex 4a – audio track 1.14, ex 4b, ex 4e – audio track 1.15, ex 4c–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Reacting to a story box on p. 9: elicit How strange / That’s bizarre, odd, weird, spooky and model them with the wide intonation they need, because flat they sound bored. Then the first two questions of ex 2 in groups of three or four: which of yesterday’s three stories was the spookiest, and is there an explanation for any of them. Four minutes; they react to each other with the phrases.
stages.aim: To give students the phrases for reacting to a story

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Ex 3a: four short dialogues with five gaps, each needing a positive or negative auxiliary — Did you?, do you?, I did see one, Neither have I, I have. Pairs complete them, then track 1.12 (ex 3b) to check. Then the second half of ex 3b: match auxiliaries 1–5 to what they do — add emphasis, say you are different, check information, show surprise, say you are the same. Monitor: the Teacher’s Book expects 1, 2 and 4 to be revision and the emphatic did in 3 to be new. Note who stumbles on which.
stages.avoid: Give nothing away while they work — the matching is the diagnosis, and it tells you what the next stage is.
stages.aim: To find out what students know about auxiliaries

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Work from their matching and Grammar Bank 1B on p. 133 (rules 2–6), teaching only what the test exposed — usually emphasis (rule 5: do/does/did before the main verb, or the auxiliary stressed and uncontracted) and reply questions (rule 4). Concept check the emphatic one: I did see one — is B contradicting A? Is did there for the past? Then the form on the board. Pronunciation sits here: track 1.14, the two dialogues in ex 4a — they notice the stressed auxiliaries (Did you? rising; So did I with the weight on So and I), then ex 4b, pairs repeat them copying the rhythm. Track 1.15 (ex 4e): is do stressed in I do like them? Yes. Drill those five lines, the whole class and then individuals.
stages.avoid: Six rules are on p. 133 and five uses on p. 9. The test tells you which two or three to teach; do not walk them through all six.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of what the test exposed

stages.name: Second test: controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 133 ex a: ten mini-dialogues, one auxiliary or modal each. Alone, then pairs, and take only the disputed ones — read them aloud with the stress, not just the word.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of auxiliaries

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4c: they complete the eight sentences about themselves — I’m not very good at …, I’ve never read …, I didn’t … last night. Then ex 4d: A reads a sentence, B answers with a reply question and then says whether they are the same or different (Aren’t you? Neither am I. / I am.), then swap. Demonstrate with your own first two sentences before they start, as the Teacher’s Book suggests. Monitor for the auxiliary and the intonation.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice reacting with auxiliaries

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three exchanges you heard on the board — a reply question with the wrong auxiliary, one that was right — and the class decides which is which. Re-drill the one that was flat.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the language

2A.context: Call the doctor? – first aid, illness and injury, and a patient who has been reading the internet (File 2A)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for specific information and for detail, checking a first-aid quiz against the Red Cross answers and explaining them to a partner.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for injuries and first aid — the ten highlighted words in the quiz: choke, lean, burn, bleed, press, wound, treat, pinch, collapse, bandage.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 14 ex 1a–1c (the quiz ‘Help save lives!’) / Communication First aid quiz: p. 105 (Student A, answers 1–3) and p. 109 (Student B, answers 4–6)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: You are first today and you set the context for the two lessons after you. Elicit first aid from the Red Cross logo or a picture of a first-aid kit, then two questions in pairs: has anyone had any first-aid training, and what would you do if someone next to you collapsed. Two minutes, two answers in open class. Board any illness or injury words that come up — they are the day’s lexis.
stages.aim: To get students into the topic of first aid

stages.name: Vocabulary for the quiz
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the ten highlighted words in the six quiz questions — choke, lean, burn, bleed, press, wound, treat, pinch, collapse, bandage. Pairs work out the meaning from the questions and the pictures. Check by miming or with the pictures, and drill the ones that will come out wrong: wound (the vowel), choke, bandage. This is the pre-teaching; the answers on pp. 105 and 109 reuse all ten.
stages.aim: To clear the words the quiz needs

stages.name: Prediction: the quiz
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the six questions, a, b or c, in pairs. Get a quick vote for each question so the room has committed itself, and confirm nothing — the reading is where they find out.
stages.aim: To have students commit to answers before reading

stages.name: Reading for specific information, then for detail
stages.todo: Pairs A and B. A reads the answers to questions 1–3 on p. 105, B the answers to 4–6 on p. 109. First read, two minutes: find the correct letter for each of your three and compare it with what the pair guessed. Second read, five minutes: the steps and the reason behind each — why cold water, why lean forward, why not straighten the leg. Then ex 1c: books covered, A tells B the right answer to 1–3 and why, B does the same for 4–6, using the quiz pictures as prompts. Finish with hands up: who had all six right.
stages.avoid: Do not let them read all six answers. Half each is what makes the telling necessary, and the telling is where the vocabulary gets used.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for specific information and detail

stages.name: Response: what would you do
stages.todo: Groups of three or four: which of the six emergencies would you feel confident dealing with now, which still frightens you, and has anyone in the group ever seen one happen — what did people do? Six minutes of talking while you collect what you hear; push them to use the words from the quiz.
stages.avoid: Ex 2f on p. 15 is not on your card — it is the next lesson’s discussion. Keep yours to the six emergencies in the quiz.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to discuss emergencies

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story from the groups that the room should hear. Then three sentences from your notes on the board, one of them right, and they correct them in pairs — make one of them a use of wound, choke or press so the vocabulary gets a second outing.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced pronouncing medical words containing the sounds /ʃ/, /dʒ/, /tʃ/ and /k/, with the correct word stress.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, talking about illness, injury and first aid in their own lives.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 ex 2a, ex 2b – audio track 1.33, ex 2d, ex 2e – audio track 1.34, ex 2f / Workbook p. 13 ex 4a and 4c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The four sound pictures at the top of ex 2a: shower, jazz, chess, key. Elicit the sound each one stands for and have the class say it. Then ask for one word from the first-aid lesson for each sound — rash, bandage, choke, ache will do — and leave the four columns on the board.
stages.aim: To get students noticing the four sounds

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the nine words sorted into the four columns, in pairs, saying them aloud as they go. Track 1.33 (ex 2b) to check. Then the teaching: /ʃ/ and /tʃ/ — the same place in the mouth, one continuous and one with a stop; /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ — the voicing; and the spelling trap the book points out, that ch is usually /tʃ/ (choking) but /k/ in ache and stomach. Drill the four columns, then across them: pressure, choking, allergy, ache. Then ex 2d–2e: the twelve longer words with their phonemics — track 1.34, they underline the stress, and you drill the ones that fall wrongly in most languages: antibiotics, paracetamol, cholesterol, emergency, injection.
stages.avoid: This is the one lesson of the day where pronunciation is the main aim, so the drilling is not a minute at the end: the whole class, then rows, then individuals, and go back to anyone who has the stop in the wrong place.
stages.aim: To clarify the four sounds and how they are made

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 13 ex 4a: six rows of four words, circle the one with the different sound. Then ex 4c: underline the stress in ten words — antibiotic, allergic, diarrhoea, dizzy, headache, medicine, swollen, temperature, vomit, unconscious. Alone, pairs, and check by having them say the rows aloud, not by reading out letters.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the sounds and the stress

stages.name: Practice in sentences
stages.todo: Pairs write three sentences about a patient, each using two words from today’s lists — I’ve got a rash on my stomach and a temperature; she needs an injection and some antibiotics. They read them to another pair, who write down which sounds they heard. Monitor for /ʃ/ against /tʃ/ and the stress on the long words.
stages.aim: To give students practice with the sounds in sentences

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2f in groups: what injuries or illnesses you might get cooking, doing sport or eating out; whether any has happened to you; whether you have ever given or been given first aid; what you should do for a high temperature, a wasp sting with an allergic reaction, bad sunburn. Eight minutes; a secretary in each group keeps the questions moving. Listen for the target sounds and for anything good.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice talking about injuries

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story from the groups. Then four or five words you heard mispronounced on the board, say them wrongly and rightly, let them tell you which was which, and re-drill the wrong ones.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the pronunciation

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using the present perfect simple and continuous to talk about illness and habits — the continuous for an unfinished or repeated action, the simple for a completed one or a number of times.
slots.sub: To practice listening for detail: a doctor and a patient who has been reading too much on the internet.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 ex 3a–3b – audio track 1.35, ex 3c – audio track 1.36, ex 3d / Grammar Bank 2A, SB p. 134, rules and ex b / SB p. 15 ex 3f

stages.name: Lead-in and listening task
stages.todo: The context is set; one line is enough — after this morning’s first aid, who would you rather have treating you, a doctor or your friend who did the course? Then ex 3a, track 1.35, books closed or the dialogue covered: what symptoms does Mr Blaine have and what does the doctor suggest? Headaches, a cough, a temperature; wait a few days. Ex 3b, second play: complete the six gaps with the verb forms they hear. Pairs compare, check on screen. Then track 1.36 (ex 3c), twenty seconds: what do the doctor and nurse think of him — a hypochondriac, which is the word the next lesson needs.
stages.avoid: This is a grammar lesson with a short listening in front of it, not a listening lesson. Two plays of 1.35 and one of 1.36, and you are at the language by minute eleven.
stages.aim: To set the context with a short listening

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 3d: the two sentences — Have you been taking / taken anything for the headaches? and How many tablets have you been taking / taken so far today? Circle the right form or tick both, in pairs, and say why. The first takes both; the second only the simple, because it asks how many. Take the answers; the teaching is the next stage.
stages.aim: To focus students on the present perfect simple and continuous

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Board two of the gapped sentences from the dialogue: I’ve been coughing a lot and I’ve taken it five or six times. Meaning first: the continuous for an action still going on, repeated, or just stopped with a result (I haven’t been feeling well for a few days); the simple when it is finished or counted (how many tablets, five or six times) and with non-action verbs (I haven’t had one for two months). Concept check with the Grammar Bank’s own pair — I’ve painted the kitchen / I’ve been painting the kitchen: which one is finished? Then the form on the board: have/has + been + -ing against have/has + past participle. Pronunciation: the weak ’ve been /əv bɪn/ — drill I’ve been coughing a lot and Have you been taking anything? as whole sentences. Grammar Bank 2A on p. 134 is the reference; have your concept questions ready before the lesson.
stages.avoid: One contrast, not two. The simple with just / yet / already / ever is on p. 134 too, but it is not what the dialogue is about and it will not fit in thirteen minutes.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the two forms

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 134 ex b: eight sentences, present perfect simple or continuous — we’ve known Jack and Ann, have you been working out, Emily hasn’t done her homework yet, we’ve been walking for hours. Individually, then compare; deal only with what they argued about; make them say which rule decided it.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the two forms

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3f: eight pairs of prompts — the first question in the present simple or continuous, the second in the present perfect simple or continuous: Do you often get colds? How many colds have you had in the last three months? Elicit the first two questions from the class so they have the shape, then pairs ask and answer from the prompts without writing the questions out. Monitor for the choice of form.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice asking about health

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right, for the class to sort. The wrong one will be a counted action in the continuous — I’ve been having three colds — so have that one ready.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the language

2B.context: Call the doctor? (continued) – cyberchondriacs, writing to a friend about being ill, and medical myths (File 2A)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced using medical vocabulary from an article about cyberchondria — life-threatening, mouth ulcer, alternative remedies, under the weather, cancer, infection, heart rate, surgery, pulse, tumour, miracle cures — to talk about health worries.
slots.sub: To practice reading for gist, in the context of a journalist who diagnoses herself online.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 16 ex 5a–5b (‘Confessions of a cyberchondriac’) / SB p. 17 ex 5c, ex 5d – audio track 1.40 (ex 5e is a detailed-reading task and is not part of this lesson)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Yesterday’s Mr Blaine, the patient who had read about brain tumours online — what did the nurse call him? Ex 5a: how would you define a hypochondriac, and what might a cyberchondriac be? Drill both words; the stress is on -chon-. Two guesses on the board and no confirmation — the first read gives it.
stages.aim: To get students thinking about hypochondriacs

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 5b in two passes, both quick. First: read the article once to check what a cyberchondriac is — two minutes, one answer. Then go through the Topic sentences box, and pairs fit sentences A–E to the five paragraph gaps, with a four-minute limit. Check: 1 B, 2 E, 3 D, 4 C, 5 A. The text has done its job; from here on it is a vocabulary lesson.
stages.avoid: No pre-teaching before the reading and no comprehension questions after it. Ex 5e is detailed reading and is not on your card; the text is here to carry the eleven phrases, nothing else.
stages.aim: To give students a reason to read the article

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 5c: the eleven highlighted words and phrases matched to definitions 1–11, in pairs with the article open, because the context decides most of them. Take no answers yet.
stages.aim: To focus students on the health words in the article

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Track 1.40 (ex 5d) to check the matching, then the teaching. Meaning the definitions have mostly done, so check the two that confuse: pulse against heart rate (you take a pulse; a rate is a number per minute), and infection against tumour. Then form and pronunciation while each is on the board: life-threatening is a compound adjective, stress on life; under the weather goes with be or feel; surgery is uncountable (have surgery, not a surgery); infection gives infected and infectious; and the sounds in tumour /ˈtjuːmə/ and ulcer /ˈʌlsə/. Drill the lot in short phrases — a life-threatening illness, feeling under the weather, take your pulse, a miracle cure.
stages.avoid: Eleven items is the top of what forty-five minutes holds. If you are running late, let cancer and alternative remedies go as passive items; the practice needs under the weather, pulse, heart rate, infection, surgery and life-threatening.
stages.aim: To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the words

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: The book gives no practice exercise for this set, so bring one: eight sentences about a patient with one phrase missing from each, first letter given — She was feeling u___ the weather, so she googled her symptoms; The doctor took his p___ and said it was normal. Alone, pairs, and check only the disputed ones.
stages.aim: To give students controlled practice of the words

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Pairs write a short exchange between a doctor and a cyberchondriac who has diagnosed himself online, using at least four of the phrases; three minutes to write, then they perform it to another pair, who count the phrases they hear. Two pairs perform to the room if there is time. Then two lines from your monitoring on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort.
stages.aim: To give students freer practice in a doctor and patient exchange

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced writing an informal email to a friend, explaining that they have not been well and saying what they have been doing recently.
slots.sub: To practice the expressions used to open, respond and close an informal email — Sorry for not writing earlier, Hope you feel better soon, That’s all for now, Take care.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 ex 4 (the task) / Writing Bank, SB p. 113, An informal email: ex a–f (Anna’s email, the Useful language box, the plan)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two questions in pairs: when did you last write to a friend to say you had been ill, and what did you tell them? Then set the task from ex 4 on p. 15 before anyone reads a model: today they write to a friend, saying they have not been well and what they have been doing. Point out that the grammar from yesterday — I haven’t been feeling well, I’ve been catching up on my emails — is exactly what this email needs.
stages.aim: To get students into the topic and set the task

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Writing Bank p. 113, Anna’s email to Sue. Read it once for content: what has happened to Anna, and what does she want from Sue? Then ex a in pairs: the twelve highlighted mistakes — four grammar or vocabulary, four punctuation, four spelling — decide which kind each is and correct it. Check on screen. Then ex b: find the three sentences that mean I haven’t written or phoned, I’ve been reading and replying to my emails, Have you been doing anything exciting? Elicit the shape of the email while you are there: an apology, news, questions, a request, a sign-off.
stages.avoid: Ex a is a proofreading exercise and it can eat the lesson. Six minutes, then the answers on screen; the point is to see what a good email looks like, not to teach spelling.
stages.aim: To give students a model email to read

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex c: the Useful language box with fourteen gaps — Thanks for your email, It was great to hear from you, Sorry for not writing earlier, Glad to hear that you’re all well, Hope you feel better soon, That’s all for now, Looking forward to hearing from you, Give my regards to, Take care. Pairs complete it, then check. Board the three groups — opening, responding to news, closing — and the form that trips them: for + -ing (Sorry for not writing), to + -ing after looking forward to. Drill three or four as whole phrases.
stages.aim: To give students the useful language for the email

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex d: they plan. Decide who the friend is and what the illness was (invented is fine), then notes under three headings — the apology and what was wrong, what you have been doing since, a question or two for the friend. Notes only, silence.
stages.aim: To give students time to plan their email

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex e: 120–180 words in two or three paragraphs, informal, with contractions, at least three expressions from the box and the present perfect simple and continuous where the content calls for it. Plan and board in front of them, in silence. Answer questions by walking over, not by talking to the room. Give a two-minute warning for ex f: check it yourself before you hand it over.
stages.aim: To give students practice in writing an informal email

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Swap emails with someone else. The reader answers one question — what has your friend been doing? — and underlines one phrase from the box they used well. Then one thing from your monitoring on the board for the class to correct: make it the -ing after for or looking forward to, because that is what you will have seen. Collect the emails and write on them before the next lesson.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the writing

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practiced reading for gist and for detail, in the context of four medical myths examined by the British Medical Journal.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, discussing medical myths and home remedies in their own country.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) Workbook p. 11, 2A Reading ‘Medical myths’: ex 1a (missing sentences), ex 1b (true or false), ex 1c (highlighted words)

stages.name: Lead-in and pre-teaching
stages.todo: Three myths on the board — we only use ten per cent of our brains; reading in dim light ruins your eyesight; shaving makes hair grow back thicker. True or false, in pairs, with a reason. A quick vote, nothing confirmed. Then three words the text needs and does not explain: blink, drowsy, short-sighted. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on.
stages.aim: To get students guessing which myths are true

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: One question over the whole text: which of the three myths on the board are in it, and does the British Medical Journal say any of them is true? Three minutes, alone. Pair check, then settle the board — all three are in it (and a fourth, about turkey), and none is true.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for gist

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1a: four sentences A–E to fit into the gaps in the four myths, one sentence not needed. Alone, then pairs justify each choice by pointing at the line before and after the gap. Then ex 1b: five statements true or false — doctors spend a lot of time on myths, unshaven hair is the same color, turkey contains less tryptophan than cheese. Pairs compare, then check both exercises on screen, with the line that gave each answer.
stages.aim: To give students practice in reading for detail

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1c: the highlighted words and phrases — guess them from the sentence they sit in, pairs, then a quick check. Spend the time on the two or three the discussion will want, not on all of them.
stages.aim: To focus students on words from the text

stages.name: Response: myths and remedies at home
stages.todo: Groups of four: what medical myths and home remedies do people in your country swear by, and who taught you them; do people trust doctors; why do so many people now look for a diagnosis online, and how reliable is it? Give each group a secretary to keep the questions moving and ask them to agree on one remedy that actually works. Nine minutes while you listen and note what to correct.
stages.aim: To give students a chance to discuss myths and remedies

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s one remedy that works, and the room’s reaction. Then two or three sentences from your notes on the board, one right, and let them find the wrong one before you say anything.
stages.aim: To give feedback on the content and the language
